title: Yachtmaster Ocean
note: Scenario questions written for study, close to the Yachtmaster Ocean syllabus. Not official exam content. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults to verify.

topics.title: The Earth, the celestial sphere & the PZX triangle

questions.q: You are at anchor off Barbados and a crew member asks what the 13°05′N on the plotter actually measures. What do you tell them?
options: The arc of your meridian from the equator to here
The arc of your meridian from the North Pole to here
The arc of your parallel from Greenwich to here
The arc of the equator from Greenwich to here
questions.why: Latitude is the arc of the meridian (the angle at the Earth's centre) from the equator: 13°05′ = 785 M north of it.

questions.q: You are crossing the doldrums on a passage up the South Atlantic. How far is it along this track?
questions.why: Contrary names add: 10°30′ + 4°15′ = 14°45′ of latitude × 60 = 885 M along a meridian.

questions.q: You log your noon position in Horta, Azores. What does the 28°38′W measure?
options: The arc of your meridian from the equator north to Horta
The arc of the equator from the date line east to yours
The arc of the equator from Greenwich's meridian west to yours
The arc of the equator from Greenwich's meridian east to yours
questions.why: Longitude is the arc of the equator (or the angle at the pole) between the Greenwich meridian and yours, 0–180° E or W.

questions.q: You plan the passage from Fiji to Samoa across the 180th meridian. What is the difference of longitude, and which way?
You sketch the celestial sphere for your position at 30°N to show the crew where the sky's axis points. Which point is the north celestial pole?
options: B — 30° above the north point of the horizon
C — 60° above the north point of the horizon
D — 60° above the south point of the horizon
questions.why: The altitude of the elevated pole equals your latitude: at 30°N the celestial pole stands 30° above due north.
questions.ref: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole

questions.q: On a night watch in the South Atlantic you work out where the Sun is. Where is it on your celestial sphere?
options: On your celestial horizon, due north
At your nadir, 90° below the horizon
On the celestial equator, due north
questions.why: The GP is your antipode, 180° of arc away, so the Sun is at the point directly below you: your nadir.

questions.q: You are watching the Sun climb to noon on the passage from Bermuda to the Azores. Which circle of the celestial sphere is it crossing now?

figure.title: Local noon, Bermuda to the Azores

options: The celestial equator — the circle 90° from the poles
Your celestial horizon — the circle 90° from your zenith
Your meridian — the great circle through the poles and your zenith
The ecliptic — the Sun's yearly path among the stars
questions.why: The observer's meridian runs through both celestial poles, your zenith and nadir; the Sun bears 180° or 000° as it crosses it.

questions.q: You take a star sight from the cockpit. Why can't you put Hs straight into the PZX triangle?

figure.title: Sight at dusk
lines: Hs read against the visible horizon

options: It needs the altitude above the horizon at the body's GP
It needs the zenith distance, which a sextant cannot measure
It needs the altitude above the visible horizon, at sea level
It needs the altitude above the celestial horizon, through the Earth's centre
questions.why: Hs is from the visible horizon at your eye; dip, refraction, SD and parallax reduce it to Ho above the celestial horizon.
questions.ref: Celestial sphere — celestial and visible horizon

questions.q: You want to know over which ocean the Sun stands at this moment. Where is its geographical position (GP)?
questions.why: GP latitude = Dec; GP longitude = GHA west up to 180°, else 360° − GHA east: 360° − 210°46.1′ = 149°13.9′E.

questions.q: You read the Sun's data for the moment of your sight. What is the position of its GP?
questions.why: Dec is the GP's latitude and GHA (under 180°) its west longitude: 7°33.3′S 48°23.4′W.

questions.q: You take a morning sight of the Sun off Bermuda. What LHA do you use?
You are approaching the Maldives and take a morning sun sight. What LHA do you use?
On the SSB net you compare sun sights with a yacht 300 miles from you on the ARC. How can both altitudes be the same?

figure.title: SSB net, 1423 UT
lines: Both sights at the same second

options: Both yachts lie on one circle of equal altitude round the GP
Both yachts lie on the same meridian as the GP
Both yachts lie on the great circle through the GP
Both yachts lie on the same parallel as the GP
questions.why: Everyone the same distance from the GP sees the same altitude: a circle of radius 90° − 52°10′ = 37°50′ = 2270 M.

questions.q: You reduce this sun sight in mid-Atlantic. What is the radius of the circle of position it puts you on?
questions.why: Zenith distance 90° − 61°20.0′ = 28°40.0′ = 1720′ of arc, and 1′ of arc = 1 M.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance

questions.q: You reduce a sun sight with Ho 41°15′ and draw the position line as a straight line on your plotting sheet. Why is that good enough?
options: On a Mercator sheet every great circle plots straight
The circle is a meridian, so it is straight on the chart
The circle's radius is 2925 M; near the AP its arc is almost straight
The intercept corrects for the curve, so it does not matter
questions.why: The circle of equal altitude is huge; the few miles of it near the AP plot as a straight line at right angles to the azimuth.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — position line

questions.q: You plot this sun sight on the plotting sheet. Which way does the position line run?
options: 045°–225°, at right angles to the azimuth
questions.why: A position line is a short piece of the circle of equal altitude, at right angles to the bearing of the GP.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — position line

questions.q: You take a dawn sight of Arcturus. How far are you from the star's geographical position?
questions.why: Distance from the GP = zenith distance: 90° − 35°45.0′ = 54°15.0′ = 3255′ = 3255 M.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance

questions.q: In the Caribbean in June the Sun near noon is almost overhead. How do you use this sight?

figure.title: Sun near noon, the Caribbean, June
lines: Sun's GP from the almanac, to the second

options: Reduce it from an AP and draw a straight line
Draw a circle of 90 M radius round the Sun's GP
Take it as a meridian altitude for latitude only
Discard it, since no sight above 80° can be used
questions.why: Zenith distance 90° − 88°30′ = 1°30′ = 90 M: too curved for a straight line, so plot the circle itself round the GP.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — high-altitude sights

questions.q: You sketch the PZX triangle for a star sight. Which side gives you the star's altitude?

figure.note: Your PZX triangle on the celestial sphere

options: PX — the altitude is PX − PZ
questions.why: ZX is the zenith distance, your distance from the star's GP, so the altitude is 90° − ZX.

questions.q: You set up the PZX triangle for Arcturus south of the Cape of Good Hope. What are the sides PZ and PX?
questions.why: In the south P is the South Pole: PZ = 90° − 35° = 55°; a north Dec lies beyond the equator, so PX = 90° + 19°06′.

questions.q: You set up the PZX triangle for Vega off Bermuda. What is the polar distance PX?
questions.why: Dec has the same name as the elevated pole: PX = 90° − Dec = 90° − 38°48′ = 51°12′.

questions.q: You set up the PZX triangle for this star. What is the angle at P, and on which side?
questions.why: LHA over 180° means the body is east: the angle at P (meridian angle) = 360° − 300° = 60°E.
questions.ref: PZX triangle — the angle at P

questions.q: You solve the PZX triangle for a sight. Which three parts do you already know?
options: PZ from your AP, ZX from the Ho, and the angle at Z from the compass
PZ from the Ho, PX from the GHA, and the angle at P from the UT
PZ from your AP, PX from the Dec, and the angle at P from the LHA
PX from the Dec, ZX from the Ho, and the angle at X from the SHA
questions.why: Co-lat, polar distance and LHA give ZX (so Hc = 90° − ZX) and the angle at Z, the azimuth.

questions.q: You solve the PZX triangle by the cosine formula. What calculated altitude Hc do you get?
You work an afternoon sun sight north of the equator. What is the true azimuth Zn?
questions.why: Z is measured from the north (elevated) pole towards the west: Zn = 360° − 100° = 260°.

questions.q: You work a morning sun sight off South Africa at 33°S. What is the true azimuth Zn?
questions.why: South of the equator Z is measured from the south pole: S86°E gives Zn = 180° − 86° = 094°.

questions.q: You notice the almanac gives Aries a GHA for every hour but each star only an SHA. Why does that work?

figure.title: Almanac, daily page
lines: Stars: SHA and Dec, once per page

options: The stars move 15° an hour, the same as the Sun
Aries is a bright star the others are measured from
The stars keep their places relative to Aries; the sky turns as one
Each star's SHA grows 15° an hour, like a GHA
questions.why: SHA is measured westward from Aries and barely changes, so GHA★ = GHA Aries + SHA at any moment.

questions.q: You are reducing a dusk sight of Vega. What is the star's GHA?
You take Sirius at dawn on the way to the Cape Verdes. What is its GHA?
You want to catch Vega on your meridian again tomorrow night at the same longitude. When will it come?
questions.why: Aries gains 2.46′ an hour on the Sun: the stars come round in 23 h 56 min, so about 4 min earlier each night.
questions.ref: First point of Aries — the sidereal day

questions.q: You take two sun sights on the same day. Between them, how far has the Sun's GP moved?
questions.why: The Earth turns 360° in 24 h, so the Sun's GHA grows 15° an hour: 4 h × 15° = 60° west.

questions.q: You explain to the crew how fast the Sun's GP races across the ocean today. About how fast is it?
questions.why: 15° an hour = 900′ of longitude; along the parallel of 23°26.3′N that is 900 × cos 23°26.3′ ≈ 826 M an hour.

questions.q: You turn to the Sun's column for the longest day in the north. About what Dec do you expect?
questions.why: The ecliptic is tilted 23°26′ to the celestial equator; at the June solstice the Sun reaches its greatest north Dec.
questions.ref: Declination through the year — the ecliptic

questions.q: You prepare for the noon sight on the first day of the ARC. About what Dec will the almanac give?
questions.why: The Dec changes fast near the equinox and slowly near the solstice: on 23 Nov it is already S20°24′.

questions.q: By mistake you work your noon sight with yesterday's Dec. In which month does that cost you the most?
options: Any month — the Dec changes 24′ every day
December — the Dec changes about 24′ a day
March — the Dec changes about 24′ a day
June — the Dec changes about 24′ a day
questions.why: Near the equinoxes the Sun crosses the equator at about 24′ a day; near the solstices its Dec barely moves.

questions.q: You are at 50°N, setting out from the Channel for the Azores. Which of these stars never sets for you?
questions.why: A body is circumpolar when Dec > co-lat (90° − 50° = 40°): only Capella (46°01′) qualifies; Vega (38°48′) just sets.

questions.q: You are south of the Cape at 35°S. Which of these stars stays above your horizon all night, every night?
questions.why: Co-lat 90° − 35° = 55°: Acrux (S63°14′) is circumpolar; Canopus (S52°43′) dips below the south horizon.

questions.q: You are waiting for the noon sight off Martinique. What altitude and bearing do you expect at meridian passage?
questions.why: The Dec is north of your latitude: z = 23°26.3′ − 14°36′ = 8°50.3′; highest altitude 81°09.7′, Sun to the north.

questions.q: You plan a meridian sight of Sirius before leaving Las Palmas. What will its altitude be?
questions.why: Contrary names: z = 28°08′ + 16°45′ = 44°53′, so the highest altitude is 45°07′, due south.

questions.q: On the passage from Horta to Mindelo, how much lower will the celestial pole stand when you arrive?
questions.why: The altitude of the celestial pole equals your latitude: 38°32′ − 16°53′ = 21°39′ lower.
questions.ref: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole

questions.q: You are crossing the South Atlantic at 40°S on the equinox. Where will the Sun rise?
questions.why: With Dec 0° the Sun is on the celestial equator, which meets every horizon due east and due west.

questions.q: You are on passage to Mauritius at 20°S. Can you use Vega for a star sight?
options: Yes — it rises to 58°48′ over the north horizon
Yes — it rises to 31°12′ over the north horizon
Yes — it is circumpolar at your latitude
No — a northern star never rises south of the equator
questions.why: Vega rises because its Dec (38°48′) is less than your co-lat (70°); z = 20° + 38°48′ = 58°48′, so at best 31°12′ high.

questions.q: A crew member wants to see the Southern Cross from the Azores. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Ponta Delgada, 37°44′N
lines: Brightest star of the Southern Cross

options: It rises only in summer, low over the south horizon
It never sets — its Dec is more than your co-lat 52°16′
It never rises — its Dec is more than your co-lat 52°16′
It rises 10°58′ above the south horizon at its highest
questions.why: Contrary name and Dec 63°14′ > co-lat 52°16′: even at meridian passage Acrux stays 10°58′ below your horizon.

questions.q: You explain to the crew why the noon sight needs no LHA, no AP and no tables. What is the reason?
options: At noon the azimuth is 000° or 180°, so Hc equals Ho
At noon the Sun stops moving, so the time does not matter
At noon the Sun's GP is always on the equator below you
P, Z and X lie on your meridian, so the triangle collapses into one arc
questions.why: On the meridian PZ, PX and ZX lie along one arc: latitude = Dec ± zenith distance, with no LHA needed.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — why it gives latitude

questions.q: You take the noon sight on your way to Tahiti. What is your latitude?
questions.why: z = 90° − 80°59.0′ = 9°01.0′; the Sun bears north, so you are z south of its GP: 7°19.0′ + 9°01.0′ = 16°20.0′S.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — why it gives latitude

questions.q: Before a dusk star fix south of Madagascar you want the GP of Canopus. Where is it?
You take Arcturus at dawn off Tahiti. What is its LHA, and where is the star?
You watch Capella through a long winter night at 50°N. What are its highest and lowest altitudes?
questions.why: Upper: 90° − (50° − 46°01′) = 86°01′ to the south. Lower: lat − polar distance = 50° − 43°59′ = 6°01′ to the north.
questions.ref: Circumpolar bodies — upper and lower transit

questions.q: You solve the PZX triangle for Regulus in the South Atlantic. What is Hc?
You consider Canopus for a meridian sight before leaving Las Palmas. Is it a good choice?
options: Yes — it is circumpolar and can be taken all night
No — at best 9°09′ high, where refraction is large
No — it never rises at Las Palmas
Yes — at its highest it stands 65°25′ due south
questions.why: z = 28°08′ + 52°43′ = 80°51′: Canopus culminates only 9°09′ above the south horizon; avoid sights below about 10°.

questions.q: You notice that the Sun's GHA on the almanac's daily page grows by almost exactly 15° every hour. Why 15°?
options: The Earth moves 15° along its orbit every hour
The Earth turns once against the stars in 24 hours
The Earth turns once against the Sun in 24 hours
The Sun moves 15° east among the stars every hour
questions.why: One turn against the Sun, 360°, takes 24 h of mean time: 360° ÷ 24 = 15° an hour; against the stars it takes 4 min less.

questions.q: You cross the equator on the way to Brazil and a crew member asks where the celestial poles are now. What do you tell them?
options: The north one 90° up, the south one 90° down
One at your zenith, the other at your nadir
Both 23°26′ above your horizon, north and south
On your horizon, due north and due south
questions.why: The elevated pole's altitude equals your latitude: at 0° both celestial poles sit on the horizon, at the north and south points.
questions.ref: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole

questions.q: At sunrise, with the Sun's centre on your celestial horizon, a crew member asks how far away its GP is. What is the answer?

figure.title: Sunrise, Indian Ocean
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

questions.why: Zenith distance 90° − 0° = 90° = 5400′ of arc = 5400 M: a quarter of the way round the Earth from the GP.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance

questions.q: At anchor off Cape Town, a crew member asks where the sky's south pole is. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Table Bay, at anchor
lines: Clear night, no star at the pole

options: 33°55′ above the south point of the horizon
56°05′ above the south point of the horizon
33°55′ above the north point of the horizon
questions.why: The elevated pole's altitude equals your latitude; south of the equator it is the south celestial pole, 33°55′ up, due south.
questions.ref: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole

questions.q: You label the parts of your PZX triangle for a star sight south of the equator. Which part does the sight reduction never use?
options: The angle at P, at the pole
The side PX, the polar distance
The angle at X, at the star
The angle at Z, at your zenith
questions.why: Reduction takes PZ, PX and the angle at P (LHA) and finds ZX (Hc) and the angle at Z (azimuth); the angle at X is not needed.

questions.q: Becalmed on the equator, a crew member asks which stars stay above the horizon all night. What do you tell them?
options: The stars within 23°26′ of the equator
Capella and the stars near the north pole
Acrux and the stars near the south pole
None — every star rises and sets
questions.why: Circumpolar needs Dec > co-lat; on the equator the co-lat is 90°, so every star spends half its daily circle below the horizon.

questions.q: On passage to Australia you work out the Sun's LHA for your sight. Where is the Sun?
options: West of your meridian — it is afternoon
East of your meridian — it is morning
Below your horizon — it is night
On your meridian — it is noon
questions.why: LHA is counted westward from your meridian: 0°–180° puts the body west of you (afternoon), over 180° east (morning).

questions.q: A crew member says it is summer in the south in January because the Earth is then closest to the Sun. What do you tell them?
options: No — the Sun's Dec is 23°26′ north in January
No — it is the axis's 23°26′ tilt to the ecliptic
Yes — the southern oceans are nearer the Sun then
Yes — the Earth is about 3% closer to the Sun then
questions.why: The equator is tilted 23°26′ to the ecliptic, so the Sun's Dec swings N and S; in January its GP is far south — and the north has winter.

questions.q: You want to catch Arcturus as it rises. Where on the horizon do you look?

figure.title: Star watch off Durban
lines: Due to rise within the hour

questions.why: A body rises on the side of east named like its Dec: a north Dec rises north of east, whichever hemisphere you are in.

questions.q: On the SSB net five yachts spread across the ocean compare sun sights taken at the same second. Which pair of values is the same for all of them?

figure.title: SSB net, 1200 UT
lines: All take a sun sight at 1200 UT

questions.why: GHA and Dec fix the GP, the same for everyone at one instant; LHA, Hc and Zn depend on each yacht's own position.

questions.q: You take a sun sight off Fiji, close to the 180th meridian. What LHA do you use, and where is the Sun?
On the passage from Vanuatu to Fiji you picture where the Sun stands. How far is its GP from your meridian, and which way?
options: 6°22.9′ east, this side of the 180th meridian

questions.q: On New Year's Day you explain the date line to the crew. At that moment, what is the local time and date at the GP, just either side of the line?
options: Midnight, 1 Jan to the west of the line; midnight, 31 Dec to the east
Noon, 31 Dec to the west of the line; noon, 1 Jan to the east
Noon, 1 Jan to the west of the line; noon, 31 Dec to the east
Noon, 1 Jan to the west of the line; noon, 2 Jan to the east
questions.why: Under the GP it is local noon; west of 180° the date is a day ahead of the east side: 1 January to the west, 31 December to the east.

questions.q: Waiting in Tonga for a weather window to New Zealand, a crew member asks on which days the noon Sun stands straight overhead here. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Nuku'alofa, Tonga
lines: Sun Dec 20 Nov S19°38′ · 30 Nov S21°36′

options: Never — only on the Tropic of Capricorn
questions.why: The Sun is overhead at noon when its Dec equals your latitude, S21°08′: passed going south in late Nov and coming back in mid-Jan.
questions.ref: The Sun's declination through the year

questions.q: Off Rio on the solstice, the crew expects the noon Sun to the north, as usual in the southern hemisphere. Which way do you face for the noon sight, and how high is the Sun?
questions.why: Dec S23°26.3′ is south of 22°54′S: the GP is 0°32.3′ south of you, so the Sun bears south, 90° − 0°32.3′ = 89°27.7′ high.

questions.q: Before leaving Cape Town for St Helena you take a noon sight. Which way does the Sun bear, and how high is it?

figure.title: Noon, 10 Jan, Table Bay
lines: The height of the southern summer

questions.why: The GP (S21°57.3′) is 11°57.7′ north of you: even in the southern summer the Sun bears north, 90° − 11°57.7′ = 78°02.3′.

questions.q: You take a noon sight in the Galápagos on the equinox. Which way does the Sun bear, and how high is it?
questions.why: Contrary names: z = 0°45.0′ + 0°03.5′ = 0°48.5′, GP north of you: the Sun bears north, 90° − 0°48.5′ = 89°11.5′ high.

questions.q: At anchor in Bora Bora you watch the noon Sun pass straight overhead. Which way does it bear a few minutes before and a few minutes after noon?
options: Nearly north before noon, nearly south after
Due north both before and after noon
Nearly south before noon, nearly north after
Nearly east before noon, nearly west after
questions.why: Its GP runs west along your own parallel and passes over you: the azimuth swings from about 090° to about 270°, never N or S.

questions.q: In the Bahamas on the longest day, a crew member says the noon Sun will stand to the north of you. Is that right?
options: No — the Sun's GP never goes north of 23°26′N
Yes — whenever the Sun's Dec is north
No — north of the equator it never does
Yes — around the June solstice, at noon
questions.why: The Sun's GP never leaves the tropics: at 25°03′N it is always south of you at noon, at best 88°23′ high on 21 June.
questions.ref: The Sun's declination through the year

questions.q: Running east in the forties, you plan a meridian sight of Antares. Which way will it bear, and how high will it be?
questions.why: Dec S26°29′ lies north of 40°S: z = 40° − 26°29′ = 13°31′, so Antares culminates to the north, 76°29′ high.

questions.q: Waiting in Horta, a crew member wants to see a body pass straight overhead. Which of these comes closest to your zenith?
options: The Sun at the June solstice
questions.why: At culmination z = |lat − Dec|: Vega 16′, Capella 7°29′, the Sun at best 15°06′, Arcturus 19°26′ from your zenith.

questions.q: A crew member asks why the Sun is highest exactly as it crosses your meridian. What do you tell them?
options: The Sun's Dec peaks at the moment of local noon
Refraction is least when the Sun bears N or S
The Earth turns most slowly at local noon
Its GP then passes closest to you on its way west
questions.why: The GP runs west along the parallel of its Dec and is nearest you as it crosses your meridian: ZX least, altitude greatest.

questions.q: Southbound from the Cape Verdes, a crew member wants Acrux to stay up all night. From which latitude will it never set?

figure.title: Cape Verdes to Cape Town
lines: Brightest star of the Southern Cross

questions.why: Circumpolar when Dec > co-lat: 63°14′ > 90° − lat once you are south of 90° − 63°14′ = 26°46′S.

questions.q: On a charter south from Ushuaia, a guest asks from which latitude the Sun stays above the horizon all day at the solstice. What do you answer (ignore refraction)?
questions.why: The Sun is circumpolar when its Dec exceeds your co-lat: 23°26′ > 90° − lat south of 66°34′S, the Antarctic Circle.

questions.q: You plan the watches for a solstice departure from Cape Town. Where does the Sun rise, and is it up for more or less than 12 hours?
options: South of east; less than 12 hours
South of east; more than 12 hours
North of east; more than 12 hours
questions.why: Dec of the same name as your latitude: the Sun rises south of east, and more than half its daily circle is above your horizon.

questions.q: Ten degrees south of the line you set up the first PZX triangle of the passage. Which pole is P, and how high does it stand?
options: The south celestial pole, 80° above the south horizon
The north celestial pole, 10° below the north horizon
The north celestial pole, right on the north horizon
The south celestial pole, 10° above the south horizon
questions.why: P is the elevated pole, named like your latitude: at 10°S the south celestial pole stands 10° up, and PZ = 80°.

questions.q: You set up the PZX triangle for a morning sun sight off Durban. What are the sides PZ and PX?
questions.why: P is the south pole: PZ = 90° − 29°53.0′ = 60°07.0′; a south Dec is on your side, so PX = 90° − 17°08.6′ = 72°51.4′.

questions.q: Bound for Brisbane, you have the azimuth angle from your afternoon sun reduction. Which true azimuth do you lay off on the plotting sheet?
questions.why: South of the equator Z is measured from south: S82°W is 180° + 82° = 262°, the Sun just south of west.

questions.q: While the GPS still works you check your sextant work against it. What Ho should the sight give?

figure.title: Sextant practice, GPS on
lines: GPS: 1500 M from the Sun's GP
At the second of the sight

questions.why: 1500 M = 1500′ of arc = 25°00′ of zenith distance, so Ho = 90° − 25°00′ = 65°00′.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance

questions.q: You draw two simultaneous star sights as whole circles of equal altitude. They cross at A and at B, about 2900 M apart. Where are you?

figure.note: Two star sights at one instant · not to scale

options: At A or B — only a third star can tell
At A, the crossing near your DR
questions.why: Two circles always cross twice, usually thousands of miles apart; your DR (or a third body) shows which crossing is yours.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — position line

questions.q: You and the mate reduce the same sun sight from different assumed positions and get different intercepts. What do you find when you plot both?

figure.title: One sun sight, two navigators
lines: Mate: AP 2, 30 M south of AP 1

options: Both give the same position line
Only the AP nearer the GP gives the line
The two lines lie 30 M apart
The two lines cross at your position
questions.why: AP 1 + 12 M south = AP 2 + 18 M north: one line. It is a piece of one circle round the GP; the AP only changes the intercept.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — the assumed position

questions.q: You discover that the index error was left out of your morning sun sight. Where does the position line you plotted lie compared with the true one?

figure.title: Morning sun line
lines: Index error found later: 2.0′ on the arc
It was not applied to this sight

questions.why: On the arc, so Ho came out 2.0′ too high: the zenith distance and the circle's radius are 2 M short, so the line sits 2 M nearer the Sun.

questions.q: You discover that the watch used for yesterday's sights was 30 seconds fast. What has that done to yesterday's fixes?

figure.title: Watch check by GPS time
lines: Used for all of yesterday's sights

options: Moved them 7.5′ of latitude south; longitude unchanged
Moved them 0.5′ of longitude west; latitude unchanged
Moved them 7.5′ of longitude west; latitude unchanged
Moved them 7.5′ of longitude east; latitude unchanged
questions.why: UT 30 s late makes every GHA 7.5′ too big and every GP too far west: the whole picture is turned 7.5′ west about the pole.

questions.q: Halfway across on the ARC you take a sun sight just as the Sun bears due east. Which way does the position line run, and what does it give you?
questions.why: A position line lies at right angles to the azimuth: with the Sun due east it runs along your meridian and fixes longitude.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — position line

questions.q: You want to mark Jupiter on your star finder, which places bodies by their SHA. What SHA do you use?

figure.title: Almanac, 1900 UT
lines: Star finder: bodies set by SHA

questions.why: SHA is measured west from Aries: SHA = GHA body − GHA Aries = 120°10.4′ − 95°40.2′ = 24°30.2′.
questions.ref: First point of Aries and SHA

questions.q: At dusk you want a star that is crossing your meridian right now. Which one is it?
questions.why: On your meridian LHA★ = LHA Aries + SHA = 360°: SHA = 360° − 279°27′ = 80°33′, which is Vega.
questions.ref: First point of Aries and SHA

questions.q: On a long night watch you picture the GP of Sirius moving across the globe. Which way does it go?
options: East along the 16°45′S parallel, 15°02.5′ an hour
West along the 16°45′S parallel, 15°00.0′ an hour
West along the 16°45′S parallel, 15°02.5′ an hour
West along a great circle, 15°02.5′ an hour
questions.why: A star's Dec is fixed, so its GP keeps to the parallel of its Dec; its GHA (Aries + SHA) grows 15°02.5′ an hour, westward.

questions.q: Before a dawn star fix on the way from Tonga to Fiji you want the GP of Antares. Where is it?
Leafing through a year of almanac pages, the crew notice that the Sun's Dec swings while Vega's stays put. Why?

figure.title: A year of almanac pages
lines: Sun Dec from N23°26′ to S23°26′

options: The Sun goes round the ecliptic, tilted 23°26′ to the equator
The Sun moves along the celestial equator, the stars do not
The Earth's axis nods 23°26′ to and fro each year
The Sun is close, so its parallax shifts its Dec
questions.why: As the Earth orbits, the Sun seems to circle the ecliptic once a year, and that circle is tilted 23°26′ to the celestial equator.

questions.q: You plan Moon sights for the week ahead. Why does the Moon cross your meridian about 50 minutes later each night?
options: Its GHA grows faster than the Sun's
It moves east among the stars about 13° a day
It moves west among the stars about 13° a day
Its Dec changes by about 13° a day
questions.why: The Moon orbits eastward about 13° a day against the stars, so its GHA grows only about 14°30′ an hour and it comes round later.

questions.q: You plotted a high sun sight as a straight line and crossed it with a star line 60 M from the foot of the intercept, F. How far is that fix from the true circle of position?

figure.note: Ho 86°00′ · circle radius 240 M · fix 60 M from F

questions.why: Offset ≈ d² ÷ 2r = 60² ÷ (2 × 240) ≈ 7.4 M: near the zenith the circle is tight, so plot the circle itself or keep the AP close.
questions.ref: Circle of equal altitude — high-altitude sights

questions.q: You find you reduced this morning's sun sight with yesterday's Dec. How far is the position line out, and which way?

figure.title: Sun sight, 21 March
lines: Dec used: yesterday's, 23.7′ too far south

questions.why: The GP sits 23.7 M too far south; along Zn 120° that is 23.7 × cos 60° ≈ 12 M, so the line lies 12 M too far towards 120°.

questions.q: You reduce a morning sun sight off the Cape in the southern summer. What are Hc and Zn?

figure.title: Morning sun, 25 Jan, off the Cape

questions.why: Lat −34°, Dec −19°00.0′: sin Hc = sin 34° sin 19°00.0′ + cos 34° cos 19°00.0′ cos 315° → 47°25.2′; Sun north of east, Zn 081°.

questions.q: You plan star sights for a long passage along 35°S. For how long is Arcturus above your horizon each day?
questions.why: Rising LHA: cos LHA = −tan lat tan Dec = tan 35° tan 19°06′ (lat S) → 76°; up for 152° of its circle ≈ 10 h.

questions.q: Running east at 45°S, you watch Acrux circle the pole through the night. What are its highest and lowest altitudes?
options: 71°46′ to the south and 18°14′ to the north
71°46′ to the north and 18°14′ to the south
questions.why: Upper: 90° − (63°14′ − 45°) = 71°46′, GP south of you. Lower: lat − polar distance = 45° − 26°46′ = 18°14′, below the pole.
questions.ref: Circumpolar bodies — upper and lower transit

questions.q: Off Mauritius at dusk you are reducing a sight of Antares. Which LHA goes into the triangle, and on which side of your meridian is the star?
On the solstice at 30°S the Sun rises south of east and swings round to the north by noon. At what altitude does it bear due east (090°)?
questions.why: Bearing 090° the triangle has a right angle at Z: sin Hc = sin Dec ÷ sin lat = sin 23°26.2′ ÷ sin 30° → 52°42′.

questions.q: You and a buddy boat, either side of the 180th meridian, take sun sights at the same second. What LHA does each of you use?
questions.why: You: 170° + 178°E = 348°. Buddy: 170° − 178°W = −8° + 360° = 352°. They are 4° east of you, so their LHA is 4° more.

questions.q: You reduce a morning sun sight in the southern summer and get an absurd intercept. Which slip is the most likely cause?
options: Yesterday's Dec used instead of today's
The index error applied the wrong way
The Dec named north instead of south
The dip added instead of subtracted
questions.why: IE, dip or a day's Dec cost minutes at most; a Dec of the wrong name moves the GP by twice the Dec, here about 45°.

questions.q: South of the Cape of Good Hope you reduce a dawn sight of Arcturus. What are Hc and Zn?
questions.why: Lat −35°, Dec +19°06′: sin Hc = −sin 35° sin 19°06′ + cos 35° cos 19°06′ cos 330° → 28°51.6′; star NE of you, Zn 033°.

questions.q: You are showing a new crew member the sextant before her first sun sight on the ARC. What moves when she turns the micrometer drum?
options: The index arm, with the index mirror on it
The shade glasses in front of the mirrors
The horizon mirror on the frame
questions.why: The drum drives the index arm along the arc and the index mirror turns with it; the horizon mirror and telescope are fixed to the frame.

questions.q: You read your micrometer sextant after a sun sight. What is Hs?

figure.title: Your sextant after the sight
lines: Index mark on the arc: just past 41°

questions.why: Degrees from the arc (the last whole degree passed, 41°), minutes from the drum (58′), tenths from the vernier (0.6′).

questions.q: You are about to bring the Sun down to the horizon. What do you swing in first?

figure.title: Sun sight, late morning
lines: Clear sky, the Sun very bright
Sextant set near 0°, all shades up

options: No shades — the telescope cuts the glare
One light horizon shade, no index shade
Index shades, enough to dim the Sun's image
Horizon shades only — the Sun is seen direct
questions.why: The Sun's image comes via the index mirror: dim it with index shades before you look. Horizon shades only cut the glare on the sea.

questions.q: The sea is lumpy and you take the sextant out of its box for the noon sight. How do you lift it?
options: By the arc — the strongest part of the frame
By the telescope — it is bolted to the frame
By the index arm, with the clamp released
By the handle or frame — never the arc or arm
questions.why: Lifting by the arc or the index arm can bend it and add an error; hold the frame or handle, and put it straight back in the box.

questions.q: You are working up a sun sight. Which altitude do you enter the main correction table with?

figure.title: Sun LL — working
lines: Main correction: enter the table with ?

options: Ha — Hs after index error and dip
Hs — the reading straight off the arc
Hc — the altitude from the sight reduction
Ho — the altitude after every correction
questions.why: Hs ± IE − dip = Ha (apparent altitude); refraction and SD depend on Ha, so the main table is entered with Ha to give Ho.

questions.q: You bought a second-hand sextant for a Pacific crossing and want to adjust it. In what order do you remove the errors?
options: Index error, perpendicularity, then side error
Perpendicularity, side error, then index error
Side error, perpendicularity, then index error
Index error, side error, then perpendicularity
questions.why: Each adjustment can upset the next: the index mirror first (perpendicularity), then the horizon mirror for side error, then index error.

questions.q: Your crew asks why you swing the sextant from side to side as the Sun touches the horizon. What are you doing?

figure.title: Sun sight from the deck
lines: Sun's lower limb near the horizon
You swing the sextant gently left and right
The Sun's image swings in an arc

options: Checking the sextant for side error
Shaking water drops off the horizon mirror
Finding the bottom of the arc — the sextant upright
questions.why: Rocking swings the Sun in an arc; at its lowest point the sextant is vertical. Set the lower limb to kiss the horizon there.

questions.q: You are alone on watch and want the time of your sight to the second. How do you get it?

figure.title: Single-handed sight
lines: GPS-checked watch at the chart table
No one on deck to call 'mark'

options: Read the watch first, then take the sight
Read the watch after you have read the sextant
Note the time as you go on deck to take it
Start a stopwatch at the sight, then read the watch
questions.why: Start the stopwatch at the instant of the sight; at the chart table read the watch and subtract the stopwatch's run.

questions.q: You take the sight on the Sun's upper limb. How does the semi-diameter go into the correction?

figure.title: Afternoon sun sight
lines: Low cloud hides the Sun's lower half
Upper limb sharp above the cloud
You bring the upper limb to the horizon

options: Subtracted — the centre is below the upper limb
Added, as for every sun sight
Added twice — for the whole diameter
Ignored — it is part of the dip
questions.why: The tables give the altitude of the Sun's centre: add SD to a lower-limb sight, subtract it from an upper-limb sight.

questions.q: You take a sight with the plastic backup sextant. What do you do about its index error?

figure.title: Backup sextant
lines: Plastic sextant from the grab bag
Left in the sun in the cockpit for an hour
IE was 2.0′ off the arc at breakfast

options: Use the 2.0′ off the arc from breakfast
Measure it again now, just before the sight
Use the metal sextant's index error
Ignore it — plastic sextants have none
questions.why: A plastic frame bends with temperature, so its index error changes within hours: check it at every sight.

questions.q: You take your sights standing at the shrouds of a 15 m ketch. What dip do you apply?
questions.why: Dip = 1.76 × √3.2 = 1.76 × 1.79 = 3.1′, always subtracted from Hs.

questions.q: You check the index error on the horizon before the morning sights. What is it, and how do you apply it?

figure.title: Index error on the horizon
lines: Direct and reflected horizon in one line

questions.why: Below zero the drum reads 60′ minus the error: 60 − 57.0 = 3.0′ off the arc, and off the arc is added to Hs.

questions.q: At twilight you check the index error on a bright star. What correction do you apply to tonight's sights?

figure.title: Index error on a star
lines: Reflected and direct star made one

questions.why: A reading on the arc for a zero angle means the sextant reads too high: subtract 2.4′ from every Hs.

questions.q: You read the sextant after a sight of Arcturus. What is the altitude after the index error?
questions.why: The reading is 52°14.6′; off the arc is added: 52°14.6′ + 1.4′ = 52°16.0′.

questions.q: You are 1300 miles from St Lucia on the ARC and take this sight of the Sun. What is Ho?

figure.title: Sun LL, 20 November
lines: IE 2.0′ on the arc · eye 2.7 m (dip 2.9′)

questions.q: Bound from Bermuda to the Azores, you catch the Sun's upper limb between clouds. What is Ho?
In mid-Atlantic you take Vega at nautical twilight. What is Ho?
questions.why: 41°20.0′ − 1.6′ IE − 2.6′ dip − 1.1′ refraction = Ho 41°14.7′; a star has no semi-diameter.

questions.q: You add Jupiter to your evening star fix. Which corrections take its Hs to Ho?

figure.title: Dusk sights
lines: Jupiter bright in the east, Ha 33°
Almanac: no additional correction for Jupiter

options: Dip and refraction — IE is for the Sun only
IE, dip and refraction — as for a star
IE, dip, refraction and the Moon's parallax
IE, dip, refraction and the Sun's SD
questions.why: Jupiter is a point of light like a star: index error, dip and star refraction. Only Venus and Mars get a small additional correction.

questions.q: You take the Moon in the afternoon to cross with a sun line. What is the parallax correction?

figure.title: Moon sight
lines: Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha

questions.why: HP × cos Ha = 57.0′ × 0.866 = 49.4′, always added: seen from the Earth's centre the Moon stands higher.

questions.q: You want a Moon sight just after sunset. Which limb do you bring to the horizon?

figure.title: Evening, west sky
lines: Thin crescent Moon above the sunset
Lit edge facing down, towards the Sun

options: Either — the semi-diameter is the same
The upper limb — the tips of the crescent
The lower limb — it is the lit edge
questions.why: Only the lit, round limb is a true edge of the Moon's disc; here it faces down, so take the lower limb and add SD.

questions.q: You take the Sun soon after sunrise because cloud is coming in. What is Ho?
Off the west coast of Barbados at 0800 you want a sun line, but the Sun is over the island. What do you do with the shoreline under it?

figure.title: Sun sight off Barbados
lines: Coast 1.5 M away, under the Sun
Eye 2.5 m: sea horizon 3.3 M off

options: Use it with no dip — land is level
Don't use it — its dip is not the table's
Use it and double the table's dip
Use it with the dip from the table
questions.why: The shoreline lies inside the sea horizon, so it dips more than the table gives; take a body over open sea instead.

questions.q: In a big Southern Ocean swell you bring the Sun down to the crest of a nearby wave. What does that do, and what do you do?

figure.title: Southern Ocean swell, 4 m
lines: In the troughs a crest hides the horizon
The boat lifts to each swell

options: No effect — the dip allows for it
Hs reads high — sight from the trough
Hs reads low — sight from the top of a swell
Hs reads low — add the wave height to the dip
questions.why: A crest above your eye stands higher than the true horizon, so Hs reads low; wait for the boat to lift and sight from the top.

questions.q: On the ARC route the horizon under the Sun is blurred by dust. What gives you a better sight?

figure.title: Hazy horizon, 0700
lines: Saharan dust in the trade wind
Horizon fuzzy from the coachroof (3.5 m)

options: Use the top of the haze as the horizon
Keep the height and add 2′ for the haze
Sight from higher up — the horizon is further off
Sight from lower down, with the dip for that height
questions.why: A lower eye brings the horizon nearer and sharper in haze; use the dip for the new height of eye.

questions.q: You take four quick sights of the rising Sun to average. Which time and Hs do you work up?
questions.why: Mean of the times 09:42:20, mean of the altitudes 31°14.0′ — fine while the altitude changes steadily over a few minutes.

questions.q: You plot five altitudes against time before averaging them. Which sight do you discard?
questions.why: The Sun rises about 3′ every 30 s: No. 3 should be near 40°08.0′, not 40°11.9′ — a bad sight; average the other four.

questions.q: You need a morning sun line in this sea. Where and how do you take the sight?

figure.title: Trade-wind sight
lines: Wind 25 kn, 3 m swell on the beam
Two crew on deck, one at the helm

options: Standing on the coachroof, holding the boom
Sitting low in the cockpit, in the troughs
Wedged in the companionway, clipped on, on a crest
At the stern, eye as high as the pushpit
questions.why: Brace yourself near the middle of the boat, hands free and clipped on, and take the sight as she lifts on a swell and the horizon clears.

questions.q: You check your sextant before the passage and see this. What is wrong, and what do you adjust?

figure.title: Checking the sextant
lines: Sextant flat, arc away from you, arm at 60°
You look into the index mirror at the arc
The reflected arc steps up from the real arc

options: Index error — the horizon mirror's second screw
Side error — the horizon mirror's screw
questions.why: If the arc and its reflection in the index mirror do not run on as one line, the index mirror is not perpendicular to the frame.

questions.q: You check the sextant on a star and see this. What does it show, and what do you adjust?

figure.title: Checking on a star
lines: Index set at 0°, telescope on a star
The reflected star passes beside the real one

options: Side error — the horizon mirror's side screw
Index error — the index mirror's screw
questions.why: If the reflected star passes beside, not through, the direct one, the horizon mirror is not perpendicular to the frame: side error.

questions.q: You check the telescope like this. What does the difference tell you?

figure.title: Collimation check
lines: Two stars 100° apart brought into contact
Contact at the top, then at the bottom edge

options: The index error is 1.5′ on the arc
The telescope is not parallel to the frame
The horizon mirror has side error
The index mirror is not perpendicular
questions.why: Collimation error: the line of sight is tilted to the frame, so large angles read too big. Adjust the collar, or keep bodies centred.

questions.q: You find this in the workbook. How far out is each position line?

figure.title: Last night's star fix
lines: Crew subtracted it from every Hs

questions.why: The right +3.0′ became −3.0′: a 6.0′ altitude error, and 1′ of altitude is 1 M, so each line is 6 M out (away from its star).

questions.q: You check the crew's working of a sun sight. What does the mistake do to the sun line?

figure.title: Sun line check
lines: Crew added the dip to Hs

options: 3 M too far towards the Sun
6 M too far away from the Sun
3 M too far away from the Sun
6 M too far towards the Sun
questions.why: Dip is always subtracted; adding 3.0′ makes Ho 6.0′ too large, so the intercept is 6 M too far towards.

questions.q: A crew member works up this star sight. How far out is the position line?

figure.title: Star sight worked up
lines: Corrected with the Sun's LL table: +14.5′

options: 16 M too far towards the star
32 M too far towards the star
16 M too far away from the star
8 M too far towards the star
questions.why: +14.5′ − (−1.7′) = 16.2′, the Sun's SD: Ho is 16.2′ too large, so the line lies about 16 M too far towards.

questions.q: You time a sun sight with the stopwatch. What is the UT of your sight?
questions.why: 14:25:00 − 1 min 37.4 s = 14:23:22.6 by the watch; it is 4 s fast, so subtract: 14:23:18.6 ≈ 14:23:19 UT.

questions.q: You measure the index error on the Sun's two limbs. What is it?

figure.title: Index error by the Sun, November

questions.why: IE = (on − off) ÷ 2 = (31.6 − 33.2) ÷ 2 = −0.8′: off the arc, add. Check: (31.6 + 33.2) ÷ 4 = 16.2′, the almanac SD.

questions.q: You take the Sun's upper limb and work it with the almanac's table. What is Ho?
You stand in the cockpit for your sights. What dip do you use?

figure.title: Where is your eye?
lines: Cockpit sole 1.0 m above the waterline
Your eye 1.6 m above the cockpit sole

questions.why: Height of eye is above the sea, not the deck: 1.0 + 1.6 = 2.6 m, and dip = 1.76 × √2.6 = 2.8′.

questions.q: How do you find Capella in the sextant before you can see it?

figure.title: Evening twilight
lines: Capella not yet visible to the eye

options: Preset 31° and sweep the horizon near 040°
Wait until it shows, then bring it down
Set 0°, aim at the star and bring it down
questions.why: With Hc and Zn worked out in advance, preset the altitude and look along the bearing: the star shows in the mirror while the horizon is sharp.

questions.q: Spray came over during the noon sight. What do you do before you stow the sextant?

figure.title: After the noon sight
lines: Spray over the cockpit during the sight
Salt drops on both mirrors and the arc

options: Box it as it is and clean it in port
Leave it on the chart table to dry
Dab the salt off, dry it, then stow it in its box
Rub the mirrors hard with a paper towel
questions.why: Salt corrodes the mirrors and arc: dab the mirrors with lens tissue (a little fresh water), dry the frame, and keep it in its box.

questions.q: Cloud clears and you could take the Sun now at 5°, or wait an hour for 15°. Why is waiting better?
options: The Sun's parallax is largest when low
The Sun's semi-diameter grows near the horizon
Dip is larger when the Sun is low
Refraction is large and uncertain near the horizon
questions.why: Refraction grows fast below 10° and varies with temperature and pressure, so its error is uncertain; keep sights above about 10–15°.

questions.q: Bound for the Marquesas, you cross a sun line with this Moon sight. What is Ho?

figure.title: Moon LL, afternoon
lines: Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha

questions.q: In the Indian Ocean you take the Moon by day to cross with the Sun. What is Ho?

figure.title: Moon UL, morning
lines: Only the upper limb is lit

questions.q: You measure the index error on the Sun, then take your sight. What is Ho?

figure.title: Sun, 25 November
lines: IE on the Sun: on 31.6′, off 33.2′

questions.q: With the lower limb in cloud, you take the setting Sun's upper limb. What is Ho?
You check the crew's sun line. How far, and which way, is their position line out?

figure.title: Checking the crew's sun line
lines: IE 1.5′ off the arc — crew subtracted it

questions.why: IE −1.5′ instead of +1.5′ = −3.0′; dip +2.9′ instead of −2.9′ = +5.8′. Ho is 2.8′ too large: 2.8 M too far towards.

questions.q: You plot this series against time, drop the bad sight and average the rest. What do you work up?

figure.title: Five sights, 40 s apart
lines: UT and Hs; the Sun climbing steadily

questions.why: The Sun climbs about 4.6′ in 40 s, so 16:07:10 should be near 28°54′: drop it. The other four average 16:06:20, 28°48.3′.

questions.q: The same sextant error is suspected in all three star sights. Where on the plotting sheet do you put your fix?
options: B — the corner where two lines cross
D — outside the triangle, past corner B
A — the centre, equally far from all three lines
C — on the line of the brightest star
questions.why: A constant error moves every line the same distance towards or away; with bodies 120° apart the true fix is equidistant from all three.

questions.q: You practise sights on the way to the Azores. When the GPS later fails, what do you do with this result?

figure.title: Practice while the GPS works
lines: Five sun sights; Hc from the GPS position

options: Set the IE to 3.6′ off the arc
questions.why: A steady +2.6′ over five sights is a personal error: subtract 2.6′ from each Ho, and keep checking it while the GPS still works.

questions.q: You check the crew's Moon sight. How far out is their position line?

figure.title: Moon LL worked by the crew
lines: Crew used the Sun LL table (SD 15.9′)
Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha

questions.why: The Sun table leaves out the Moon's parallax: 47.4′ + 15.8′ − 15.9′ = 47.3′ too small an Ho, so about 47 M too far away.

questions.q: What do you do before the dusk star sights?

figure.title: Sextant knocked off the chart table
lines: At 0° a star passes beside its reflection

options: Zero the index error first, then side error
Remove the side error, then measure IE again
Use 3.5′ on the arc and ignore the side error
Average the two: use 1.5′ on the arc
questions.why: Side error is set on the horizon mirror, which moves the index error: remove side error first, then measure IE again and apply it.

questions.q: Your crew looks through the sextant for the first time: the horizon in one half of the field, the Sun beside it. Where does the Sun's image come from?

figure.title: First look through the sextant
lines: One half of the field: the sea horizon
The other half: the Sun, dimmed by shades

options: The horizon mirror's clear half, seen direct
The telescope's lens, without any mirror
The index mirror, via the horizon mirror's silvered half
The shade glasses, by their own reflection
questions.why: Sunlight hits the index mirror, then the silvered half of the horizon mirror, then the telescope; the clear half shows the horizon direct.

questions.q: Twilight is coming and you fit a telescope for the star sights. Which do you choose?

figure.title: In the sextant box
lines: Boat rolling in the trade-wind swell

options: The 7× telescope, a little out of focus
The 7× telescope, for the most magnification
The Sun telescope, with its dark filter on
questions.why: A low power (about 3×) with a wide field finds the star, holds it in a rolling boat and shows it while the horizon is still sharp.

questions.q: At night the horizon is lost in the dark but the stars are bright. A crew member suggests the old aircraft bubble sextant aboard. What is the catch at sea?

figure.title: Night sights?
lines: Aircraft bubble sextant in a locker

options: The boat's motion moves the bubble: errors of miles
None — it is more accurate than a marine sextant
It needs a larger dip than a marine sextant
It works only on the Sun, never on stars
questions.why: A bubble sextant needs no horizon and no dip, but the yacht's roll and pitch throw the bubble about: a single sight can be many miles out.

questions.q: You are stowing the gear for a three-week Atlantic crossing. Where does the sextant box live?
options: In the forepeak, out of everyone's way
Wedged low near the middle of the boat, in a dry locker
On the chart table, ready for the next sight
In a cockpit locker, close to where you sight
questions.why: Low and amidships the motion is least; wedge the box so it cannot slide, and keep it dry and out of the sun.

questions.q: In the tropics the Sun will pass about 87° high at noon. What makes this sight hard?
options: Refraction is largest near the zenith
No shade is dark enough for a high Sun
Finding the vertical — the Sun sweeps along the horizon
Dip grows as the Sun climbs higher
questions.why: Near the zenith the Sun's azimuth swings fast and rocking shows no clear bottom of the arc, so it is hard to tell where the vertical meets the horizon.

questions.q: The almanac gives Venus an additional altitude correction that Jupiter does not get. Why?

figure.title: Dusk sights
lines: Venus bright in the west, Ha 18°

options: Venus is so bright that it dazzles the eye
Venus has a semi-diameter like the Sun's
Venus is refracted more than a star
Venus comes close: its parallax and its phase
questions.why: Venus passes close to the Earth, so it has a small parallax, and its phase shifts the centre of its light: the almanac lists a small extra correction.

questions.q: Bound for Svalbard, the air is far colder than the almanac's standard. When does its temperature and pressure correction matter?

figure.title: Cold air, 74°N
lines: Sights planned at Ha 5° and Ha 40°

options: Only for the Moon, never for the Sun
At every altitude by the same amount
questions.why: The extra correction scales with refraction itself: up to a minute at 5°, nothing worth applying above about 10–15°.

questions.q: You move from the cockpit up onto the coachroof to see over the swell. What happens to the dip you apply?
options: It is larger — and now it is added
It is the same — dip depends on the sea
It is smaller — the horizon is clearer
questions.why: Dip grows with height of eye (1.76 √h): the higher you stand, the lower the horizon looks, so more is subtracted.

questions.q: You can buy one sextant for an ocean crossing and already own a plastic one. Which do you make the main instrument?
options: The plastic one — light, and it never corrodes
The plastic one — it needs no adjustment
A metal one — its index error stays steady
Either — both hold their errors equally
questions.why: A metal frame keeps its shape through heat and knocks, so its errors stay put; a plastic one drifts with temperature — keep it as the backup.

questions.q: You call 'mark!' at the instant of the sight and your crew reads the watch. What does she note first?

figure.title: Sight with a timekeeper
lines: You at the shrouds with the sextant
Crew at the chart table with the watch

options: The hour, then the minutes and seconds
The seconds, then the minutes and hour
questions.why: The seconds change while she reads; note them first and the minutes and hour after, which will not have moved.

questions.q: The morning horizon is too hazy for an index check, so you use the Sun's two limbs instead. What is the index error, and which way does it go?

figure.title: Index error by the Sun, 15 October

questions.q: You measure the index error on the Sun twice, a few minutes apart. Which measurement do you trust, and what is the error?

figure.title: Index error by the Sun, 10 March

options: The second — IE 1.7′ off the arc
The first — IE 0.3′ on the arc
The second — IE 1.7′ on the arc
The first — IE 0.3′ off the arc
questions.why: (on + off) ÷ 4 should be the SD: 64.4 ÷ 4 = 16.1′, good; 62.8 ÷ 4 = 15.7′, a poor contact. IE = (32.5 − 31.9) ÷ 2 = 0.3′ on.

questions.q: You step up from the cockpit onto the coachroof for the sight. What dip do you apply now?

figure.title: Height of eye
lines: Cockpit: eye 2.4 m above the sea

questions.why: Height of eye 2.4 + 0.9 = 3.3 m above the sea; dip = 1.76 × √3.3 = 1.76 × 1.82 = 3.2′.

questions.q: You and a crew member take the Sun's lower limb at the same moment. Whose Hs reads higher, and by how much?
questions.why: A higher eye sees the horizon lower: dip 3.4′ at 3.7 m against 2.6′ at 2.2 m, so your Hs is 0.8′ more; after dip both give the same Ho.

questions.q: You are crossing to the Marquesas on a 14 m catamaran in a big swell. Where do you take the morning sun sight, and with what dip?

figure.title: Catamaran, 4 m swell
lines: Cockpit: eye 2.1 m, crests hide the horizon

options: The flybridge, with the dip for 4.8 m (3.9′)
The cockpit, with the nearest crest as horizon
The flybridge, with the cockpit dip (2.6′)
The flybridge, no dip — the horizon is clear
questions.why: Sight where the horizon is clear and use the dip for that height: 1.76 × √4.8 = 3.9′. A nearby crest is not the horizon.

questions.q: Crossing the Arabian Sea in May, you take the Sun just after sunrise, before the haze thickens. What is Ho?
Cold air lies over the warm Gulf Stream and you suspect the dip is not what the table says. How do you plan the dusk star sights?
options: Only the two highest, clear of the dip
A, B and C — three are always enough
A and B only — 90° apart cuts best
questions.why: A dip error moves every line the same way, towards or away; in opposite pairs it cancels — the fix lies midway between each pair.

questions.q: Off the Cape Verdes you take Venus at dusk to add to the star fix. What is Ho?
questions.why: 22°36.4′ − 1.1′ − 2.5′ = Ha 22°32.8′; − 2.4′ refraction + 0.3′ Venus = Ho 22°30.7′. A planet takes no SD.

questions.q: In the early afternoon you want the Moon to cross with your sun line. Which limb do you bring to the horizon, and what happens to the SD?

figure.title: Afternoon sky
lines: The Moon's lit side faces up, to the Sun

options: The upper limb — subtract the SD
The lower limb — add the SD
The upper limb — add the SD
The centre — no SD at all
questions.why: Take the lit, round limb: with the Sun higher than the Moon it is the upper one, and an upper-limb sight takes the SD off.

questions.q: Going over the crew's Moon sight at the chart table, you spot this slip with the parallax. Where does it put their Moon line?

figure.title: Moon sight, crew's working
lines: Crew added the whole HP as parallax

options: About 27 M too far towards the Moon
About 31 M too far towards the Moon
About 58 M too far towards the Moon
About 31 M too far away from the Moon
questions.why: Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha = 58.4 × 0.466 = 27.2′; adding 58.4′ makes Ho 31.2′ too large: about 31 M too far towards.

questions.q: A crew member took the Moon's HP and SD from the wrong day's page. How far out is her Moon line?

figure.title: Moon LL, Ha 40°00′
lines: Parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha

options: About 4 M too far away from the Moon
About 6 M too far towards the Moon
About 6 M too far away from the Moon
About 2 M too far away from the Moon
questions.why: Parallax 60.1 × 0.766 = 46.0′ vs 41.8′ (4.2′) and the SD 1.5′ short: Ho 5.7′ too small, so the line is about 6 M too far away.

questions.q: Bound from the Caribbean to the Azores in May, you take the Sun a few minutes before it crosses your meridian. How do you plot this sight?

figure.title: Sun near the zenith, 25 May, 1512 UT

options: A straight position line from an AP, as usual
A circle of 160 M radius round your DR
A circle of 320 M radius round the Sun's GP
A circle of 160 M radius round the Sun's GP
questions.why: At 87°20′ the circle of equal altitude is small: radius = zenith distance 2°40′ = 160 M. Plot it as a circle round the GP, not a straight line.

questions.q: You plot five sun sights against time and draw the line of best fit. What Hs do you take off the line for 10:24:00 UT?

figure.title: Five sights of the rising Sun
lines: UT and Hs; the Sun climbing steadily

questions.why: The line follows the steady climb (about 8.6′ a minute); at 10:24:00 it reads 33°19.3′, smoother than any single sight.

questions.q: Last night's three star lines: two cross neatly, the third is far off. What most likely went wrong with the third?
options: The drum misread by ten minutes
The arc misread by a whole degree
The dip added instead of subtracted
The index error applied the wrong way
questions.why: With the drum near 60′ the index sits almost on the next degree: an Hs read 1° high gives an intercept near 60′ instead of the real one.

questions.q: Checking the sextant after your sun sight, you see that the reading you wrote down is wrong. What had that done to your sun line?

figure.title: Sun sight, rechecked
lines: Sextant still shows: 23° on the arc

options: It was 1 M too far towards the Sun
It was 10 M too far away from the Sun
It was 10 M too far towards the Sun
It was 20 M too far towards the Sun
questions.why: The true Hs is 23°32.6′, 10′ less than worked: Ho was 10′ too large, so the line was 10 M too far towards the Sun.

questions.q: The sextant slid off the cockpit seat. You check it as below. What do you do with the index error?

figure.title: Checks after the knock
lines: IE now 2.2′ on the arc (was 0.4′ off)

options: Apply the mean, 0.9′ on the arc
Apply 2.6′ on the arc — the change
Apply the old 0.4′ off the arc
Apply 2.2′ on the arc, rechecked at each sight
questions.why: A small new index error is simply measured and applied; adjusting it at sea risks upsetting the side error. Recheck it before each sight.

questions.q: Evening twilight is starting and the horizon is still sharp all round. Which star do you take first?
options: A — bright, over the eastern horizon
C — faint, over the eastern horizon
B — bright, over the western horizon
D — faint, over the western horizon
questions.why: At dusk the eastern horizon fades first, and only bright stars show in the telescope yet: bright eastern stars first, western ones last.

questions.q: Morning twilight: the horizon is just showing in the east, still dark in the west. Which star do you take first?
options: A — brighter, over the eastern horizon
B — fainter, over the eastern horizon
C — brighter, over the western horizon
D — fainter, over the western horizon
questions.why: At dawn the eastern horizon sharpens first and faint stars fade first: start with faint eastern stars, finish with bright ones in the west.

questions.q: At 0300 a bright Moon lights the sea to the south; elsewhere the horizon is lost in the dark. Which body gives you a usable sight?

figure.title: Night sky, 0300
lines: Star Q: Zn 060° · Star R: Zn 300°

options: Stars Q and R — the best angle of cut
Star Q — the brightest star in the sky
Star P — its horizon is lit by the Moon
Star R — farthest from the Moon's glare
questions.why: At night a sight needs a horizon you can see, and only the sea under the Moon shows one: take the Moon and stars near its bearing.

questions.q: Ashore before the voyage, you practise with an artificial horizon, bringing the Sun and its reflection together. What is the apparent altitude of the Sun's centre?

figure.title: Artificial horizon on the quay
lines: Tray of oil, sheltered from the wind
Sun and its reflection made to coincide

questions.why: Correct the reading for IE first, then halve it: (71°36.4′ − 1.2′) ÷ 2 = 35°47.6′. No dip — the oil surface is truly level.

questions.q: Bound from Cape Town to St Helena, you take Canopus at dusk and correct it with the almanac's tables. What is Ho?
questions.why: 38°42.0′ + 0.9′ − 3.0′ = Ha 38°39.9′, inside the row; − 1.2′ = Ho 38°38.7′. A star needs no SD or parallax.

questions.q: In the South Atlantic in January it is high summer. Which column of the almanac's Sun table do you use?
options: Apr–Sept — it is summer in the south
Oct–Mar — the column goes by the date
Either — the two columns are the same
questions.why: The columns follow the Earth–Sun distance, not the local season: in January the Sun is nearest and its SD largest, in both hemispheres.

questions.q: The horizon is a little soft, so you measure the index error four times. What correction do you apply?
questions.why: Give each reading its sign (on −, off +): (+0.6 − 0.2 + 0.8 + 0.4) ÷ 4 = +0.4′, a mean of 0.4′ off the arc, so add it.

questions.q: You watch a new crew member take the Sun without rocking the sextant; it leans a little to one side. What does that do to her sun line?

figure.title: Watching the crew's sight
lines: Lower limb set on the horizon there

options: No effect while the limb touches
Hs too small — the line too far away
Hs too large — the line too far away
Hs too large — the line too far towards
questions.why: A tilted sextant measures down to a point of the horizon off to one side, a larger angle than the altitude: Ho too big, the line towards the Sun.

questions.q: Each time you bring Sirius down from the sky you lose it in the mirror. What is the other way to get it onto the horizon?

figure.title: Twilight star sight
lines: Index at 0°, star in the telescope
Lost each time you swing the arm

options: Hold the sextant upside down and bring the horizon up
Use more index shades so the star stands out
Bring it down faster, before the boat rolls
Defocus the telescope so the star looks bigger
questions.why: Inverted, the sextant shows the star direct and the horizon reflected: lift the horizon to the star, turn the sextant upright and fine-tune.

questions.q: In the morning the Sun climbs quickly. How do you get a clean contact of the lower limb?
options: Set the limb just above and wait for it to sink
Set the limb just below the horizon; mark as it rises to touch
Bring it down fast and mark the first contact
Keep turning the drum until you see it touch
questions.why: A rising Sun brings itself to the horizon: set the limb a touch low, keep rocking, and mark the instant it just kisses the horizon.

questions.q: With the index error removed, you look at the horizon and tilt the sextant like this. What does it show?

figure.title: Checking on the horizon
lines: Set so the horizon is one line
Tilted 45° to the left, then the right
The horizon stays one unbroken line

questions.why: If the horizon mirror leans, tilting the sextant breaks the horizon into a step. An unbroken line at any tilt means no side error.

questions.q: In mid-Pacific the micrometer drum turns stiffly and feels gritty. What do you do?

figure.title: Sextant after a month at sea
lines: Salt crystals on the rack teeth

options: Leave it — the grit beds in after a while
Tighten the clamp until it runs smoothly
Clean the rack and worm, then a drop of light oil
questions.why: Salt and grit on the rack wear the worm and spoil readings: brush them off, wipe clean, and put a trace of light oil on the worm and rack.

questions.q: You borrow an older vernier sextant for the passage. What does it read?
questions.why: The arc to the last division passed, 46°40′, plus the vernier's 3′20″: 46°43′20″, and 20″ = 0.3′, so 46°43.3′.

questions.q: Through dark index shades and a horizon shade the Sun is a crisp disc, but the horizon under it has almost vanished. What do you change?

figure.title: Sun sight, late afternoon
lines: Index shades: the two darkest in
Horizon under the Sun: barely visible

options: Lift the index shades, keep the horizon one
Lift the horizon shade; try a lighter index shade
Add a darker horizon shade for contrast
Fit the star telescope to gather more light
questions.why: Horizon shades darken the sea too: use them only against glare. Dim the Sun with index shades just enough to see both images clearly.

questions.q: On a catamaran bound for Tahiti, you measure the index error on the Sun, then take the sight from the flybridge. What is Ho?

figure.title: Sun, 5 March, flybridge
lines: IE by the Sun: on 33.6′, off 31.2′

questions.q: Bound for Greenland through the Denmark Strait, you take Mars low in the twilight. What is Ho?
Off the Galápagos a crew member works up this Moon sight to cross with the morning sun line. What should Ho be?

figure.title: Moon UL, the crew's working
lines: Only the upper limb is lit

questions.why: Upper limb: the SD is subtracted. 33°05.0′ − 1.5′ + 51.1′ − 16.6′ = Ho 33°38.0′; the crew's line was 33 M too far towards the Moon.

questions.q: At dawn you take six sights of a setting star, plot them against time and fit a line. What Hs do you take off the line for 06:48:00 UT?

figure.title: Six sights of a setting star
lines: UT and Hs; the star dropping steadily

questions.why: The star drops about 8.8′ a minute; 06:47:19 sits 6′ off the line — drop it. The line through the other five reads 27°35.6′ at 06:48:00.

questions.q: On 18 June, some minutes before local noon near the Tropic of Cancer, you work up this sight of a very high Sun. What radius do you draw round the Sun's GP?
questions.why: 86°50.4′ − 0.4′ − 2.9′ + 15.7′ = Ho 87°02.8′; zenith distance 90° − Ho = 2°57.2′ = 177′, so a 177 M circle round the GP.

questions.q: You check the crew's star sight against the sextant, still untouched since the sight. What intercept should they plot?
questions.why: The index is short of 42°, so Hs is 41°57.3′: + 0.8′ − 2.8′ − 1.1′ = Ho 41°54.2′; minus Hc 41°49.6′ = 4.6 M towards.

questions.q: A breaking wave threw the open sextant box across the saloon. Star sights are due soon. Which instrument do you use?

figure.title: After the fall
lines: Metal sextant: IE 5.8′ to 7.2′ on, unsteady
Its index arm wobbles on the arc
Plastic backup: IE 2.0′ off, steady 3 times

options: The plastic backup, its IE checked at each sight
The metal one, with the mean IE of 6.5′ on
Both, and average the two sextants' altitudes
The metal one, after adjusting its index mirror
questions.why: An IE that wanders and a loose arm mean damage the mirror screws can't fix: use the steady backup tonight and get the metal sextant repaired.

questions.q: Early in the dusk the sky is still bright. Which three stars do you take for the fix?

figure.title: Dusk: magnitude, Zn, Hc
lines: Telescope shows mag 1.0 or brighter now

questions.why: Bright enough for the telescope (A, E, D), between 15° and 70° high (not C at 72°), and about 120° apart in bearing: A 050°, E 180°, D 290°.

questions.q: You and a crew member take the Sun's lower limb at the same moment, each with your own sextant. After IE and dip, how far apart are your altitudes?
With the dip in doubt over the Gulf Stream, you take two stars on opposite bearings from the same AP. What do the intercepts tell you?
questions.why: A common error e adds to both: e = (4.2 + 1.8) ÷ 2 = 3.0′ too high; the true position is (4.2 − 1.8) ÷ 2 = 1.2 M from the AP towards 010°.

questions.q: You are halfway across on the ARC, converting the almanac's LMT to UT by hand. What is your longitude in time?
Your ship's clocks keep the Caribbean zone time. What do you write in the UT column of the log?
questions.why: West longitude, ZD +4: UT = zone time + ZD = 1530 + 4 h = 1930.

questions.q: You take a sun sight on the passage from Bermuda to the Azores. What UT goes into the reduction?

figure.title: Deck watch
lines: Error on GPS this morning: 12 s fast

questions.why: A fast watch shows too much: UT = 14 23 10 − 12 s = 14 22 58.

questions.q: Checking the watch after landfall, you find it was 8 seconds out during the last day's sights. How much longitude error did that put in your sun lines?

figure.title: After landfall
lines: Not applied to the last day's sights

questions.why: The Earth turns 15′ of arc per minute of time: 4 s = 1′ of longitude, so 8 s = 2′.

questions.q: Bound west from Tonga to Fiji, you cross the 180th meridian at 2100 on Tuesday 9 June, ship's time. What do you write in the log a moment later?
questions.why: Westbound across 180° the date goes forward a day (ZD +12 becomes −12); the clock time stays the same.

questions.q: Your logs hold noon sights from passages all through the year, and the almanac's Mer Pass for the Sun moves. Why?
options: The true Sun runs ahead of or behind the mean Sun
The Earth's spin speeds up and slows down
The ship's clocks are changed for summer time
questions.why: Mean time runs evenly, the true Sun does not (elliptic orbit, tilted axis): the difference is the equation of time, up to ~16 min.

questions.q: Your crew asks whether the radio's UTC must be corrected before you open the almanac. What do you tell them?
options: Apply the zone description to it first
Add 37 s to it to get UT
Use it as UT; the difference is under a second
Add 18 s to it to get UT
questions.why: UTC is kept within 0.9 s of UT; 0.9 s is about 0.2′ of longitude, below what a sextant can give.

questions.q: Your crew keeps the deck log in ship's time, which changes as you go west. Which time do you write against every sight and fix?

figure.title: Nav log, day 9
lines: Ship's clocks retarded 1 h last night
Crew log events in ship's time

options: Ship's time, as the crew does
The zone time of the port you left
UT, read from the deck watch
questions.why: Sights and fixes are worked in UT; ship's time jumps an hour at every zone change, UT never does.

questions.q: You are alone on deck at dawn with the sextant, and the deck watch is below at the chart table. How do you time the star sight?
options: Start a stopwatch at the sight; compare it with the watch later
Note the minute only; the seconds hardly matter
Take the time of the plotter's last GPS fix
Read the watch when you get back to the chart table
questions.why: Start the stopwatch at the instant of the sight, then subtract its reading from the watch time; never guess the seconds.

questions.q: You work a sun sight by hand. How do you get the GHA for the moment of the sight?
options: The 14h GHA plus 0°23′10″ for the minutes
The 14h GHA plus the increment for 23m 10s
The 14h GHA plus the v correction for 23m
The 14h GHA alone; minutes are below sextant accuracy
questions.why: The daily page gives GHA for each whole hour; the increments page adds the minutes and seconds (15° an hour for the Sun).

questions.q: South of Hispaniola with the GPS down, you time the moment the Sun stops rising at noon. What longitude does that give you?
questions.why: 16 37 20 − 12 00 00 = 4h 37m 20s: 60° + 9°15′ + 5′ = 69°20′, west because local noon comes after Greenwich's.

questions.q: You plan the evening star sights off the Queensland coast. At what UT does the Sun set?
questions.why: 147°45′ = 9h 51m; east longitude: UT = LMT − 9h 51m = 1735 − 0951 = 0744 UT, the same date.
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: You keep ship's time by the zone you are in. Which zone description belongs to this noon position?
questions.why: Zone +3 runs from 37°30′W to 52°30′W, centred on 45°W; 37°40′W is just inside it.

questions.q: You want to compare the deck watch with a radio time signal. What UT and date is it now?
questions.why: East longitude, ZD −10: UT = 0930 − 10 h = 2330 on the day before, 13 May.

questions.q: You sail the ARC from Las Palmas to Rodney Bay and keep ship's time by the zone you are in. How do the clocks change on the way?
options: Retard 4 h, an hour each at 15°W, 30°W, 45°W and 60°W
Advance 3 h, an hour each at 22°30′W, 37°30′W and 52°30′W
Retard 3 h, an hour each at 22°30′W, 37°30′W and 52°30′W
Retard 3 h, an hour each at 30°W, 45°W and 60°W
questions.why: Westbound the zones go from +1 to +4: retard an hour at each boundary, 7°30′ past each multiple of 15°.

questions.q: You keep zone time on the passage east. What do you do with the ship's clocks now?
questions.why: Eastbound you enter zone +3 at 52°30′W: advance the clocks an hour; the ZD falls by one.

questions.q: You clear in at Horta, and the office closes at 1730 local time. What time is it ashore as you tie up?
questions.why: UT = 1500 + 2 h = 1700; the Azores keep UT +0 in summer, so it is 1700 ashore.
questions.ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

questions.q: After the Puddle Jump you anchor in Taiohae Bay. What is the local time ashore?
questions.why: UT = 1400 + 9 h = 2300; the Marquesas keep UT −9 h 30 m: 2300 − 0930 = 1330 local.
questions.ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

questions.q: You are on passage to Fiji and join the cruisers' SSB net. When do you switch the radio on, by ship's time?
questions.why: ZD −12: ship's time = UT + 12 h = 0300 + 12 h = 1500 on the same Thursday.

questions.q: On 16 November you still have no time signal. What are the watch's daily rate and its error now?
options: Losing 2 s a day; 3 s fast
Gaining 14 s a day; 115 s fast
Gaining 2.4 s a day; 34 s fast
Gaining 2 s a day; 31 s fast
questions.why: (17 − 3) s / 7 days = gaining 2 s a day; 17 s + 7 × 2 s = 31 s fast on 16 Nov.

questions.q: You check the deck watch against the GPS just before a morning sun sight. What UT do you use for the sight?
questions.why: The watch is 7 s ahead of the GPS, so 7 s fast: 09 41 18 − 7 s = 09 41 11 UT.

questions.q: Mid-Atlantic, your watch is 20 seconds fast and you do not know it. Where does that put your positions from sun lines?

figure.title: Celestial-only passage
lines: Sun lines worked with that time

questions.why: Too late a UT gives too big a GHA; west longitude = GHA − LHA comes out 20 s × 15″ = 5′ too far west.

questions.q: Your crew set the deck watch from the plotter, which shows GPS time. What error does that put in your longitude?
questions.why: GPS time runs 18 s ahead of UTC (no leap seconds); 18 s × 15″ = 270″ = 4.5′ of longitude.

questions.q: You need a reliable time check for your sights. Where do you get it?

figure.title: Day 12, no GPS
lines: Plotter and both GPS sets dead

options: The VHF's log of the last DSC call
The bulkhead clock, set before departure
The laptop clock, synced in port
Time signals on the SSB, e.g. WWV on 10 MHz
questions.why: Shortwave time stations (WWV/WWVH on 5, 10, 15 MHz) give UTC to the second; clocks set weeks ago have unknown errors.

questions.q: Alone on deck, you time a sun sight this way. What is the UT of the sight?
questions.why: 10 15 00 − 1m 37s = 10 13 23 by the watch; it is 4 s fast, so UT 10 13 19.
