questions.q: Your crew misread the minute when calling the time of a sun sight. How big an error does that put in your longitude?
questions.why: The Sun's GHA moves 15° an hour, 15′ a minute: one minute of time wrong moves the line 15′ of longitude.

questions.q: Bound east from New Zealand to Tahiti, you cross the 180th meridian on Friday 15 May, ship's time. What date goes in the log after the next midnight?
questions.why: Eastbound across 180° you repeat a day (ZD −12 becomes +12): Friday 15 May comes twice.

questions.q: Bound west from Suwarrow to Samoa, you take a star sight at dusk. Which almanac page and hour do you open?
questions.why: ZD +11: UT = 1850 + 11 h = 0550 the next day: the 5 May page, the 05h row.

questions.q: Approaching Suva, you take a morning sun sight. With which date and time do you enter the almanac?
questions.why: ZD −12: UT = 0745 − 12 h = 1945 on 14 March; the almanac is entered with the UT date, not the ship's.

questions.q: Between Tahiti and the Cook Islands you download a GRIB file. At what ship's time is this forecast valid?
questions.why: ZD +10: ship's time = UT − 10 h = 1200 − 10 h = 0200 on the same date.

questions.q: On the ARC you work a sun sight by hand. What is the Sun's GHA at the moment of the sight?
In the Indian Ocean at dawn you take a star sight. What is GHA Aries at the moment of the sight?
In the trade winds on the day of the equinox you work a sun sight. Which declination do you use?
questions.why: d 1.0′ an hour × 48/60 = 0.8′ northward: S 0°00.6′ − 0.8′ crosses the equator, Dec N 0°00.2′.

questions.q: West of the Cape Verdes you plan the noon sight. At what UT does the Sun cross your meridian?
questions.why: Mer Pass is LMT: 23°15′W = 1h 33m; west, so UT = 1144 + 0133 = 1317 UT.
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: Leaving Cape Town for St Helena, you want a noon sight. What is the UT of local noon?
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: A crew member says you must also apply the equation of time to the Mer Pass to get local noon. When is local noon, in LMT?
questions.why: The Mer Pass is already 1200 + 14m 13s with the EoT applied; only your longitude is left, to turn it into UT.

questions.q: On the ARC you want the watch called for sunrise. At what ship's time does the Sun rise?
questions.why: UT = 0625 + 2h 44m = 0909; ship's time = 0909 − 3 h = 0609, 16 min before LMT since you are east of 45°W.
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: You want to be on deck with the sextant when morning nautical twilight begins. What ship's time is that?
questions.why: UT = 0536 − 3h 50m = 0146; ship's time = 0146 + 4 h = 0546, 10 min after LMT since you are west of 60°E.
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: Bound from Rio towards Tristan da Cunha, you plan the dusk star sights. At what UT does the Sun set?
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: You arrive at the marina in Mindelo. What time is it ashore?

figure.title: Mindelo, Cape Verde
lines: Cape Verde keeps UT −1 all year

questions.why: UT = 1000 + 2 h = 1200; the islands keep UT −1, so 1100 ashore: legal time need not match the nautical zone.
questions.ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

questions.q: Between the Cook Islands and Niue you plan the dusk star sights. What are the UT and the date of sunset?
questions.why: 165° = 11h 00m; west, so UT = 1823 + 11 h = 0523 UT on the next day, 4 March.
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: The GPS has been dead since 1 December. What UT do you use for this sight?
questions.why: 6 s slow, then 20 days × 1.5 s gained = 30 s: now 24 s fast; UT = 10 14 32 − 24 s = 10 14 08.

questions.q: Approaching the Bay of Biscay you find the watch was 30 seconds slow for the whole crossing. How far, and which way, is your fix wrong?

figure.title: Bound for Brittany, lat 48°N
lines: Fix from sun and star lines

questions.why: 30 s = 7.5′ of longitude; a slow watch puts you east; 7.5′ × cos 48° = 5.0 M on the ground.

questions.q: You plan your arrival in Tonga and book the customs officer. What will the local time and date be when you arrive?
questions.why: UT out 1800 on 1 June + 7 d 2 h = 2000 UT on 8 June; Tonga keeps UT +13: 0900 on 9 June.

questions.q: You take the first star of the morning round. Which almanac entries do you use?

figure.title: Dawn stars, Indian Ocean
lines: Deck watch keeps UT, 3 s slow

questions.why: 23 59 58 + 3 s = 00 00 01 UT on 7 Nov: the 00h row of 7 Nov plus the increment for 1 second.

questions.q: On your way into the South Atlantic you plan the dusk star sights. At what ship's time does the Sun set?
questions.why: 5°N is halfway: 1742 LMT; UT = 1742 + 2h 20m = 2002; ship's time = 2002 − 2 h = 1802.
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: You want to time the noon sight exactly, to get a longitude from it. At what UT does the Sun cross your meridian?

figure.title: Noon to the second, 4 November
lines: EoT 16m 29s, Sun ahead of mean time

questions.q: At the end of the ARC you work a sun sight timed by the cockpit watch. What is the Sun's GHA?

figure.title: Almanac, 10 December
lines: Watch on ship's time (ZD +3), 5 s slow

questions.q: You want to close the coast after sunrise. What will the ship's clock show when the Sun rises?
questions.why: UT = 0612 + 4h 04m = 1016; on ZD +3 the clock shows 1016 − 3 h = 0716 (0616 only after you go to ZD +4).
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: You plan the evening star sights for the window between civil and nautical twilight. What is that window by ship's time?
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: Closing Western Australia from Mauritius, you turn the almanac's LMT of sunrise into UT. How much time does your longitude give, and which way do you apply it?

figure.title: DR, approaching Fremantle
lines: Almanac sunrise is given in LMT

questions.why: 115° × 4 min = 460 min, 45′ = 3 min: 7h 43m. East of Greenwich LMT is ahead of UT, so UT = LMT − 7h 43m.

questions.q: On passage to the Maldives you log a fix taken at this time. What UT goes beside it?
questions.why: East longitude, ZD −5: UT = zone time + ZD = 1400 − 5 h = 0900. The ZD, not the exact longitude, sets ship's time.

questions.q: Running south well off the Brazilian coast, you take an afternoon sun sight. What UT goes into the reduction?

figure.title: Deck watch
lines: Compared with GPS at noon: 9 s slow

questions.why: A slow watch shows too little: add the error. UT = 16 05 54 + 9 s = 16 06 03.

questions.q: Bound west from Niue for Fiji, you cross the 180th meridian tonight and change the ship's date. What do you do with the deck watch you keep on UT?
options: Put its date forward a day with the ship's
Nothing — UT and its date run on unchanged
Reset it to the new zone time, ZD −12
Put its date back a day for the crossing
questions.why: The date line changes zone time and the ship's date only; UT is the same on both sides, so the deck watch and its date are left alone.

questions.q: You check the deck watch against the hourly time signal on the radio. At which moment is it exactly the hour?

figure.title: Broadcast time signal
lines: Five short pips, then one long one

options: At the start of the first pip
At the end of the fifth, short pip
At the start of the sixth, long pip
At the end of the sixth, long pip
questions.why: The pips count down the last five seconds; the hour is the start of the last, longer pip.

questions.q: Last night you watched the Moon cross your meridian. About when will it cross tonight?
questions.why: The Moon moves east round the sky about 13° a day, so it reaches your meridian some 50 min later each day (40–66 min).

questions.q: Your rate book shows the deck watch gaining faster since you reached the tropics. What is the likely cause, and what do you do?

figure.title: Rate book
lines: Falmouth to Madeira: gaining 0.4 s a day
Since the Cape Verdes: gaining 1.6 s a day
Watch kept in the chart table

options: Heat; use the new rate from recent checks
A failing battery; average the two rates
Magnetism; move it from the chart table
Zone changes; add 1 s per hour retarded
questions.why: A quartz watch's rate changes with temperature: predict its error with the rate measured in the present climate.

questions.q: You work a dawn sight of Canopus by hand. Which increment do you add to the 03h GHA of Aries?
questions.why: Stars go through GHA Aries, which turns 15°02.46′ an hour, so it has its own column; the seconds count too (4 s = 1′).

questions.q: Westbound on the trade-wind crossing, you retard the clocks tonight. How long is watch B on deck?
questions.why: At 0200 the clock goes back to 0100: B stands 0000 to 0400 by the clock, which is 5 hours of real time.
questions.ref: Time — ship's time and the watch rota

questions.q: Your old handheld GPS from the grab bag shows this. What do you take from its display?

figure.title: Spare handheld GPS
lines: Time agrees with the radio signal

options: Nothing; its clock is corrupt as well
Its time less 19 years of leap seconds
Its date and time; a GPS is never wrong
Its time of day; the date comes from the log
questions.why: An old receiver's week counter rolls over after 1024 weeks: the date jumps back 19.6 years, but the time of day stays right.

questions.q: Between Cocos Keeling and Christmas Island with the GPS down, you time the Sun at its highest. What longitude does that give?

figure.title: Noon, 15 February
lines: Watch checked on the radio today

questions.why: Local noon = 12 00 00 + 14m 08s = 12 14 08 LMT; less 05 31 44 UT = 6h 42m 24s east = 100°36′E.

questions.q: Crossing the Indian Ocean from Cocos Keeling to Rodrigues, you plan the ship's clock changes for the crew. What are they?
questions.why: Westbound the zones go from −6 to −4: retard an hour at each boundary, 82°30′E and 67°30′E (7°30′ past 75° and 60°).

questions.q: On the last clock change watch B stood five hours, and three more changes come before St Lucia. How do you plan them?

figure.title: ARC rota, westbound
lines: Clocks back 1 h four times on passage
Last change at 0200: B stood 5 h

options: Give B the extra hour each time, then a lie-in
Retard the full hour at 0200 each time, as before
Retard 20 minutes in each of the three night watches
Advance the clocks instead, and catch up at landfall
questions.why: Retarding 20 min in each night watch shares the hour: each watch stands 4h 20m, and no one stands five hours.
questions.ref: Time — ship's time and the watch rota

questions.q: On passage from Richards Bay to Mauritius the boat crosses a zone boundary on this watch. What happens to the ship's clocks?
questions.why: Eastbound the clocks go forward an hour at each boundary; in east longitude the ZD grows more negative: −2 becomes −3.

questions.q: Off New Caledonia on New Year's morning you take a sun sight. Which almanac and which page do you open?
questions.why: ZD −11: UT = 0730 − 11 h = 2030 on 31 December 2026 — the last page of last year's almanac.

questions.q: Approaching Port Vila, you note the time of sunrise in the log in UT. What UT and date do you write?
questions.why: 168°E = 11h 12m; UT = 0535 − 11h 12m = 1823 on the day before, 9 October. East of Greenwich, UT is behind.
questions.ref: Time — sunrise, sunset and twilight in UT

questions.q: Off the Brazilian coast at 20°S you plan the evening star sights. Which planets can you add to them?
questions.why: Venus and Mars cross with the Sun and are lost in its glare; at dusk Saturn is high in the west and Jupiter low in the east.
questions.ref: Time — planets' and stars' meridian passage

questions.q: Bound for Reykjavik in June, you look up tonight's star sights in the almanac. What does it tell you?
options: The Sun stays up: take sun lines all night too
The data is missing: interpolate from 60°N
Twilight lasts all night: shoot stars at any hour
The sky never gets dark: plan on sun lines, not stars
questions.why: //// means the Sun never gets 6° below the horizon at 64°N: no dark sky with a horizon for stars; the Sun is up 21 hours.

questions.q: You arrive at Puerto Williams in the Beagle Channel for Christmas. At what time by the clocks ashore does the Sun set?

figure.title: Puerto Williams, 20 December
lines: Ship's clock ZD +5; Chile keeps UT −3

questions.why: UT = 2039 + 4h 30m = 0109 the next day; ashore UT − 3 h = 2209: far south at midsummer, on a zone east of its longitude.
questions.ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

questions.q: In the Bay of Bengal you want the Moon on your meridian for a latitude. At what UT does it cross tonight?
questions.why: East: use the difference from the day before, 45 min × 90/360 = 11 min earlier: 2014 LMT; UT = 2014 − 6 h = 1414.

questions.q: Under the midnight sun off Svalbard you want to time the Sun at its lowest, due north. At what UT does that come?

figure.title: Off Svalbard, night of 24–25 June
lines: The Sun stays about 9° up all night

questions.why: Lower transit at 0000 LMT + 2m 35s = 0003 LMT on 25 June; 15°E is 1 h, so UT = 2303 on 24 June.

questions.q: Off Mauritius before dawn you want Jupiter on your meridian for a latitude. At what ship's time does it cross?
questions.why: A planet's Mer Pass is LMT, much the same at any longitude: UT = 0421 − 3h 52m = 0029; ship's time = UT + 4 h = 0429.
questions.ref: Time — planets' and stars' meridian passage

questions.q: In the Indian Ocean in February you plan to catch Sirius as it crosses your meridian. When is that by the ship's clock?
questions.ref: Time — planets' and stars' meridian passage

questions.q: The GPS failed a week ago. Before the morning sights you compare your three watches. Which one do you set aside, and what is UT?

figure.title: Watch comparison
lines: Rate book (+ fast): A +20 s, B −5 s, C +8 s

questions.why: Corrected, A and B both give 10 00 00 and C gives 10 00 30: C has jumped, and the two that agree give UT.

questions.q: You carry two deck watches and compare them every morning. Today they disagree. What do you conclude?

figure.title: Two watches, day 10 without GPS
lines: A gains 1.0 s a day, B loses 0.5 s a day
Predicted A − B = 22 s; today 52 s

options: A has jumped 30 s; it has the bigger rate
Each is 15 s out; split the difference
One has jumped 30 s; a time signal must decide
Both are right; the heat changed the rates
questions.why: Two watches show only their difference: one has jumped 30 s, but which one takes a third clock or a radio time signal.

questions.q: Six days after the last GPS check, deep in the trades, you need the deck watch error for a sight. What is it now?

figure.title: Rate book
lines: Rate at 15 °C: gaining 0.5 s a day
Rate in the tropics: gaining 1.8 s a day
Six warm days since the check

questions.why: Use the rate for the temperature it is running at: 4 s + 6 × 1.8 s = 14.8 s, so 15 s fast.

questions.q: In the Indian Ocean at 70°E your watch is 12 seconds fast and you do not know it. What does that do to the longitude of your fixes?

figure.title: Indian Ocean, no GPS
lines: Sun and star lines worked with it

options: 3′ too small — the fix lies too far west
12′ too large — the fix lies too far east
3′ too large — the fix lies too far east
12′ too small — the fix lies too far west
questions.why: Too late a time makes GHA too big; LHA = GHA + long E, so the east longitude comes out 3′ (12 s ÷ 4) too small: too far west.

questions.q: In the Southern Ocean at 60°S you want each sun line good to a mile east–west. How large a watch error can you accept?
questions.why: At 60° a mile of easting is 1′ ÷ cos 60° = 2′ of longitude, and 2′ of longitude is 8 s of time.

questions.q: Checking the watch on a radio signal, you find it was two minutes wrong all yesterday. Which of yesterday's results can you still trust?
options: The running fix from all three
questions.why: A meridian altitude needs no exact time, only the Dec, which barely moves in 2 min; the sun lines are 30′ of longitude out.

questions.q: At dawn you shoot three stars alone, timing them with the stopwatch's lap button. What UT do you write for the second star?
questions.why: The watch read 06 12 00 at UT 06 12 03; the second lap adds 4m 51s: UT 06 16 54.

questions.q: You take a star at the very end of the hour. What is GHA Aries for the sight?
questions.why: 02h row plus the Aries increment for 59m 59s, 15°02.2′: 83°11.6′ + 15°02.2′ = 98°13.8′, a hair short of the 03h value.

questions.q: Heading for the Cape Verdes in February you work a sun sight. Which declination do you use?
questions.why: The d correction for 37m at d 0.7 is 0.4′; the Dec is falling, so subtract: S 16°42.9′ − 0.4′ = S 16°42.5′.

questions.q: Arriving in the Galápagos from Panama, you want to enter Academy Bay after sunrise. When does the Sun rise ashore, and by your ship's clock?

figure.title: Santa Cruz, Galápagos, 15 Feb
lines: Islands keep UT −6; ship still UT −5

questions.why: UT = 0610 + 6h 01m = 1211; ashore UT − 6 h = 0611; your clock, still on Panama's UT − 5, shows 0711.
questions.ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

questions.q: After the passage from Tonga you berth at the Opua quarantine dock in November. Customs want you before 1700 New Zealand time. What is the time ashore now?
questions.why: UT = 1500 − 12 h = 0300; New Zealand summer time is UT + 13: 1600 ashore, an hour ahead of your zone time.
questions.ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

questions.q: Looking at the almanac's Sun column in July, a crew member asks why the GHA at 12h is not 0°. When is the Sun actually on the Greenwich meridian?
questions.why: It still needs 1°38.4′ to reach 360°: at 15° an hour that is 6m 34s, so 12 06 34 UT. That gap is the equation of time.

questions.q: Two yachts in company talk on the SSB either side of 180°, each keeping its zone time. At 0003 UT on Thursday 12 November, what does each write in its log?

figure.title: Either side of the date line
lines: Radio call at 0003 UT, Thu 12 Nov

questions.why: West of 180° (ZD −12): 0003 + 12 h = 1203 Thursday; east of it (ZD +12): 0003 − 12 h = 1203 Wednesday. Same clock, a day apart.

questions.q: Running east at 48°S towards New Zealand at midsummer, you plan the evening stars. What window between civil and nautical twilight do you plan for?
questions.why: Interpolate 3/5 of the way from 45°S to 50°S: civil 2042, nautical 2142 LMT. An hour, twice the tropics: the Sun sets at a slant.

questions.q: You keep a rate book from the radio time signals. What daily rate do you write in it?
questions.why: 7.2 s gained in 4½ days, from 3 Nov 0800 to 7 Nov 2000: 7.2 ÷ 4.5 = gaining 1.6 s a day.

questions.q: Your morning sun sight works out to this LHA. How long until the Sun crosses your meridian for the noon sight?

figure.title: Morning sun sight, worked
lines: The Sun's LHA grows 15° an hour

questions.why: The Sun is 360° − 341°15′ = 18°45′ east of your meridian; at 15° an hour, 18°45′ is 1h 15m.

questions.q: Mid-Pacific, you take the time from WWV some 4000 miles away. How much does the radio signal's travel time matter?
options: About 0.5 s; subtract it from UT
About 0.02 s, far below sight accuracy
About 4 s, a whole minute of longitude
About 2 s, half a minute of longitude
questions.why: 4000 M is about 7400 km; ÷ 300 000 km/s ≈ 0.025 s ≈ 0.006′ of longitude: ignore it.

questions.q: Bound for the Marquesas, you plan a Sun–Moon fix with the Moon on your meridian. At what time by the ship's clock does it cross?
The GPS has been dead since 1 November, and you have sailed from Biscay into the trades. What UT do you use for this sight?

figure.title: Rate book, Biscay to the trades
lines: 1 Nov: watch 2 s slow (last GPS check)
1–10 Nov, cool: gaining 0.6 s a day
From 10 Nov, tropics: gaining 2.1 s a day

questions.q: Bound west from Tonga for the Lau group of Fiji, you keep ZD +12 and plan the noon sight. At what UT is local noon, and on which almanac date?
questions.why: UT = 1213 + 11h 54m = 2407, so 0007 UT on 27 January: just past UT midnight, the almanac date is a day ahead of the ship's.

questions.q: Approaching Orkney from the Atlantic at midsummer, you want the time of sunrise for the morning sights. What is it in UT?
questions.why: 59°10′N is 70/120 of the way to 60°N: 0256 − 11.7 min ≈ 0244 LMT; 4°30′W = 18 min, so 0302 UT. Up here it moves fast.

questions.q: Closing Rodrigues from Cocos, you want a dawn star fix before the reef pass. When does morning nautical twilight begin by your ship's clock, and what time is it ashore then?

figure.title: Rodrigues, 15 September
lines: Ship still on ZD −6; island keeps UT +4

questions.ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

questions.q: You have sailed from Opua to Papeete and want the true passage time for the log's summary. How long were you at sea?

figure.title: Opua to Papeete
lines: Left 0800 Fri 1 May, NZ time UT +12

questions.why: In UT you left at 2000 on 30 April and arrived at 1800 on 15 May: 14 days 22 hours. The repeated day makes the dates look short.

questions.q: South of Java at dawn you take a star by the cockpit watch, which keeps ship's time. What is GHA Aries for the sight?

figure.title: Almanac and watch
lines: Watch on ship's time, 4 s fast: 05 48 30

questions.q: With 12 days to go to Barbados and no time signal, you know the watch's rate only to a second a day either way. How far off could your longitude be at landfall?

figure.title: Landfall planning, no GPS
lines: Rate known to ±1 s a day

questions.why: 12 days × 1 s = 12 s = 3′ of longitude; at 15°N, 3′ × cos 15° = 2.9 M east or west. The latitude is not affected.

questions.q: You leave Neiafu for Savusavu and tell friends in Fiji when to expect you. At what local time, and on which day, will you arrive?
questions.why: UT out = 1900 Friday; + 2 d 5 h = 0000 UT Monday; Fiji is UT + 12: 1200 Monday. The date line bends east round Tonga.
questions.ref: Time — shore time and ship's time

questions.q: Before a sight you compare the deck watch with the chronometer below. What is the UT of the sight?

figure.title: Chronometer and deck watch
lines: Its rate: losing 1.5 s a day

questions.why: Chronometer now 5 + 4 × 1.5 = 11 s slow; the watch reads 13 s more, so it is 2 s fast: UT = 10 41 27 − 2 s = 10 41 25.

questions.q: You are on the ARC route, the GPS has failed and you want a noon latitude. At what UT is the Sun on your meridian?
questions.why: Mer Pass 1148 LMT + 35°20′ of west longitude in time (2h21m) = 1409 UT; longitude west is added.

questions.q: On passage from Cocos Keeling to Mauritius you plan the noon sight. At what UT do you expect the Sun on your meridian?
questions.why: Mer Pass 1205 LMT − 72°45′ of east longitude in time (4h51m) = 0714 UT; longitude east is subtracted.

questions.q: Your ship's clock keeps zone time +3 and you want to call the navigator on deck for noon. What will the ship's clock show at meridian passage?
questions.why: 1153 + 3h09m for 47°10′W = 1502 UT; zone +3 means ship's time = UT − 3 h = 1202.

questions.q: You are running west in the trades and want the UT of noon, allowing for your run. When will the Sun be on your meridian?
questions.why: First guess 1149 + 2h40m = 1429; 4.5 h at 7 kn = 31 M = 33′ of longitude W → 40°33′W → 1149 + 2h42m = 1431 UT.

questions.q: Your noon is predicted for 1409 UT. How do you take the meridian altitude?

figure.title: Noon sight
lines: Watch checked against UT this morning

options: Start ten minutes early and follow the Sun up until it stops rising
Start at 1409 UT and average the sights of the next ten minutes
Take one sight at exactly 1409 UT, timed to the second
Take sights from 1400 to 1420 UT and use the last one
questions.why: Before noon the Sun climbs ever more slowly: keep it on the horizon until it stops rising — that highest altitude is the meridian altitude.

questions.q: You follow the Sun up to noon and note these sextant readings. Which Hs do you reduce for your latitude?
questions.why: The meridian altitude is the maximum: 50°46.4′ at 1410. A mean of readings either side of noon always comes out low.

questions.q: Cloud covers the Sun through your predicted noon. At 1427 UT it comes out and you take a sight. What do you do with it?
options: Use it as the meridian altitude — the top is flat
Discard it — after noon a sight gives nothing
Reduce it as an ordinary sun sight for a position line
Add 18′ to it, a minute of arc for each minute late
questions.why: 18 minutes after noon the Sun has dropped some 15′: work it with LHA, Hc and an intercept as a normal sun line.

questions.q: Your noon sight on the ARC route gives this. Which working gives your latitude?
questions.why: Sun south of you: Lat = Dec + z. With Dec south (−21°22.1′): −21°22.1′ + 38°59.1′ = 17°37.0′N.

questions.q: Halfway from Bermuda to the Azores you take the noon sight on the longest day. What is your latitude?
Bound for Hawaii in July, you find the noon Sun bearing north of you. What is your latitude?
On the Puddle Jump, well out from the Galápagos, you take the noon sight. Where are you?
Sailing from St Helena to Ascension just before Christmas, you see the noon Sun south of you. What is your latitude?
Two days out of Cape Town for St Helena, the noon Sun bears north. What latitude do you plot?
Crossing the Bay of Bengal from Phuket to Sri Lanka in the NE monsoon, you take this noon sight but forget to note the Sun's bearing. What is your latitude?
questions.why: Dec is south and you are north of the equator, so the Sun bears south: Lat = Dec + z = −21°09.2′ + 28°17.5′ = 7°08.3′N.

questions.q: Your noon on the ARC route falls at 1409 UT. Which Dec do you use?
questions.why: Dec changes 0.4′ an hour and is increasing: for 9 minutes add 0.4′ × 9/60 = 0.06′, so S21°22.0′ becomes S21°22.1′.

questions.q: You are three minutes late for noon and take the sight anyway, treating it as the meridian altitude. How much lower than the true maximum is it?

figure.title: ARC route, 28 Nov 2026
lines: Noon (LAN) 1409 UT, you sight at 1412 UT

options: About 45′ — 15′ of arc per minute of time
About 1.3′ — it falls as fast as it rose
About 4.4′ — over a minute of arc per minute
About 0.4′ — the top of the curve is flat
questions.why: Near noon the altitude changes as the square of the time from noon: three minutes off costs only about 0.4′ here.

questions.q: At dusk between Bermuda and the Azores, Arcturus crosses your meridian bearing south. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Evening twilight, 20 Jun 2026
lines: Arcturus on the meridian, bearing south

questions.q: North of the Caribbean at evening twilight, you catch Capella on your meridian, bearing north. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Evening twilight, 1 Mar 2027
lines: Capella on the meridian, bearing north

questions.q: Bound for the Azores in early May, you take Jupiter on the meridian at dusk, bearing south. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Jupiter at dusk, 3 May 2027
lines: Jupiter on the meridian, bearing south

questions.why: A planet on the meridian works like the Sun: z = 18°06.5′, south of you, so Lat = Dec + z = 17°08.4′ + 18°06.5′ = 35°14.9′N.

questions.q: On the long leg to the Marquesas, Canopus crosses your meridian in evening twilight, bearing south. Where are you?

figure.title: Evening twilight, 15 Mar 2027
lines: Canopus on the meridian, bearing south

questions.q: Between the Azores and Lisbon at morning twilight, you take Kochab on the meridian below the pole. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Morning twilight, 25 Aug 2027
lines: Kochab at lower transit, bearing north

questions.why: Below the pole Lat = Ho + polar distance: 22°15.5′ + (90° − 74°04.0′ = 15°56.0′) = 38°11.5′N.

questions.q: Leaving Newport, Rhode Island, for the Azores, you want a star to take below the pole at twilight. Which of these is circumpolar at your latitude?
questions.why: Circumpolar when Dec exceeds the co-latitude, 90° − 41°30′ = 48°30′: only Dubhe (N61°38′) stays above the horizon below the pole.

questions.q: Bound from the BVI to Bermuda, you take Polaris at evening twilight. What is your latitude?
At morning twilight on the ARC route you take Polaris. With which LHA Aries do you enter the a0 table?
questions.why: LHA = GHA − west longitude: 171°44.8′ − 22°14′ = 149°30.8′. a0 comes from LHA Aries, a1 from latitude, a2 from the month.

questions.q: At dusk you want Polaris, but it is faint and the sky is still bright. How do you find it in the sextant?
options: Set your DR latitude on the sextant and sweep the horizon due north
Take the brightest star low in the north and use that
Wait for full darkness, when it is the brightest star in the north
Bring it down from overhead, as you would a bright star
questions.why: Polaris is only magnitude 2: preset its altitude (about your latitude), look due north, and it shows near the horizon in the scope.

questions.q: On the leg from Panama to the Galápagos, a crew member suggests a Polaris sight for latitude. What do you decide?

figure.title: Polaris, DR 4°10′N 084°W
lines: Haze low on the northern horizon

options: Take it — Polaris gives latitude anywhere north of the equator
Not worth it — a low, hazy sight with large refraction
Take it, and add the refraction instead of subtracting it
Take it — at low latitude a0, a1 and a2 are all zero
questions.why: Below about 10° refraction is large and uncertain and the horizon poor: use the noon Sun or a star well up for latitude.

questions.q: In the South Pacific you find the south celestial pole by eye from the Southern Cross and the Pointers. What does its altitude give you?
options: Your latitude to the minute, as Polaris does in the north
Your south latitude, after the a0, a1 and a2 corrections
A rough check on your south latitude, not a fix
Your longitude, if you note the time of the sight
questions.why: The pole's altitude equals your latitude, but with no bright star on it an estimate by eye can be a degree or more out.

questions.q: On your plotting sheet you have run the morning sun line up to noon and drawn the noon latitude. Which point is your noon position?
questions.why: The noon fix is where the run-up morning line (blue) cuts the noon latitude: A. B uses the line before it was run up.

questions.q: You want a noon position from this morning's sun line. How do you bring the morning line up to noon?
options: Move it 18.4 M along 250°, keeping its direction
Turn it east–west to lie like the noon line
Move it 18.4 M along the Sun's azimuth, 118°
questions.why: A position line is transferred by the run between the sights — course and distance made good — and keeps its direction.

questions.q: You are running down the latitude of Hiva Oa on the Puddle Jump, and today's noon sight puts you here. What do you do?

figure.title: Noon, latitude sailing
lines: About 400 M still to the west

options: Make good 6 M to the south
Make good 12 M to the south
Make good 24 M to the south
Make good 12 M to the north
questions.why: In the south 9°48′S is 12′ further from the equator than 9°36′S: 12′ of latitude is 12 M to make good to the south.

questions.q: You have reached the latitude of Bridgetown, Barbados, and are running down it to the west. How far have you still to go?
questions.why: Departure = DLo × cos lat = 151′ × cos 13°06′ = 147 M along the parallel.

questions.q: Later in the day you find you never applied the index error to your noon sight. How does that move your noon latitude?
questions.why: On the arc is subtracted, so your Ho was 2.4′ high and z 2.4′ small: Lat = Dec + z came out 2.4′ too far south.

questions.q: On the ARC route you want a star on the meridian for a latitude at dusk. Which of these can you take?
options: Fomalhaut — between civil and nautical twilight
Enif — as soon as it crosses the meridian
Altair — the brightest and highest of them
Alpheratz — in full darkness, stars are sharpest
questions.why: A star sight needs both the star and the horizon: only Fomalhaut crosses the meridian between 1750 and 1817.

questions.q: Bound from the Galápagos to the Marquesas, a crew member suggests a Polaris sight for latitude tonight. What do you tell them?
options: Only at midnight, when it is highest
It is below the horizon south of the equator
Fine, but add the 1° instead of subtracting it
Fine — it gives latitude anywhere on Earth
questions.why: Polaris' altitude is about your north latitude: in south latitudes it is below the horizon.

questions.q: On a clear night north of the Azores you look for Polaris. Which star is it?
questions.why: Follow the Plough's pointers, Merak to Dubhe, about five times their gap: Polaris sits alone in a dim patch of sky.

questions.q: On a night watch in the South Pacific you look for the south celestial pole. Which point is it?
questions.why: Extend the Cross's long axis, Gacrux to Acrux, about 4½ times its length; the Pointers' perpendicular bisector meets it there.

questions.q: A new crew member asks why a single Polaris sight gives you your latitude. What do you tell them?
options: It sits within 1° of the pole, whose altitude equals your latitude
Its declination equals your latitude every night
It is always on your meridian, like the Sun at noon
Its altitude depends only on the date, as in the almanac
questions.why: The celestial pole's altitude equals your latitude; Polaris is within 1° of it, and a0, a1, a2 correct for the difference.

questions.q: You are making for Barbados across the Atlantic without GPS, by latitude sailing. Where do you plan to reach the island's latitude?
options: Right at the island, on the great circle
Well east of it, then run down the latitude to the west
Well west of it, then work back to the east
A little north of it, then search either way
questions.why: Reach the latitude well up-wind and up-stream of the island: it is then dead ahead, and noon sights keep you on the parallel.

questions.q: You are at 12°N in the southern Caribbean in mid-June. Where will you see the Sun at noon?
questions.why: Dec N23°20′ is north of your 12°10′N, so at noon the Sun bears north: altitude 90° − (23°20′ − 12°10′) ≈ 79°.

questions.q: Low cloud hides the Plough, but Cassiopeia's W is clear high in the north-east. Where do you look for Polaris?
options: In the middle of Cassiopeia's W
At the end of the Plough's handle
On the far side of Cassiopeia from the Plough
About midway between Cassiopeia and the Plough
questions.why: Cassiopeia and the Plough lie on opposite sides of Polaris at about the same distance, so either one leads you to it.

questions.q: Mid-Atlantic, your only watch has stopped and the GPS is dead. Which sight still gives you a reliable position line?
options: A noon latitude — it needs only the date's Dec
A morning sun line for longitude
A Sun and Moon fix by day
questions.why: A meridian altitude needs no accurate time (Dec moves under 1′ an hour); every other sight needs UT to the second.

questions.q: You cross the run-up morning sun line with your noon latitude, working by plane sailing. What is the longitude of your noon position?
questions.why: Run the point 21.2 M on 260° → 15°19.4′N 41°25.5′W; down the line (219°) to 15°14.0′N is 4.4 M of westing → 41°30.0′W.

questions.q: With the Sun nearly overhead, a crew member takes the noon sight at 1927 UT, four minutes early, and you work it as a meridian altitude. How far out is your latitude?
questions.why: With the Sun 3° from the zenith the top is sharp: 4 min early it is 9′ low, so z is 9′ too big and Lat = Dec − z 9′ too far south.

questions.q: Crossing from Cocos Keeling to Mauritius, you reduce this noon sight. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Noon sight, 15 Aug 2027
lines: IE 1.8′ off the arc, height of eye 2.5 m

questions.q: Between Bermuda and the Azores you take Polaris at dusk. What is your latitude?
Bound from the Azores to Falmouth, you take Dubhe below the pole at morning twilight. What is your latitude?
South of the Azores you want Vega on the meridian at dusk. At what UT will it cross your meridian?
questions.why: On the meridian LHA★ = 0, so GHA Aries = 25° − 80°33′ = 304°27′: 10°52.8′ past 2000 at 15°02.5′ an hour is 43 min → 2043 UT.

questions.q: Mid-Pacific, just east of the date line, you work the noon sight for the ship's date. For which date and UT do you take the Sun's Dec?
questions.why: 1210 LMT + 11h52m for 178°W = 2402 on 10 March, which is 0002 UT on 11 March: use the 11 March page.

questions.q: At the spring equinox your noon latitude disagrees with the GPS, which has just come back. Which slip explains it?
options: Dec named N instead of S
SD for the upper limb used
questions.why: The error is 59.8′ = 2 × 29.9′: Dec S was used as N. Dip added costs a few minutes, the wrong limb 32′, a late sight a fraction.

questions.q: Your noon fix puts you north of Barbados' latitude. You want to reach 13°06′N 120 M to the west of you and then run down it. What true course do you steer?
questions.why: Lose 14′ (14 M) of latitude over 120 M of departure: tan C = 14/120, 6.7° south of west → 263°.

questions.q: On passage from Tonga to New Zealand you bring the Sun's upper limb down to the horizon at noon. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Noon sight, 10 Nov 2026
lines: IE 2.2′ on the arc, height of eye 2.8 m

questions.q: Between Mauritius and the Seychelles you take the noon Sun by its upper limb. What Ho do you work your latitude from?

figure.title: Noon sight, 20 Jul 2026
lines: IE 1.4′ off the arc, height of eye 2.0 m

questions.why: Hs 55°27.7′ + 1.4′ IE off the arc − 2.5′ dip − 0.7′ refraction − 15.7′ SD (upper limb) = Ho 55°10.2′.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — from Hs to Ho

questions.q: Two days out of the Canaries for Cape Verde, you take the noon sight at 1325 UT. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Noon sight, 20 Oct 2026
lines: IE 1.6′ on the arc, height of eye 2.4 m

questions.q: Bound from Fremantle to Mauritius, you took the noon Sun by its upper limb but worked it with the lower-limb correction. How does that move your latitude?

figure.title: Noon, 12 Jan 2027
lines: Upper limb observed, Sun bearing north

questions.why: +SD instead of −SD makes Ho 2 × 16.3′ = 32.6′ too high; z is that much too small, and with the Sun north of you Lat = Dec − z comes out 32.6′ too far north.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — from Hs to Ho

questions.q: At noon thin cloud covers the lower half of the Sun, but its upper edge is sharp against the sky. What do you do?

figure.title: Noon sight
lines: Thin cloud over the Sun's lower half

options: Give up the noon sight until tomorrow
Bring the centre to the horizon and apply no SD
Bring the upper limb to the horizon and subtract the SD
Guess where the lower limb is and use that
questions.why: Use the limb you can see: the upper limb's correction subtracts the semi-diameter (about 16′) where the lower limb's adds it.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — from Hs to Ho

questions.q: A day short of Rio on passage from Cape Town, you find the noon Sun will pass almost overhead. How do you get your latitude today?
options: Take the maximum as usual — a high Sun gives the best noon
Average the sights taken ten minutes either side of noon
Note the Sun's bearing at noon and take your latitude as the Dec
Time sights either side of noon and plot each as a circle round the GP
questions.why: Within a degree of the zenith the bearing swings fast and the peak is hard to catch: each timed sight is a small circle, radius z, round the GP.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — Sun near the zenith

questions.q: Bound from Tahiti to Hawaii, you plot a sight taken four minutes after noon as a circle round the Sun's GP. What radius do you draw?
questions.why: Radius = zenith distance: 90° − 87°50.0′ = 2°10.0′ = 130 minutes of arc = 130.0 M, centred on the GP.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — Sun near the zenith

questions.q: South of Bermuda, bound for the Virgin Islands, the crew hand you this noon altitude but cannot say which way they faced. Which latitude can it give?
options: 18°04.5′N only — in May the Sun bears north
questions.why: z = 90° − 88°41.6′ = 1°18.4′: Sun north gives Dec − z = 18°04.5′N, Sun south Dec + z = 20°41.3′N. Only the bearing or a good DR decides.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — Sun near the zenith

questions.q: You are delivering a motor yacht from Newport to Bermuda at 24 knots, heading south towards the noon Sun. When will the sextant show the greatest altitude?
options: At 1200 ship's time, whatever the longitude
At LAN exactly — the boat's speed makes no difference
A few minutes after LAN — you are closing the Sun
A few minutes before LAN — your speed brings noon forward
questions.why: Running towards the Sun adds about 24′ of altitude an hour, so it keeps rising after LAN: the peak comes late, and a little too high.

questions.q: Bound north from Bermuda to Newport at 25 knots, you follow the Sun up at noon. When will you see its greatest altitude?

figure.title: Motor yacht, 20 Nov 2026
lines: Near LAN the altitude falls 0.030′ × t²

options: At LAN, as on any boat
questions.why: Running away from the Sun costs 25′/h = 0.42′ a minute; the curve falls 0.030′ × t², so the top comes 0.42 ÷ (2 × 0.030) ≈ 7 min early.

questions.q: On a fast motor yacht running north or south, how do you get a true meridian altitude at noon?
options: Take the altitude at the predicted time of LAN by the watch
Take the sight ten minutes after LAN, when it settles
Take the maximum, as on any boat — it always falls at LAN
Take the maximum and add your speed in minutes of arc
questions.why: A fast north–south run shifts the peak off the meridian: take the sight at the computed LAN by the watch, or slow down for it.

questions.q: Between Bermuda and the Azores in June, the first-quarter Moon crosses your meridian at dusk, bearing south. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Moon at dusk, June
lines: Moon (LL) on the meridian, bearing south

questions.q: In the Marquesas you want the Moon on your meridian tonight. At what UT will it cross?
questions.why: The Moon is 49 min later each day: 1752 + 49 × 140/360 = 1811 LMT at 140°W; + 9h20m = 2731, i.e. 0331 UT on 15 July.

questions.q: Crossing from Mauritius to Durban in late February, you catch Venus on the meridian in the afternoon sky, bearing north. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Venus by day
lines: Venus on the meridian, bearing north

questions.q: You take Jupiter on the meridian at dusk. From which Ho do you work your latitude?
questions.why: A planet takes IE, dip and refraction only: 44°36.2′ − 1.2′ − 2.8′ − 1.0′ = 44°31.2′. No semi-diameter: it is a point of light.

questions.q: You took the Moon on the meridian at 0352 UT but worked it with the Dec for 03h. How far out is your latitude?
questions.why: The Moon's Dec moves 13.5′ an hour: 52 minutes is 11.7′. The Dec you used is that much too far south, and so is your latitude.

questions.q: Hove-to for a day in a winter gale south of the Azores, with no almanac to hand, you take Kochab at both its transits. What is your latitude?
questions.why: Above and below the pole the star is the same distance from it, so Lat = (50°14.4′ + 18°22.4′) ÷ 2 = 34°18.4′N, with no Dec needed.

questions.q: Approaching Svalbard at midsummer, you have lost the almanac overboard. You take the Sun at noon, bearing south, and at midnight, bearing north. What is your latitude?
questions.why: The Sun crosses on both sides of the zenith: Lat = 90° − (36°12.5′ − 10°35.9′) ÷ 2 = 77°11.7′N. The mean, 23°24.2′, is its Dec.

questions.q: North of Norway in July, a crew member plans a Polaris sight for tonight's latitude. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Barents Sea, 10 Jul 2027
lines: Sun at local midnight: 8° up, bearing north

options: No darkness, no Polaris — take the midnight Sun bearing north
Take it — at 76°N it is nearly overhead, so z is tiny
Take it, but this far north skip a0, a1 and a2
Take it at local midnight, the darkest moment
questions.why: At 76°N in July the Sun stays about 8° up at midnight: no stars. Its lower transit gives latitude: Lat = Ho + (90° − Dec).

questions.q: On the southern route from Cape Verde to Grenada, you take Polaris low in the north at dusk. What is your latitude?
You have taken Polaris near 10°N and, on another passage, near 50°N. What is true of the low sight?

figure.title: Two Polaris sights
lines: Same sextant, same height of eye

options: It needs no dip correction, being so low
It gives you longitude as well as latitude
Its refraction is larger and less certain — the horizon needs care
Its a0 correction is larger, as the star circles wider
questions.why: a0 depends on LHA Aries, not on latitude. Polaris 10° up carries about 5′ of refraction, which haze and temperature can upset.

questions.q: Bound from Oman to India in January, you take Polaris at dusk. With which LHA Aries do you enter the a0 table?
questions.why: LHA = GHA + east longitude: 317°21.7′ + 64°30′ = 381°51.7′; take off 360° to enter the table at 21°51.7′.

questions.q: At dusk on the ARC route you take Polaris. What is your latitude?
Sailing the South Atlantic, a new crew member asks how you will get a latitude at dusk with no pole star. What do you tell them?
options: The south celestial pole's altitude, corrected by a0
A bright star's meridian altitude, such as Achernar or Canopus
The Southern Cross's altitude at any time
Polaris, low on the northern horizon
questions.why: No bright star marks the south pole: take a bright star as it crosses your meridian in twilight and use Lat = Dec ± z.

questions.q: Between Rodrigues and Mauritius at dusk just after Christmas, Achernar crosses your meridian, bearing south. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Evening twilight, 28 Dec 2026
lines: Achernar on the meridian, bearing south

questions.q: Crossing the Tasman from Hobart to New Zealand in early December, you take Acrux below the south pole at dusk. What is your latitude?

figure.title: Evening twilight, 1 Dec 2026
lines: Acrux at lower transit, bearing south

questions.why: Below the pole Lat = Ho + polar distance: 14°22.5′ + (90° − 63°14.0′ = 26°46.0′) = 41°08.5′, named like the pole: S.

questions.q: At evening twilight in the Indian Ocean you see the Southern Cross standing upright like this. What does it tell you?
options: Acrux is on your meridian — time for its meridian altitude
The Cross is due east — a good star for longitude
Acrux is at its lowest, at lower transit
The Cross is setting — too low to use
questions.why: With Gacrux straight above Acrux the long axis is vertical: the Cross is at upper transit, bearing south, on your meridian.

questions.q: Your crew points out a cross of stars, larger and dimmer than you expected, with no bright pair beside it. What is it most likely to be?
options: The Southern Cross upside down, at lower transit
The False Cross — the true one is smaller, with the Pointers by it
The Northern Cross, seen from the south
The Southern Cross, looking larger near the horizon
questions.why: The False Cross (in Carina and Vela) is bigger and fainter; the real Cross is compact, with α and β Centauri pointing to it.

questions.q: A crew member asks for the 'southern Polaris' to take for latitude tonight. What do you tell them?
options: Canopus — work it with the a0 tables
Acrux — it sits on the south pole
There is none to use — Sigma Octantis is too faint
Achernar — it never moves in the sky
questions.why: Sigma Octantis, about 1° from the south pole, is only magnitude 5.4, too faint for a sextant. Use a bright star's meridian altitude.

questions.q: Two days out of Fremantle for Mauritius, at 30°S, you want a star to take below the south pole at twilight. Which of these stays above your horizon all night?
questions.why: Circumpolar when the Dec exceeds the co-latitude, 90° − 30° = 60°: only Acrux (S63°14′) stays up; Achernar (S57°06′) just sets.

questions.q: Running down the latitude of Antigua, you find the noon sights creeping north. Which course now keeps you on the latitude?

figure.title: Latitude sailing to Antigua
lines: Back on 17°00′N today after a correction

questions.why: A set of 7 M a day to the north is 0.29 kn; at 6.5 kn that needs asin(0.29/6.5) ≈ 3°: steer 3° south of west, 267°.

questions.q: Bound for Bermuda from the Azores, your noon fix puts you north of the latitude you want, with a current setting north. What course do you steer?

figure.note: Current 000° 0.5 kn · speed 6 kn · not to scale

questions.why: The track to the target is 261° (25 M south in 150 M west); to cancel 0.5 kn of set to the north at 6 kn, steer about 5° further south: 256°.

questions.q: On the run from the Marquesas to the Tuamotus, today's noon latitude differs from your DR. What does it tell you about the current?

figure.title: Noon, 24 h after the last fix

options: Nothing — a latitude cannot show current
questions.why: 13′ south of the DR after 24 h of good steering and log: 13 M ÷ 24 h ≈ 0.5 kn of southerly set. The east–west part stays unknown.

questions.q: Running down the latitude of Ascension with no good longitude, at noon you have the island 60 M ahead by DR, give or take 25 M. What is your plan?

figure.title: Noon, latitude sailing
lines: On 7°56′S, Ascension 60 M ahead by DR

options: Alter 30° north to be sure of passing clear
Speed up to arrive before dark
Hold 6 kn — its light will show you at night
Slow down and close the island at first light
questions.why: With 25 M of doubt you could arrive any time from dusk to the small hours: slow down, keep to the latitude, close the island in daylight.

questions.q: You advance your noon latitude to dusk and cross it with this star line. What is the longitude of the fix?
questions.why: Noon lat run 39 M on 225° → 23°42.4′N; intercept point 23°58.4′N 45°26.3′W; along 165° to 23°42.4′N is 4.3 M east → 45°21.6′W.

questions.q: At dusk on the ARC route you want one star to cross with your noon latitude, run up to the time of the sight. Which do you choose?
questions.why: A latitude runs east–west, so the best cut comes from a star bearing near east or west: Altair at 256° crosses it at 76°.

questions.q: Two days out of Cape Town for St Helena, you advance your noon latitude to dusk for a star fix. Where does the advanced latitude lie?
questions.why: A latitude line moves only by the run's change of latitude: 36.0 M × cos 315° = 25.5′ north, so 25°42.0′S becomes 25°16.5′S.

questions.q: Cloud hides the Sun from mid-morning until 1530, when it comes out. You have a 0900 sun line. How do you get a fix?
options: Wait for tomorrow's noon — one sun line is worthless
Work the 1530 sight as a late meridian altitude
Cross the 0900 and 1530 lines without running up
Run the 0900 line up to 1530 and cross it with a 1530 sun line
questions.why: Sun–run–sun: transfer the morning line by the run and cross it with the afternoon line; the Sun's bearing has swung 135°.

questions.q: Bound from Bermuda to Antigua, with cloud closing in, you take the Sun six minutes before noon and reduce it as an ex-meridian. What is your latitude?
Cloud hid the Sun at its peak, but you caught the same sextant altitude before and after noon. What is your longitude?
questions.why: LAN is midway, 2025:45½ UT. The Sun crosses Greenwich at 1144:45, so 8h41m00½s × 15 = 130°15.1′ of west longitude.

questions.q: Leaving Fiji for Vanuatu, the ship's clock still on Fiji time (zone −12), you plan the noon sight at 177°30′E. When, in UT, is the Sun on your meridian?
questions.why: 1209 LMT − 11h50m for 177°30′E = 0019 UT on the same date, 15 January: east longitude is subtracted, and no day is crossed.

questions.q: On the ARC route the crew took today's noon sight standing on the coachroof, but you reduced it for your usual cockpit height. How does that move your latitude?

figure.title: Noon sight
lines: Sun bearing south, you in north latitude

questions.why: Dip for 3.5 m is 3.3′, for 2.0 m 2.5′: Ho came out 0.8′ too high and z too small, so with the Sun south Lat = Dec + z is 0.8′ too far south.
questions.ref: Meridian altitude — from Hs to Ho

questions.q: A new watchkeeper offers to take the noon sight 'at 1200 by the ship's clock'. What do you tell them?
options: Noon is when the Sun crosses our meridian — from Mer Pass and longitude
Fine, as long as the clock is checked against UT
Fine — the ship's clock is set to local noon
Take it at 1200 UT, the almanac's noon
questions.why: Local noon is the Sun's meridian passage: Mer Pass in LMT plus or minus your longitude in time — rarely 1200 on any clock.

questions.q: On the South Atlantic crossing from Cape Town to Brazil in July, a crew member used to the Med starts the noon sight facing south. Where should they look?
questions.why: Dec N21° is north of your 30°S, so the noon Sun bears north at 90° − (30° + 21°) = 39°.

questions.q: Jupiter crosses your meridian at 0130 local time, high and brilliant in a moonless sky. Do you take it for latitude?
options: Only if it bears north of you
Yes — a planet is bright enough at any hour
No — there is no horizon to bring it down to
Yes, and add 15′ for the dark horizon
questions.why: A sextant sight needs a sharp horizon: stars and planets are taken in twilight, when both the body and the horizon can be seen.

questions.q: A day out of Cape Town in mid-April, you preset the sextant before noon so the Sun is ready in the telescope. What do you set, and where do you look?
questions.why: Dec N11°20′ and your 33°40′S are on opposite sides of the equator: z = 33°40′ + 11°20′ = 45°, so the Sun is about 45° up, to the north.

questions.q: Overcast all day has cost you the noon sight, but the sky is clearing from the west at dusk. What is the next best latitude tonight?

figure.title: Noon sight lost
lines: Clearing from the west at dusk

options: A star on the meridian, or Polaris, in evening twilight
A star low in the east, as soon as it rises
The Moon at midnight, whatever the horizon
Tomorrow's noon — no other sight gives latitude
questions.why: Any body on your meridian gives latitude, and Polaris does at any hour in the north — in twilight, with a sharp horizon.

questions.q: You plan to take the Moon on the meridian. Which almanac figure do you need that you never use for the Sun?
questions.why: The Moon is so close that its parallax reaches a degree: parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha. The Sun's is only about 0.1′.

questions.q: At dusk in early March you take Capella and Rigel on the meridian minutes apart, and the two latitudes disagree. Which do you plot?
questions.why: An error common to both sights (IE, dip) moves a north star's latitude one way and a south star's the other: their mean cancels it.

questions.q: After plotting your noon fix from the run-up morning line, you find the noon latitude was 4.0′ too far north. How does the fix move?

figure.title: Noon fix
lines: Noon latitude found 4.0′ too far north

questions.why: The fix slides along the run-up line (030°–210°): 4.0′ of latitude south along it is 4.0 ÷ cos 30° = 4.6 M towards 210°.

questions.q: You are 600 miles west of the Canaries on the ARC route and have just reduced this sight. What does it give you?

figure.title: Morning sun sight
lines: Reduced from the DR as the AP

options: A position line running 038°–218°, not a fix
Your latitude, as the Sun is still rising
A position line along 128° through the DR
A fix 3.1 M from the DR along 128°
questions.why: One sight gives one position line, at right angles to the azimuth: 128° ± 90° = 038°/218°. A fix needs a second line.

questions.q: Your DR longitude is in doubt after two days of cloud. At which of these times does a sun sight do most for your longitude?
options: 1145 — the Sun is highest, so the sight is most accurate
0845 — the Sun is well clear of the meridian and above 15°
0715 — the Sun is nearest east, so the line is nearest north–south
1215 — just after noon, when the Sun's bearing is steady
questions.why: A line lies at right angles to the azimuth, so a Sun well east or west of the meridian gives longitude; below 15° refraction is large and uncertain.

questions.q: The watch leader wants to take the first sun sight of the day right now. What do you tell him?

figure.title: Just after sunrise
lines: Sun's lower limb 6° above the horizon
Cool air, slight haze to the east

options: Wait until noon: morning sights are never usable
Take it now and apply twice the refraction to be safe
Wait until the Sun is above about 15°: refraction is large and uncertain
Take it now: the bearing is nearest east, the best for longitude
questions.why: Low down, refraction is big and varies with air temperature and pressure; above about 15° its uncertainty is small.

questions.q: You take a sun sight in the trade winds and time it with this watch. What UT do you take into the almanac?

figure.title: Timing the sight
lines: Watch kept on ship's time, ZD +3
Watch 11 s fast by the GPS check

questions.why: Remove the error (fast: subtract 11 s) = 11:23:30 ship's time; UT = zone time + ZD (+3) = 14:23:30.
questions.ref: Sight reduction — UT from the watch

questions.q: You are three weeks out from the Galápagos on the Puddle Jump. Which almanac page and hour do you open for this sight?
questions.why: UT = zone time + ZD = 1648 + 9 h = 2548, i.e. 0148 on the next day: the 01h line of 15 April.
questions.ref: Sight reduction — UT from the watch

questions.q: You work an afternoon sight on the ARC route. What is the Sun's GHA at the moment of the sight?
You work this morning sight on passage to St Lucia from your DR longitude. What is the LHA?
You take an afternoon sun sight between the Galápagos and the Marquesas on the day of the equinox. What declination do you use?

figure.title: Almanac, 20 March 2027
lines: d 1.0′ an hour, Sun moving north

questions.why: d correction for 42 min = 0.7′ northward: S0°00.4′ → N0°00.3′ — the Sun has crossed the equator, so the name changes.

questions.q: Your GPS has failed mid-Atlantic. How far east or west could your sun-sight longitude be wrong because of the watch alone?

figure.title: The watch
lines: Last checked by GPS 9 days ago
Error now unknown: up to ±12 s

questions.why: The Earth turns 15′ of arc a minute: 4 s of time = 1′ of longitude, so 12 s = 3′.

questions.q: You take a morning sun sight from the cockpit, 400 miles west of the Cape Verdes. What is Ho?
Only the Sun's upper limb shows clearly above a bank of low cloud, so you take that. What is Ho?

figure.title: Sun, upper limb
lines: Hs UL 28°41.6′ · IE 2.4′ off the arc
Lower limb lost in low cloud

questions.why: Hs 28°41.6′ + 2.4′ IE off − 3.3′ dip − 1.8′ refraction − 16.2′ SD (upper limb) = Ho 28°22.7′.

questions.q: You are in the trade winds 1000 miles from Antigua and work the sight from your DR. What is the LHA?
questions.why: LHA = GHA − longitude West (+ longitude East): 312°40.2′ − 45°20.0′ = 267°20.2′.

questions.q: Checking the crew's working of the 1530 sight on the way to the Marquesas, you find this. What has gone wrong?
options: The longitude was added instead of subtracted
The watch error was applied the wrong way
The GHA was taken for the wrong day
Nothing: an afternoon LHA is always over 180°
questions.why: In the afternoon the Sun is west of you, so LHA is 0–180°: 180°36.2′ − 128°05.0′ W = 52°31.2′, not 308°41.2′.

questions.q: You work this ARC morning sight by calculator from the AP. What Hc do you get?
questions.why: LHA = 352°41.6′ − 38°41.6′ = 314°; Dec S is negative against a north latitude: sin Hc = sin L sin D + cos L cos D cos LHA → 30°50.5′.

questions.q: You reduce this afternoon sight half-way from Bermuda to the Azores. What is the Sun's true azimuth, Zn?
questions.why: LHA 48° (under 180°) puts the Sun west of the meridian: azimuth angle N 094° W, so Zn = 360° − 094° = 266°.

questions.q: You are crossing the Indian Ocean from Cocos Keeling to Rodrigues. What is the Sun's Zn for this afternoon sight?
questions.why: South latitude, LHA under 180°: Zn = 180° + Z = 180° + 96° = 276°.

questions.q: You reduce a sight from a chosen AP on passage from Bermuda to the Azores. What is Hc?
You have no calculator aboard, only HO 249 sight reduction tables. Why do you work the sight from a chosen AP rather than from the DR?
options: The tables only work for west longitudes
The tables are entered with whole degrees of latitude and LHA
A chosen AP removes the need for an intercept
The DR is always less accurate than an AP
questions.why: HO 249 tabulates whole degrees: take the AP's latitude to the nearest degree and its longitude so that the LHA comes out whole.

questions.q: You want to reduce this ARC morning sight with HO 249. Which AP and LHA do you use?
questions.why: In west longitude give the AP the GHA's minutes (50.3′), within 30′ of the DR: 356°50.3′ − 38°50.3′ = LHA 318°.

questions.q: Your co-skipper works the morning sight from the DR by calculator; you work the same sight with HO 249. Which position line do you plot?
options: The DR one: an AP is further from the boat
The AP one: tables are more exact than a calculator
Neither: different intercepts mean an error
Either: both give the same line on the sheet
questions.why: Moving the AP along the azimuth changes the intercept by the same amount, so both workings plot the same position line.

questions.q: You reduce this morning sun sight from your DR. What is the intercept?
questions.why: Ho − Hc = 42°18.4′ − 42°12.1′ = +6.3′ = 6.3 M; Ho greater than Hc means towards.

questions.q: You are plotting this afternoon sight on the plotting sheet. How do you lay off the intercept from the AP?
questions.why: Ho is less than Hc: 5.4′ away, so lay it off from the AP on the reciprocal of Zn, 236° − 180° = 056°.

questions.q: On the plotting sheet you have marked the AP and drawn the Sun's azimuth. How do you plot this sight?
options: Measure 6 M from the AP towards 310° and draw the line at right angles there
Measure 6 M from the AP towards 130° and draw the line along the azimuth
Measure 6 M from the AP towards 130° and draw the line at right angles there
Draw the line at right angles to the azimuth through the AP itself
questions.why: Lay off the intercept along the azimuth (towards the Sun for 'towards'); the position line is drawn at right angles to the azimuth there.

questions.q: You plot this sun sight from the AP shown. Which line is its position line?
questions.why: Ho 32°14.0′ < Hc 32°22.0′: 8.0 M away, so lay off 8 M along 240° and draw the line at right angles to the azimuth: line B.

questions.q: You are plotting a 9-mile intercept on a plotting sheet in 40°N. Where do you measure the 9 miles with the dividers?
options: On the latitude scale, where 1′ = 1 M
On either scale: they are the same at 40°N
On the longitude scale, where 1′ = 1 M
On the longitude scale, corrected by cos 40°
questions.why: Distance is measured on the latitude scale; a minute of longitude is only cos 40° × 1 M ≈ 0.77 M here.

questions.q: Your afternoon sight, 600 miles east of Bermuda, has the Sun exactly due west. Combined with the noon latitude, what does it give you?
questions.why: Sun due west: the line runs north–south, a meridian. 6.0 M west at 36°40′N = 6.0 / cos 36.7° = 7.5′ of longitude: 52°22.5′W.
questions.ref: Sun sights — a line and a latitude

lines: Run to the 1530 sight: 250° T, 18 M
