questions.q: You have an 0900 sun line and will take a noon sight for a running fix. Between the two you sail 245° T, 26 M by the log. What do you do with the 0900 line?
options: Move it 26 M along 245° and redraw it parallel to itself
Move it 26 M along the Sun's 0900 azimuth
Turn it to the noon azimuth through the noon DR
Leave it: a position line holds all day
questions.why: A position line is carried forward by the run (course and distance through the water) and stays parallel to itself.

questions.q: You carry the morning sun line forward by moving its AP. Where is the AP after the run?

figure.title: Running the line on
lines: Zn and intercept stay the same

questions.q: You want a sun-run-sun fix whose lines cut at 45° or more, but with as short a run as possible. When do you take the second sight?
questions.why: Two lines cut at the change of azimuth: 173° − 127° = 46° at 1130; a longer run only adds run error.

questions.q: You plot a sun-run-sun fix on the passage to St Lucia. Which point is your noon position?

figure.note: Plotting sheet · C noon DR · D 0915 DR

questions.why: Run the 0915 line on by the run (252°, 31 M) and cross it with the noon latitude: A. B uses the line before it was run on.

questions.q: You run the morning sun line on to noon and cross it with the noon latitude. What is the longitude of your noon fix?
questions.why: Transferred AP 16°50.4′N 39°21.1′W; the line through 4.6 M towards 131° meets 16°55.4′N 10.9′ east of it: 39°10.2′W.

questions.q: You are crossing the Equatorial Current with a four-hour run between two sun sights. How far out could your running fix be from the current alone?
questions.why: The earlier line is carried by the run through the water: 0.8 kn × 4 h = 3.2 M of set that the run does not include.

questions.q: You are south of Bermuda with the Moon in a clear afternoon sky. What do these two sights give you?
options: A running fix once the Moon line is run on 24 hours
Only one line: the Moon cannot be used in daylight
A fix from two lines cutting at 54°, with no run between them
Two lines cutting at 126°, too wide to give a fix
questions.why: Simultaneous sun and Moon lines need no run; they cross at 238° − 112° = 126°, the same as 54° — a fair cut.

questions.q: You are sailing from the Canaries to Mindelo in the Cape Verdes. Which sight tells you best whether you are left or right of your track?
options: 1430 — the Sun is ahead, so the line crosses the track
1200 — the Sun is highest, so the line is most accurate
0730 — the Sun is lowest, so its bearing is steadiest
0900 — the Sun is abeam, so the line runs along the track
questions.why: Sun abeam (134° ≈ 225° − 90°): the line lies parallel to the course — a course line, showing any offset to either side.

questions.q: You are steering 265° on the Puddle Jump in April, and the morning Sun rises almost dead astern. What does your first sun line of the day tell you best?
options: How far you have run along the track
Your latitude, as the Sun is near the east
Your compass error, as the Sun is astern
Whether you are north or south of the track
questions.why: Sun astern: the position line lies across the track — a speed line that checks the distance run, not your offset to either side.

questions.q: Bound from Bermuda to the Azores, you plot this morning sun line. What does it tell you?

figure.title: Approaching Faial, 10 June
lines: Sun line crosses the track 46 M short

options: That you are 46 M south of the track and must alter north
About 7 hours to go, but nothing about your offset north or south
Your exact position: a sun line along the track is a fix
Your latitude, because the Sun is on the prime vertical
questions.why: The Sun dead ahead gives a speed line across the track: 46 M ÷ 6.5 kn ≈ 7 h to go; it says nothing about your offset to either side.

questions.q: You are approaching Tobago in May, with the Sun passing nearly overhead. Why are these two sights, 40 minutes apart, worth taking?
options: The altitude barely changes, so they average to a better latitude
Two sights cancel the index error, so no corrections are needed
The bearing swings 66° in 40 minutes: a quick running fix with almost no run
The Sun is north of you, so each gives longitude directly
questions.why: With the Sun near the zenith its azimuth swings fast past noon: two lines 40 min apart cut at 66° after a run of only a few miles.

questions.q: 250 miles east of Martinique you get a sight with the Sun almost overhead and plot it as a circle round the Sun's geographical position. What centre and radius do you use?
questions.why: GP: latitude = Dec N15°08.8′, longitude = GHA 60°43.3′ west; radius = 90° − 86°05.0′ = 3°55.0′ = 235 M.

questions.q: You find this mistake after plotting the morning line. Where does the correct position line lie?

figure.title: Morning sight, rechecked
lines: IE was not applied to Hs

options: 2 M further towards the Sun, along 112°
2 M further away from the Sun, along 292°
2 M along the line itself, to the north
questions.why: Off the arc is added: the true Ho is 2.0′ higher, so the intercept grows by 2 M towards the Sun; 1′ of altitude = 1 M.

questions.q: Your morning sun-run-sun fix was worked with the watch as read. How is the fix wrong?

figure.title: Noon time check
lines: Radio time signal: watch 8 s fast
Morning sights used the watch as read

questions.why: A fast watch gives a UT that is too late, so GHA is 2′ too big (8 s × 15′ a minute): the fix is 2′ of longitude too far west.

questions.q: You take a quick series of morning sights in a lumpy sea. Which one do you throw out?
questions.why: The Sun climbs evenly, about 7′ every 40 s here; the third jumps 11′ then 3′, so it is off the line — reject it.
questions.ref: Sun sights — a series of sights

questions.q: You decide to reduce one sight from this series instead of all four. Which time and altitude do you use?
questions.why: Average the times (10:15:02) and the altitudes (41°27.55′ ≈ 41°27.6′) and reduce once; it works because the altitude rises steadily.
questions.ref: Sun sights — a series of sights

questions.q: You cross three sun lines from one day on the passage. What most likely makes the triangle?

figure.title: Three sun lines run on to 1600

options: Errors in the course and distance used to run the lines on
The Sun's declination changing between sights
Using a different AP for each sight
questions.why: Each line is good to about a mile; the hours of run (leeway, current, log error) carried by the earlier lines open the hat.

questions.q: Your three sun lines of the day make a small, neat triangle. If all three altitudes carry the same unknown error, where can you be?

figure.title: Three sun lines, run on to 1500
lines: Index error checked once, at dawn

options: On the noon line, since it needs no run
Possibly outside the triangle: the azimuths span less than 180°
Inside it, at the centre of the triangle
At the corner made by the two latest lines
questions.why: A constant error moves every line the same way along its azimuth; with azimuths spanning only 100° the true spot can lie outside.

questions.q: Bound from the Canaries to the Cape Verdes, you reduce an afternoon sight and the intercept comes out nil. What do you plot?

figure.title: Afternoon sun sight
lines: Worked from the DR as the AP

options: The AP itself, as a fix
No line: a nil intercept means a slip
A line through the AP itself, running 124°–304°
A line through the AP along 034°–214°
questions.why: Ho = Hc puts you on the circle through the AP: draw the line through the AP at right angles to Zn 214°, i.e. 124°–304°.

questions.q: You are working a sun sight timed at 14h 36m 20s UT. Which increment do you add to the Sun's GHA for 14h?
options: 9°05.0′, from the Sun and planets column
questions.why: The Sun's GHA grows exactly 15° an hour: 36m 20s = 36.33 min × 15′ = 545′ = 9°05.0′ — the Sun and planets column.

questions.q: Crossing the Indian Ocean from Mauritius towards the Chagos, you work this sight from your DR. What is the LHA?
On a February delivery from Antigua to Bermuda, you check the crew's GHA roughly before going on. Which GHA is about right for this sight?
questions.why: GHA ≈ (UT − 12 h) × 15°, give or take the EoT: 3.5 h × 15° = 52.5°, less 3.6° for an EoT of −14 min → about 049°.

questions.q: Your crew, on their first passage south of the equator, say the towards/away rule is reversed down here. How do you lay off this intercept?

figure.title: Sight at 28°S, Sun to the north

questions.why: Ho greater than Hc is towards the Sun in either hemisphere: lay off 5.5 M from the AP along Zn 028°.

questions.q: You will reduce this sight with HO 249 on the approach to Rio de Janeiro from St Helena. What latitude do you give the AP?
questions.why: HO 249 is entered with a whole degree of latitude: take the one nearest the DR, 23°38′S → 24°S.

questions.q: Your HO 249 tables are soaked, and you now reduce sights by calculator with the cosine formula. Which position do you work them from?
options: The DR as it is — the formula takes any position
Yesterday's noon fix, unchanged all day
A whole-degree AP, as you would for the tables
questions.why: The formula needs no whole-degree LHA, so work from the DR: one point to plot from and the shortest intercept.

questions.q: On passage from Samoa to Fiji you cross 180° during the night. What changes in the way you work the morning sun sight?
options: The longitude is now east: subtract it from the GHA
The longitude is now east: add it to the GHA
Nothing, until you reset the ship's clock
UT jumps a day too: open the almanac a day later
questions.why: The date line changes the ship's date and the longitude's name, not UT: in east longitude LHA = GHA + longitude.

questions.q: The navigator wants to shift this morning's sun line for the current before he plots it. What do you tell him?
options: Move it 1.2 M along the Sun's azimuth
Draw it through the DR moved for the current
Leave it: at its own time the line is where the sight puts it
Move it 1.2 M along 270°, for the hour
questions.why: Current matters only when a line is carried forward in time; a sun line plotted for its own time needs no allowance.

questions.q: In the Tuamotus you are passing a long reef that runs 150°–330° on your port hand. At what Sun bearing does a sun line best show your distance off it?
options: Overhead at noon — the latitude is exact
150° or 330° — the Sun is along the reef
Any bearing, once the line is run on
060° or 240° — the line then runs along the reef
questions.why: A line lies at right angles to the azimuth: with the Sun on 060° or 240° it runs 150°–330°, parallel to the reef — your distance off.

questions.q: A few hours out of Cape Town for St Helena, you reduce a morning sight with HO 249. What is the Sun's Zn?

figure.title: HO 249, south latitude
lines: AP 34°S · LHA 318° · Dec S21° same name

questions.why: South latitude, LHA over 180°: Zn = 180° − Z = 180° − 98° = 082°.

questions.q: Bound from Bali to Cocos Keeling, you reduce this sight with HO 249. Which AP and LHA do you use?
questions.why: In east longitude the AP's minutes are 60′ − the GHA's: 331°27.4′ + 102°32.6′E = 434° → LHA 074°; 11°40′S → 12°S.

questions.q: Two days out of Tonga for Fiji, past the date line, you take a morning sun sight. Which almanac page and hour do you open?
questions.why: UT = zone time + ZD = 0915 − 12 h = 2115 on the day before: 13 August, the 21h line.
questions.ref: Sight reduction — UT from the watch

questions.q: Off Madeira, bound for Las Palmas, you find the crew took the Sun's Dec for this sight from yesterday's page. Where does that put the line?
options: Less than a mile out: the Dec barely moves in a day
questions.why: Yesterday's Dec is 18.8′ further north, so Hc comes out 18.6′ too high: the line sits 19 M too far from the Sun — north.

questions.q: On a February delivery from Cape Town to Salvador, you take a sun sight at 14h 47m UT. What Dec do you use?
questions.why: d 0.8′ × 47/60 = 0.6′; the Dec is getting smaller (S14°18.3′ → S14°17.5′), so subtract it: S14°17.7′.

questions.q: You are going to reduce a July sight with HO 249 on the passage from Tahiti to Rarotonga. Which page and declination do you enter?
questions.why: Lat S with Dec N is contrary name; enter the whole degree below the Dec (21°) and take the 14′ with the d correction.

questions.q: Bound from New Zealand for Cape Horn, you lay off this intercept from the AP. Where is the end of the intercept?
questions.why: dLat = 7.0 × cos 60° = 3.5′ N, so the south latitude gets smaller; dLong = 6.06 / cos 47° = 8.9′ E, so the west longitude gets smaller.

questions.q: In the Southern Ocean you make up a plotting sheet for 47°S. How far apart do you draw meridians one degree apart?
questions.why: A degree of longitude is a degree of latitude × cos lat: 120 mm × cos 47° = 82 mm.

questions.q: On the way from Cape Town to Punta del Este, a new crew member works her first sight and gets this. What is most likely wrong?
options: The latitude went in as north, not south
The SD was taken for the wrong limb
The dip was added, not subtracted
The index error went in the wrong way
questions.why: A slip in a correction moves a line a few miles; an intercept of 1316 M is a blunder in the entries — here sin L with the wrong sign.

questions.q: Heading west from Hawaii, you time an afternoon sight with this watch. Which almanac line do you use?

figure.title: Timing the sight
lines: Watch kept on UT, 35 s slow

questions.why: Slow: add 35 s: 23:59:40 + 35 s = 00:00:15 UT on 1 December — the next day's 00h line, plus 15 s of increments.
questions.ref: Sight reduction — UT from the watch

questions.q: You correct a July sun sight with the almanac's Sun table. Which main correction do you apply?
questions.why: The table has two seasons because the Sun's SD changes through the year: in July use Apr–Sep, and the limb you brought down.

questions.q: After three days of gale with no sights, your first sun sight, worked from the DR, gives a very large intercept. What do you do with it?

figure.title: First sight after the gale
lines: DR from log and compass only

options: Retake the sight until it agrees with the DR
Plot it as it is: an intercept of any length is exact
Throw it out: an intercept over 30 M is a blunder
Plot it, then rework it from a point on that line
questions.why: A long intercept is not wrong, but the straight line is only a tangent to the circle near its foot: rework from a point on it.

questions.q: After plotting a sun-run-sun fix you find the index error was left out of both sights. Where is the true fix?

figure.title: Sun-run-sun fix
lines: IE 2.0′ off the arc, not applied

options: Where it is: the error cancels out
questions.why: Both Ho were 2′ low, so each line moves 2 M towards its Sun; with azimuths 120° apart the fix moves 2 / cos 60° = 4 M along 170°.

questions.q: At landfall you find the log under-read on the run between your sun sights. How far out was the morning line after you ran it on?
questions.why: A run error moves the line only by its part along the azimuth: 3.0 M × cos (250° − 120°) = 3.0 × 0.64 ≈ 1.9 M.

questions.q: Practising with the GPS still working, you compare five days of sun lines with the GPS position. What do they tell you?

figure.title: Sun lines against the GPS
lines: Each line 0.5–1.5 M from the GPS fix,
always on the side away from the Sun

options: The GPS is about 1 M out: trust the sextant
A watch error: reset the watch to UT
A constant error of about 1′: recheck the IE and your eye
Normal scatter: there is nothing to correct
questions.why: Random errors scatter both ways; lines always about a mile 'away' point to a constant altitude error — index or personal.

questions.q: In the tropics in August you get three sun lines spread over the day. Allowing for a constant sextant error you cannot rule out, where in this cocked hat are you?

figure.title: Three sun lines, 27 August, 15°N
lines: Lines run on to 1615 · triangle 2 M across
Index error checked once, at dawn

options: At the corner where the two latest lines cross
Anywhere outside it: a constant error moves you out
Outside it, beyond the side of the noon line
Inside it: the azimuths span more than 180°
questions.why: A constant error shifts all three lines alike; with azimuths spanning 187° (086° to 273°), the true spot lies inside.

questions.q: Running east in the Southern Ocean in June, you want a sun-run-sun fix today. Which pair of sights do you take?
options: 0900 and 1500 — the widest cut of the day
1130 and 1230 — the Sun at its highest
questions.why: Refraction is unreliable below about 10°, and the Sun barely tops 18° at noon: 1000 and 1400 (14°, 57° apart) give the best usable cut.

questions.q: On a June morning between Bermuda and the Azores the Moon is up in daylight. When do you take the Sun and the Moon together for a fix?
questions.why: Take the best cut with both bodies above about 15°: at 1200 the Moon is only 7° up, so 0700 (49°) is best.
questions.ref: Sun and Moon — a fix by day

questions.q: You take a Moon sight 25 minutes after your Sun sight. How do you get the fix for 1505?
options: Run the Moon line back 2.9 M along 255°
Cross them as they are: 25 minutes is simultaneous
Run the Sun line on 2.9 M along 255°
questions.why: Lines from different times need a run: carry the 1440 Sun line forward by the 25-minute run (255°, 2.9 M) and cross it with the Moon's.
questions.ref: Sun and Moon — a fix by day

questions.q: Between your two sun sights you altered course for a squall line. What run do you carry the first line by?
questions.why: Add the legs as vectors, not their courses and distances: 245° 12.4 M + 195° 11.0 M = 222° T, 21.2 M.

questions.q: Beating north from Antigua to Bermuda, you will run the 0900 sun line on to noon. Along which direction do you move it?
questions.why: Leeway sets you away from the wind: on starboard tack, heading 015°, the water track is 015° − 8° = 007°; carry the line along that.

questions.q: On day 12 of the ARC your noon sun-run-sun fix lies away from the noon DR worked up from yesterday's noon fix. What current has the boat had?

figure.title: Noon, day 12
lines: Noon DR from log and compass
Noon fix: 14 M on 260° from the DR

questions.why: The set runs from the DR to the fix, and the drift is spread over the time since the last fix: 14 M ÷ 24 h ≈ 0.6 kn on 260°.

questions.q: Bound for Bermuda from the Virgin Islands, you plot an afternoon sun line that runs along your course. What do you do?

figure.title: Afternoon sun line
lines: Course 000° T for Bermuda, 140 M to go
The line passes 9 M east of Bermuda

options: Hold 000°: a course line shows no offset
Alter about 4° to starboard: you are 9 M west of it
Alter about 4° to port: you are 9 M east of the track
Slow down: the line puts you 9 M ahead
questions.why: Sun abeam: the line lies along the course and shows the offset — 9 M east with 140 M to go is about 4° (9/140): alter to port.

questions.q: South of Bermuda you work a Sun and a Moon sight taken together, each from its own AP for HO 249. Which point is your fix?

figure.note: Plotting sheet · APs ringed · azimuths dashed

questions.why: Lay off each intercept from its own AP — the Sun's 4 M towards 232°, the Moon's 6 M away from 128° — and the two lines cross at C.
questions.ref: Sun and Moon — a fix by day

questions.q: Bound from the Galápagos to the Marquesas, you run the 0800 sun line on to the noon latitude in the South Equatorial Current. Which point is your noon fix?
questions.why: Carry the line by the run and the current together — 250° 26 M plus 280° 6 M — then cross it with the noon latitude: B.

questions.q: Cloud closes in after your only sun sight of the morning, worked from a chosen AP for HO 249. Which point do you log as your best position?

figure.note: Plotting sheet · AP chosen for HO 249

questions.why: With one line, the most likely position is the foot of the perpendicular from the DR to the line; the AP's end point is only a plotting point.

questions.q: In a short swell you take five sights of the morning Sun and plot them against time. What do you take into the reduction?

figure.note: Five sights · the line drawn by eye

options: 16:43:00 with Hs 42°21.9′, the mean of all five
16:43:00 with Hs 42°20.8′, read off the line
16:44:09 with Hs 42°36.5′, the last sight as taken
questions.why: Draw the best line through the sights, ignore the one off it, and take a round time with its altitude off the line.
questions.ref: Sun sights — a series of sights

questions.q: Coming down on the Tuamotus from the Marquesas, you work a morning sight with the Sun at right angles to the reef. How far off the reef edge are you?
questions.why: The line runs parallel to the reef: the AP is 14.0 M off it, and the line lies 5.2 M towards the Sun and the reef — 14.0 − 5.2 = 8.8 M.

questions.q: Approaching Falmouth from the Azores, your deep-water sounder first finds bottom at 190 m just as you take a sun sight. Where are you?

figure.note: Depths in metres · contours dashed · B the AP · C the DR

questions.why: Cross the sun line with the 200 m contour, the edge of the shelf: D. Where the bottom rises steeply, a sounding is a position line of its own.

questions.q: Making landfall on the Marquesas, you have a radar range of Ua Huka and a sun line at the same moment. Where are you?

figure.note: Radar range 16 M, dashed · C Ua Huka · D the DR

questions.why: A range and a line cross twice; the DR decides which cut you are at — here B, close to the DR, not A on the far side of the island.

questions.why: Upper limb: SD subtracted. Ho 37°01.9′; LHA 302°04.4′; Hc 36°56.1′, Zn 098°: 5.8 M towards.

questions.q: Running before the SW monsoon from the Seychelles to the Maldives, you work this early-afternoon sight from the DR. What do you plot?

lines: Hs LL 70°59.6′ · IE 0.6′ off the arc

questions.q: Bound from Hawaii to San Francisco, north of the Pacific High, you time this morning sight on a watch kept on UT. What do you plot?

lines: Hs LL 52°13.9′ · IE 1.0′ on the arc

questions.q: Running down the forties from New Zealand to Cape Horn, you work this afternoon sight from the DR. What do you plot?
questions.why: UT 00:34:20 on 22 March — the next day's page. GHA 186°49.1′, LHA 058°19.1′; Ho 20°47.9′, Hc 20°54.1′: 6.2 M away.
questions.ref: Sight reduction — UT from the watch

questions.q: Bound from Tonga to Fiji, you crossed 180° in the night. You work this morning sight from the DR. What do you plot?

figure.title: Sun sight after crossing 180°
lines: Hs LL 37°06.2′ · IE 1.4′ off the arc

questions.q: In the forties between Cape Town and Fremantle in July, you reduce this afternoon sight with HO 249 from a chosen AP. What do you plot from the AP?
On the NE-monsoon run from Phuket to Galle, you work this morning sight from a chosen AP for HO 249. What do you plot, and from where?

figure.title: Sun sight, 18 January 2027
lines: Hs LL 36°43.4′ · IE 0.8′ on the arc
Reduce from an AP for HO 249

options: From the DR 6°50′N 88°40′E: 8.2 M away, Zn 122°
questions.why: AP 7°N 88°22.1′E makes the LHA 314°; Ho 36°54.7′, Hc 37°02.9′: 8.2 M away, Zn 122°, laid off from the AP.

questions.q: Between Bermuda and the Azores you take the Sun and the crescent Moon together and work both from the DR. Where is your fix?
questions.why: Moon Ho = Hs − dip − R + SD + HP × cos Ha (27.9′) = 62°48.0′: 3.9 M away; crossed with the Sun line → 38°13.0′N 40°21.6′W.
questions.ref: Sun and Moon — a fix by day

questions.q: Bound from Tonga to New Zealand, you will pass Minerva Reef after dark and want at least 5 M off it. What does this afternoon sun line tell you?

figure.title: 1500 sun line, reef to the west
lines: Reef edge 020°–200°, parallel to the line
AP 11.0 M east of the reef edge

options: About 3.8 M abeam: alter away now
About 7.2 M abeam: hold your course
About 4.8 M abeam: alter away now
About 9.6 M abeam: hold your course
questions.why: The line is 11.0 − 3.8 = 7.2 M off; four hours of 0.6 kn set towards the reef take 2.4 M: 4.8 M abeam, inside your margin.

questions.q: Crossing the Gulf Stream from Newport to Bermuda, you run the 0900 sun line on to the 1300 sight. Where is your 1300 fix?
questions.why: Carry the 0900 line by the run and the stream together — over the ground 148° 26.5 M — and cross it with the 1300 line: 36°42.3′N 69°36.1′W.

questions.q: You are running down the trades at 20°N and want a dawn star fix. When do you have both the stars and a usable horizon?
options: From 0630 LMT, once the Sun is up
questions.why: Between nautical twilight (Sun 12° down: the horizon appears) and civil twilight (6° down: the stars fade) you have both.

questions.q: You are on the ARC route at 16°N, planning the evening stars. What time do you take for the end of civil twilight?
questions.why: Interpolate between the rows: 16°N is 0.6 of the way from 10°N to 20°N; 1800 − 0.6 × 16 min = 1750 LMT.

questions.q: You have sailed from the Channel down to 10°N. What does this almanac extract mean for your evening star sights?
options: The window is the same — only the clock changes
The window is longer — there is no need to hurry
The window is shorter — be on deck and ready early
Stars can be taken only after nautical twilight here
questions.why: In low latitudes the Sun sinks steeply: civil to nautical twilight takes 24 min at 10°N against 38 min at 50°N.

questions.q: Your crew wants one more star before supper. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Dusk, 20 Jan, lat 14°N
lines: Now 1849: the horizon is a grey blur

options: Go on, and add 5′ for the dim horizon
Go on, with a darker shade on the telescope
Go on — the stars are at their brightest now
Stop — the horizon is too dim to trust
questions.why: After nautical twilight the horizon fades; an altitude measured to a blurred horizon can put the line miles out.

questions.q: You are 600 miles west of the Cape Verdes at dusk with time for three stars before the horizon goes. Which three do you take?
questions.why: Altitudes 20°–70°, azimuths about 120° apart: 073°, 168°, 330°. Peacock is too low; the other sets lie within 180°.

questions.q: Your star finder offers six stars, all between 25° and 60° high. Which three azimuths give you the best three-star fix?
questions.why: Three lines cut best with the bodies about 120° apart; reciprocal bearings give parallel lines, a narrow fan gives shallow cuts.

questions.q: Bound for St Helena, you have planned these four stars for the evening fix. In what order do you shoot them?
questions.why: At dusk the brightest stars show first while the horizon is still sharp: take Sirius first and leave fainter Aldebaran for last.

questions.q: Before dawn you work out where Arcturus will be, so you can find it in the half-light. What do you preset on the sextant, and where do you look?
questions.why: LHA = 217°09.0′ + 145°48′ − 52° = 310°57.0′; the formula gives Hc 43°28′, Zn 080°, east of you (LHA over 180°).

questions.q: Before evening twilight you set up the star finder to see which stars will be up. Which two things do you set it for?
options: Your latitude and LHA Aries at twilight
LHA Aries and the Moon's declination
Your latitude and the Sun's declination
Your longitude and the Sun's GHA
questions.why: Take the template for your latitude and set it to LHA Aries at twilight; it then shows each star's altitude and azimuth.

questions.q: You want the star finder set for tonight's twilight on the Puddle Jump. Which LHA Aries do you set?
You plan tonight's stars with HO 249 Volume 1. What do you enter the table with?
options: Your latitude and each star's SHA
Each star's LHA and its Dec
Your longitude and the time in UT
questions.why: Vol 1 is entered with Lat and LHA Aries: it lists seven selected stars with Hc and Zn, the best three for a fix marked ◆.

questions.q: You have plotted a fix from Volume 1's selected stars. What must you still do to it?

figure.title: HO 249 Volume 1
lines: Fix plotted from three selected stars

options: Correct each Hc by 1′ for every year
Apply the v and d corrections to each Hc
Move it by the precession correction in Table 5
questions.why: Precession slowly shifts the stars; Table 5 gives the small move of the fix for years either side of the tables' epoch.

questions.q: Halfway from Bermuda to the Azores, the cloud clears for a moment and you shoot a bright star you cannot name. Which star was it?
questions.why: sin Dec = sin Lat sin Ho + cos Lat cos Ho cos Zn: Dec N11°44′; LHA 43° (west), SHA = LHA − LHA Aries ≈ 207°.

questions.q: On the trade-wind route at 24°N, an unknown star crosses your meridian due south. Which star is it?
questions.why: z = 90° − 54°32′ = 35°28′; star bearing south: Dec = Lat − z = S11°18′. On the meridian LHA = 0, so SHA = 360° − 201°36′ = 158°24′.

questions.q: At dusk a gap in the cloud shows a bright star you do not recognise, and you take its altitude. What else do you note to identify it afterwards?
options: The Moon's bearing at the same moment
The exact time and its compass bearing
Its colour and how much it twinkles
questions.why: Altitude, azimuth and time give its Dec and SHA by formula or the star finder; then you find it in the almanac's star list.

questions.q: Off the Leeward Islands, you reduce a dawn sight of Sirius from the DR. What is the star's LHA?
You have already worked LHA Aries for your AP and now want Regulus's LHA. What is it?
questions.why: LHA★ = LHA Aries + SHA: 312°10.4′ + 207°36′ = 519°46.4′; take off 360°: 159°46.4′ (the star is west of you).

questions.q: You are crossing the Indian Ocean from Chagos towards the Seychelles. What is Rigel's LHA?
questions.why: Longitude east is added: 298°33.2′ + 72°14.5′ = 370°47.7′; take off 360°: LHA 10°47.7′.

questions.q: Bound from Bermuda to the Azores, you reduce your evening sight of Vega from the DR. What intercept and azimuth do you plot?
On passage from Cape Town to St Helena, you reduce an evening sight of Canopus from the DR. What do you plot?
You compare your observed and calculated altitudes of Spica. What is the intercept?
questions.why: Ho 37°02.6′ − Hc 36°55.9′ = 6.7′; Ho is greater, so the intercept is towards the star.

questions.q: Bound from Tahiti for Rarotonga, at 23°S, you take Z from the tables for a star. What is its true azimuth Zn?
questions.why: South latitude with LHA over 180°: Zn = 180° − Z = 180° − 094° = 086°.

questions.q: You shot an unnamed star and want to identify it with the star finder. How do you use it?
questions.why: Set the template to LHA Aries at the sight; the star is under Ho 52° and the true bearing, 105° − 2°W = 103°.

questions.q: You will reduce a sight of Antares off the coast of Brazil with HO 249. Which assumed position do you use?
questions.why: AP latitude: the nearest whole degree. AP longitude: the one nearest the DR that makes LHA whole: 251°36.8′ − 36°36.8′ = 215°.

questions.q: You plot your Deneb sight from its assumed position. Where do you draw the position line?
options: At right angles to the azimuth, 6 M towards Deneb
At right angles to the azimuth, 6 M away from Deneb
At right angles to the azimuth, through the AP
Along the azimuth line, through the AP
questions.why: Measure the intercept from the AP along the azimuth (towards the body), then draw the position line at right angles there.

questions.q: All three of your stars lie in the eastern sky, and their lines give this cocked hat. What do you make of it?
options: You are at its centre — plot it and go on
You may be outside it — add a star in the west
You are at the corner nearest the DR
It is small, so the fix is good to a mile
questions.why: With all the bodies on one side, a constant error moves every line the same way, so the true position can lie outside the triangle.

questions.q: Four star lines give this plot: three meet in a point and the Spica line passes 8 miles off. What do you do?
options: Average all four and take the middle
Trust Spica — it was the brightest star
Take the point where three meet; recheck Spica
Discard the lot and wait for noon
questions.why: Three lines agreeing in a point outweigh one; the odd line is likely the wrong star, a mistimed sight or a slip in the working.

questions.q: You reduce three stars with HO 249, so each has its own assumed position with a different longitude. How do you plot them?
options: Use the first star's AP for all three
Average the three APs and plot from that
Plot every intercept from the DR
Plot each intercept from its own AP
questions.why: Each intercept belongs to the AP it was worked from; plot each from its own AP and the lines cross at the fix.

questions.q: Your Antares sight comes out 4.5′ away. How do you lay off the intercept?
options: Measure 4.5 M from the AP towards 321°
Measure 4.5 M from the AP towards 051°
Measure 4.5 M from the AP towards 231°
Measure 4.5 M from the AP towards 141°
questions.why: Away: measure from the AP in the reciprocal of Zn, 141° + 180° = 321°, and draw the position line at right angles there.

questions.q: You want the fix for 1911, the time of your last sight. What do you do with the Capella line?
questions.why: 1854 to 1911 is 17 min at 7.5 kn = 2.1 M: transfer the Capella line 2.1 M along the course, 250°.

questions.q: Instead of moving the Deneb line on the plot, you correct its intercept for the run to 1916. What intercept do you plot?
questions.why: Run 24 min at 8 kn = 3.2 M; its part towards Deneb is 3.2 × cos 60° = 1.6 M; 3.4′ + 1.6′ = 5.0′ towards.

questions.q: You reduce an evening sight of Venus taken at 1823:40 UT. What is its GHA?
questions.why: 142°17.6′ + 5°55.0′ = 148°12.6′; v −0.9 for 24 min gives −0.4′: GHA 148°12.2′. Venus's v can be negative.

questions.q: Working a sight of Mars taken at 2142:08 UT, you open the increments page. What is Mars's GHA?
questions.why: Planets use the Sun/planets column: 77°31.4′ + 10°32.0′ + v 0.8′ (1.1 × 42/60) = 88°04.2′.

questions.q: You want a fix this afternoon, not at dusk. What do you do?

figure.title: Afternoon, mid-Atlantic
lines: Venus mag −4.6, 45° east of the Sun
Clear sky; Venus's Hc and Zn worked out

options: Wait for dusk — planets cannot be seen by day
Preset Venus's Hc and sweep along its Zn
Take a second sun line five minutes later
Take the Sun's upper limb for a second line
questions.why: Bright Venus can be found by day with the sextant preset to its Hc on its Zn; its line crosses the sun line for a fix.

questions.q: Jupiter is the bright, steady light in the east at dusk, and you have shot it. Where do you find its GHA and Dec?
options: In the star list, from its SHA
In its own column on the almanac's daily page
From the Sun's GHA and declination
questions.why: Planets move against the stars, so each has GHA and Dec hourly in its own daily-page column; only stars are worked from SHA.

questions.q: Bound from Cocos Keeling to Rodrigues, you take Jupiter at dawn and work it from the DR. What intercept and azimuth do you plot?
At 0930 you want a Moon sight to cross with the Sun. Which limb do you bring down to the horizon?

figure.title: Morning Moon
lines: Last-quarter Moon, low in the west
Sun well up in the east
The Moon's bright side faces up

options: The upper limb — the lit edge
The centre — judge it by eye
The lower limb — the dark edge is sharper
The lower limb — it is always the lower
questions.why: Always use the lit limb, and the lit side faces the Sun: with the Sun higher than the Moon, the top edge is lit.

questions.q: You correct an upper-limb Moon sight with the almanac's Moon tables. What is Ho?
questions.why: Ha + first part 54.1′ + second part, U column 1.7′ − 30′ for the upper limb = 41°43.8′.

questions.q: Approaching Fernando de Noronha, you work your afternoon Moon sight from the DR. What intercept and azimuth do you plot?
You need Venus's declination for a sight at 1845 UT. What is it?
questions.why: The next hour shows Dec increasing: d 0.9′ × 45/60 = 0.7′; S21°14.2′ + 0.7′ = S21°14.9′.

questions.q: You take the Sun and the half Moon within minutes of each other in the afternoon. What do the two position lines give you?
options: They cut at about 74° — a good fix
They cut at about 37° — latitude only
They cut at about 16° — too fine to use
They run parallel — no fix by day
questions.why: Lines cut at the angle between the azimuths: 238° − 132° = 106°, i.e. 74°. Near the quarters the Moon is about 90° from the Sun.

questions.q: What is the Moon's GHA for your sight at 1531:20 UT?
Your GPS has failed mid-ocean and you want Sun–Moon fixes by day. Around which days of this month do you plan them?
options: Around the 16th and the 31st — the quarters
Any day the Moon is in the sky
questions.why: Near the quarters the Moon is about 90° from the Sun and up by day; at new Moon it is lost in the glare, at full Moon up only at night.

questions.q: One of your three dawn sights gives this. What do you do with it?

figure.title: “Sirius”
lines: The other two stars agree within 1.5′

options: Move the fix halfway towards its line
Plot it — the DR must be 128 miles out
Rework the other two from its AP
Leave it out — it was not Sirius
questions.why: A huge intercept and a bearing 40° off the prediction mean the wrong body; fix from the two good lines and a re-shot star.

questions.q: At dusk you look for Capella where you predicted it and see this. Which light do you bring down?

figure.title: Dusk, looking for Capella
lines: At 046°: a brilliant steady light, 28° up
At 043°: a star as bright as Vega, 31° up

options: Whichever is easier to hold in the mirror
Neither — Capella cannot be up yet
questions.why: Capella matches the predicted Hc and Zn and is about as bright as Vega; a brilliant steady light near it is a planet.

questions.q: Your star finder still has Jupiter marked where you plotted it a month ago. What do you do before tonight's planning?

figure.title: Star finder, before twilight
lines: Venus and Mars not yet plotted

options: Move it by the Table 5 precession correction
Re-plot it from this week's almanac SHA and Dec
Nothing — a planet keeps its SHA like a star
Leave it off — planets cannot go on a star finder
questions.why: Planets wander among the stars; the almanac's daily pages give their current SHA and Dec to plot them afresh.

questions.q: Cloud let you have only one star at dawn. You want a running fix at 0935 with your sun line. What do you do?
options: Advance the star line 21 M along 080°
Advance the sun line 21 M along 260°
Advance the star line 21 M along 260°
Advance the star line 6 M along 260°
questions.why: 0605 to 0935 is 3h30m at 6 kn = 21 M: advance the earlier star line 21 M along 260° to cross the sun line.

questions.q: Cloud is building and you may get only one star at dusk to cross with your advanced afternoon sun line. Which star do you take first?

figure.title: Sun line 1530, Zn 239°
lines: Dusk stars from the star finder:

questions.why: Deneb's line cuts the sun line at about 91°; the others bear within 30° of the Sun's azimuth or its reciprocal.

questions.q: You come on deck for dawn sights and the stars are still bright. What are you waiting for before the first sight?
options: The horizon to sharpen below the stars
The Moon to light up the horizon
The stars to grow brighter in the dark
The Sun's upper limb to show
questions.why: At dawn the stars are there first and you wait for the horizon; at dusk the horizon is sharp and you wait for the stars.

questions.q: At dawn you plan these four stars. In what order do you take them?
questions.why: At dawn the faintest stars fade first: start with Dubhe and keep bright Arcturus for last, as the sky lightens.

questions.q: A crew member on her first ocean passage asks which planets she can use for sights. Which four have their own columns in the almanac?
questions.why: The almanac tabulates GHA and Dec for the four navigational planets: Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn. Mercury keeps too close to the Sun.

questions.q: Bound from Rio for Cape Town, you take Achernar at dusk and work it from the DR. What Hc and Zn do you get?
questions.why: LHA = 335°27.5′ + 335°21′ − 22°40′ = 288°08.5′: west longitude is subtracted. The formula then gives Hc 35°23.9′, Zn 141°.

questions.q: Bound from Shetland to Norway at midsummer, you want a star fix tonight. When do you take it?
options: Between 2314 and 0049 LMT, bright stars only
After nautical twilight ends, as usual
Between 2128 and 2314 LMT, in civil twilight
Not tonight — no star will show at all
questions.why: The Sun never gets 12° down, so the horizon stays all night; between the two civil twilights only the brightest stars and planets show.

questions.q: South of St Helena in July, you will have a noon latitude today. Which dawn star gives the best line to cross with it?
questions.why: The noon Sun bears north, so its line runs east–west; Rigel at Zn 086° gives a north–south line that cuts it near 90°.

questions.q: It is 0200 under a bright Moon and you doubt your DR. What is the catch if you take star sights now?

figure.title: 0200, mid-ocean
lines: Full Moon 50° up in the south-west

options: Stars near the Moon need its parallax
The bright horizon under the Moon may be false
The stars are too faint to find by moonlight
questions.why: The Moon's glitter can show a line short of the true horizon: trust a moonlit horizon only when other lines confirm it.

questions.q: Leaving Cape Town for Brazil, you plan the first dusk fix. Which three stars do you take?
questions.why: The bright southern stars bunch in the south: take Canopus 137°, Fomalhaut 252° and Aldebaran 012°. Acrux and Peacock are low.

questions.q: Bound from Sydney for Lord Howe Island at 33°S, you work Antares with HO 249. What is its true azimuth?
questions.why: South latitude, LHA under 180° (the star is west of you): Zn = 180° + Z = 180° + 095° = 275°.

questions.q: At dawn off the Marquesas the eastern horizon is sharp but the west is still dark and hazy. In what order do you take these four stars?

figure.title: Dawn, 15 Mar, 15°S 140°W
lines: Horizon: sharp in the east, hazy in the west

questions.why: At dawn the eastern horizon sharpens first and the western last: start with Altair in the east and leave Spica, in the west, till last.

questions.q: Crossing the Arabian Sea from Salalah towards Cochin, you take Fomalhaut at dusk and work it from the DR. What Hc and Zn do you get?
questions.why: LHA = 252°58.7′ + 15°18′ + 60°18′ = 328°34.7′. Dec S with Lat N: contrary names, so Dec goes in negative: Hc 36°55.4′, Zn 145°.

questions.q: On passage from the Faroes to Iceland in October, you plan the dusk fix at 62°N. Which three stars do you take?
questions.why: High in the north many stars stand near the zenith: Deneb is 71° up. Arcturus, Altair and Mirfak are 20°–70° up and about 120° apart.

questions.q: Hove-to in a gale in the Agulhas Current, you get two stars 39 minutes apart. How do you bring the first line up to the time of the second?

figure.title: Hove-to off South Africa, dusk
lines: Drift from the last fixes: 225°, 1.5 kn

questions.why: Hove-to, the boat still drifts: 39 min at 1.5 kn = 1.0 M. Move the first line 1.0 M along the drift, 225°.

questions.q: On your first night in the South Pacific, you want Acrux for the dusk fix. Where on the Southern Cross do you look?
options: In the middle, where the two arms meet
At the foot — the bright star nearest the pole
At the head — the top of the long arm
At the east end of the cross-bar
questions.why: Acrux is the foot of the Cross; the long arm, from the head through Acrux, points towards the south celestial pole.

questions.q: Leaving Fremantle for Mauritius, you will reduce Spica with HO 249. Which assumed position do you use?
questions.why: East longitude is added: choose the minutes that make LHA whole, 287°23.6′ + 115°36.4′ = 403° = LHA 43°, and the latitude nearest the DR.

questions.q: In the afternoon mid-Atlantic, you have a sun line and two other bodies in the sky. Which do you take to cross with the Sun?
options: Neither — wait for the dusk stars
Venus — it is the brighter of the two
Venus — it is nearer the Sun in the sky
The Moon — its line cuts the sun line at 85°
questions.why: Lines cut at the difference in azimuth: Sun–Moon 85°, Sun–Venus 49°. The Moon, near first quarter, gives the better fix.

questions.q: Crossing the trades, you shoot three stars over 32 minutes while the North Equatorial Current sets you west. How do you move the first line to the time of the last?
questions.why: Advance by the run over the ground: 3.5 M along 255° plus 0.5 M along 280° = 4.0 M along 258°.

questions.q: Bound for Tristan da Cunha, you look over tonight's planned stars. Which one do you leave out?
options: Achernar — it is too near the meridian
Peacock — it is too far south
questions.why: At 87° the azimuth is hard to judge and the sextant hard to swing; keep to 20°–70° — Hamal at 21° still serves.

questions.q: You plot three star intercepts from one AP. Which point is the fix?
questions.why: Lay off 3.5′ towards 040°, 0.9′ away from 160° and 2.6′ away from 280°: the lines meet 3 M east and 2 M north of the AP.

questions.q: You want the fix for 1910, the time of your middle star. What do you do with the Rigel line taken at 1920?
options: Leave it — it is the last sight
questions.why: Retire it to 1910: 10 min at 7 kn = 1.2 M back along the track, 075°. The 1858 line goes 1.4 M forward along 255°.

questions.q: Halfway along the ARC to St Lucia, you add Saturn to the dusk fix and work it from the DR. What do you plot?
Approaching the Virgin Islands, you want Venus in tonight's dusk fix. When do you take it?
options: With the stars, once they all show
First, at about 1800, while it is over 10° up
Last, at the end of nautical twilight
Never — a planet is too bright to use
questions.why: Venus shows long before the stars and sinks fast: take it first, above 10°, before the large and uncertain refraction near the horizon.

questions.q: The dusk sky is clear and you have time for five stars. A crew member says three is enough. Why take all five?
options: The almanac's corrections need five sights
Five lines always make the hat smaller
An odd line shows up and can be left out
Each extra star halves the error of the fix
questions.why: With three lines a bad sight hides inside the hat; with four or five, the lines that agree show up the one that does not.

questions.q: Venus is crossing the equator this morning. What declination do you use for your sight at 1145 UT?
questions.why: Dec moves 1.2′ an hour northward: S0°00.7′ + 0.9′ north (45/60 of 1.2′) crosses the equator: N0°00.2′.

questions.q: Your afternoon sun line, run up to dusk, passes 5 miles south of a neat three-star fix. What do you make of it?

figure.title: Dusk, 1840
lines: Sun line at 1500, run up 22 M (6 kn)
It passes 5 M south of the star fix

options: Trust the stars — the 22 M run carries the error
Trust the sun line — the Sun is the surer body
Rework the stars — three lines cannot all be wrong
Move the fix halfway to the sun line
questions.why: The stars were taken together, with no run; the sun line was carried 22 M on the log and compass, so any current or leeway sits in it.

questions.q: You will correct tonight's Moon sight. Where do you find the Moon's horizontal parallax?
options: On the increments page, beside v and d
On the daily page, beside its GHA and Dec for the hour
In HO 249 Volume 1, with the selected stars
In the star list at the back of the almanac
questions.why: The Moon's HP changes through the month (about 54′ to 61′), so the daily page gives it hour by hour with GHA, v, Dec and d.

questions.q: South of Madagascar, bound for Durban, you take the Moon at dusk and work it from the DR. What do you plot?
Working tonight's Moon sight, what declination do you take for 0438 UT?
questions.why: The next hour shows Dec falling: d 9.5′ × 38/60 = 6.0′; N23°35.7′ − 6.0′ = N23°29.7′. The Moon's d is large: never skip it.

questions.q: Mid-Atlantic at dusk, your Rigel sight comes out 87 miles away. What do you make of it?
options: You took Betelgeuse — rework it as Betelgeuse
The horizon was poor — leave it out
Rework it as Rigel from a new AP
The DR is 87 miles out — plot it
questions.why: Its altitude and bearing fit Betelgeuse, Orion's other bright star, about 20° from Rigel: rework it with Betelgeuse's SHA and Dec.

questions.q: Your mate's three-star plot gives a 7-mile cocked hat, and you find he plotted Altair's intercept the wrong way. How far does the Altair line move when you correct it?
questions.why: The line lay 3.5 M on the wrong side of the AP; corrected, it moves 2 × 3.5 = 7.0 M towards Altair.

questions.q: At dawn between the Azores and the Caribbean, you work Jupiter and Rigel from the same DR. Where is your fix?
questions.why: Rigel away at 181°: 2.9′ north. Jupiter towards at 088°: 3.9 M east = 4.4′ of longitude at 28°N: 28°12.9′N 40°20.6′W.

questions.q: Planning tonight's dusk fix, you read the almanac's planet notes for the month. Which planets can you add to your stars?

figure.title: Planet notes, this month
lines: Venus: a morning star, rises before the Sun
Mars: too close to the Sun to observe

questions.why: Only planets above the horizon at dusk help: Jupiter and Saturn. Venus rises before dawn and Mars is lost in the Sun's glare.

questions.q: Approaching the Tuamotus from the Marquesas at dusk, you most want your distance off the atolls. Which star do you take first?

figure.title: Dusk, 11 May, 30 M from the Tuamotus

questions.why: A position line runs at 90° to the bearing: Canopus at 214° gives a line along the chain, 124°–304°, so your distance off it.

questions.q: Your three stars were spread about 120° apart and their lines give this small cocked hat. Where do you put the fix?
options: On the line of the brightest star
In the middle of the triangle
Outside the triangle, towards the stars
At the corner nearest the DR
questions.why: With the bodies spread round the horizon, the true position most likely lies inside a small hat: take its centre.

questions.q: At dawn you chose two stars on almost opposite bearings, and their lines lie parallel, 3 miles apart. What does that tell you?
options: You are 3 M beyond the farther line
You are on the line of the brighter star
You are near the line midway between them
Nothing — parallel lines are of no use
questions.why: A constant error (dip, index error) moves the two lines opposite ways; the mean line between them is free of it.

questions.q: Bound from Fiji to Tonga, you have just crossed the 180th meridian eastbound. You take Rigil Kent at dusk and work it from the DR. What do you plot?
You plan dawn stars on the way from the Marquesas to Tahiti. When do you come on deck?
options: Before 0516, to find the stars in the dark
After 0602, once the horizon is bright
questions.why: Find the stars and preset the sextant while it is still dark; shoot as the horizon sharpens, between nautical and civil twilight.

questions.q: At 0300 you took three stars by the light of a nearly full Moon and plotted them. Which line do you distrust?
options: None — moonlight gives a true horizon
Hamal's — it bore under the Moon
Dubhe's — it was the lowest of the three
questions.why: The horizon under the Moon's glitter may be false; the line of the star taken beneath it is the one to doubt and re-shoot at dawn.

questions.q: After two cloudy days your DR may be 40 miles out. How far from your preset Hc may Sirius appear when you look for it?

figure.title: After two cloudy days
lines: DR uncertain by up to 40 M

options: Not at all — a DR error does not change Hc
Up to about 4′ — it will be in the eyepiece
Up to about 40′ — sweep a little up and down
Up to about 4° — use the star finder instead
questions.why: 1′ of altitude is 1 M of distance: a 40 M error in the DR can put the star up to 40′ off the preset Hc, and its Zn a little out too.

questions.q: Four dusk stars from one AP: three lines meet within a mile, but Regulus comes out like this. What most likely went wrong?
options: Its time was a minute out — rework the GHA
Refraction was left out — add it to Hs
It was the wrong star — leave it out
Its sextant reading was 1° out — add 1° and rework
questions.why: 58.7′ away, against 1.3′ towards that fits the other three, is 60′: Hs was read or written 1° low.

questions.q: Leaving the Bay of Islands for Tonga, you list the dusk stars. Which two would give almost the same position line?
questions.why: Two stars on almost the same bearing give almost the same line; keep the higher one and spend the time on another bearing.

questions.q: At 0100 LMT a brilliant, steady white light stands high in the sky, and your crew calls it Venus. Which planet is it?

figure.title: 15 Jan, 20°N 60°W, 0100 LMT
lines: The Sun set seven hours ago

options: Venus — it is the brightest planet
Jupiter — Venus is never far from the Sun
Saturn — it is the slowest planet
Mars — it is brightest at midnight
questions.why: Venus is never more than about 47° from the Sun, so it is never high in the middle of the night; a brilliant white planet there is Jupiter.

questions.q: Cloud leaves you only two stars, and their lines cut at 30°. If one line is a mile out, how far can that move the fix?

figure.title: Two-star fix
lines: Each line good to about 1 M

options: About 0.5 M along the other line
About 1.0 M along the other line
About 2.0 M along the other line
About 1.2 M along the other line
questions.why: Moving one line 1 M shifts the cut 1 / sin 30° = 2 M along the other line; at a 90° cut it would be only 1 M.

questions.q: After two days of cloud your star intercepts are all about 30 miles, though the lines meet in a small hat. What do you do next?
options: Shorten each intercept by a tenth
Take a point halfway back to the DR
Plot it as it is — the hat is small
Rework the sights with the fix as a new DR
questions.why: A position line is a short straight piece of a large circle; with intercepts over about 30′ the curve tells, so rework from the new position.

questions.q: Bound from Iceland for Newfoundland, you take Kochab at dusk at 58°N and work it from the DR. What Hc and Zn do you get?
questions.why: GHA★ = GHA Aries + SHA: LHA = 349°10.8′ + 137°18′ − 30°10′ = 96°18.8′. Kochab never sets here, so a slip still gives a believable Hc.

questions.q: Your dusk and dawn star fixes are 11 hours apart. The dawn fix lies here against your DR. What current has set you overnight?
questions.why: DR to fix over the 11 h is the current: 6.6 M ÷ 11 h = 0.6 kn, setting 290°, from the DR towards the fix.

questions.q: You will reduce tonight's Jupiter and Moon sights with HO 249. Which volume do you open?
options: None — HO 249 is for stars only
Vol 1, with Lat and LHA Aries
Vol 2 or 3, with Lat, LHA and Dec
Vol 1 for Jupiter, Vol 3 for the Moon
questions.why: Vol 1 holds selected stars only; Vols 2 (Lat 0°–39°) and 3 (40°–89°) take any body with Dec up to 29°, planets and the Moon included.

questions.q: Before dawn you want a Moon sight to go with the stars. Which limb do you expect to bring down to the horizon?

figure.title: 0330, three days after full Moon
lines: The Sun rises at 0610, in the east

options: Either — a gibbous Moon is lit all round
The lower limb — the Sun is below the horizon
The lower limb — it is the one used at night
The upper limb — the lit side faces up
questions.why: The lit limb faces the Sun along the great circle to it; from a Moon high in the west that circle runs up over the zenith, so the top is lit.

questions.q: On your first night in the southern sky, you look for the Southern Cross to find Acrux and see this. Is it the Cross?

figure.title: Looking south at dusk
lines: A cross of four stars, mag about 2
No bright pair of stars beside it

options: Probably the False Cross — find the Pointers first
No — that shape is Orion's Belt
Yes — it is the only cross in the sky
Yes — take its brightest star as Acrux
questions.why: The False Cross is bigger and fainter; the real Cross is small, with two bright Pointers, Rigil Kent and Hadar, leading to it.

questions.q: Bound for Nouméa at night, your three-star fix gives this large cocked hat, with the barrier reef to the south-west. What do you do?
options: Take the corner nearest the DR and hold on
Assume the corner nearest the reef and rework
Ignore the fix and trust the DR
Take the centre and hold your course
questions.why: A big hat means a bad sight or a slip: until you find it, navigate from the most dangerous corner, keep sea room, and rework or re-shoot.

questions.q: Cloud closes in after Jupiter and Spica, whose lines cut at about 90°. How far do you trust this fix?
options: Fully — two lines at 90° cannot be wrong
Not at all — a planet and a star do not mix
A good cut, but no check against a bad sight
For latitude only — Spica is near the meridian
questions.why: Two lines always meet somewhere, so a blunder in either goes unseen; use the fix with care and add a third body as soon as you can.

questions.q: Off the Queensland coast, bound for New Caledonia, you work Achernar at dusk. What is its LHA?
You plan a compass check by amplitude at sunrise on the ARC route. At which moment do you take the Sun's bearing?

figure.title: Sunrise amplitude
lines: Clear eastern horizon, light trade wind

options: Lower limb half a diameter above the visible horizon
Upper limb just clearing the visible horizon
Sun's centre about 5° above the visible horizon
Lower limb just touching the visible horizon
questions.why: The amplitude is for the Sun's centre on the celestial horizon: with refraction and dip, the lower limb then shows about half a diameter up.

questions.q: You check the steering compass by the Sun's amplitude at sunrise. What is the compass error?

figure.title: Sunrise, 25 November
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

questions.why: sin Amp = sin 20°46′ / cos 17° → Amp E21.8°S, true bearing 111.8°; error = true − compass = 111.8° − 118° = 6°W.

questions.q: You are on the Pacific Puddle Jump and take an amplitude at sunset. What true bearing do you compare with the compass?

figure.title: Sunset, 10 April
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

questions.why: sin Amp = sin 8°11′ / cos 12° → Amp 8.4°, from west toward the Dec's name (N): 270° + 8° = 278°T.

questions.q: You want to catch the sunrise for an amplitude. Where on the horizon do you look for the Sun?
questions.why: The Sun rises toward the name of its Dec in either hemisphere: sin Amp = sin 23°26′ / cos 20° → E25°N, about 065°.

questions.q: You take an amplitude at sunset to check the compass. Which true bearing do you use?

figure.title: Sunset, 20 March
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

questions.why: With Dec 0° sin Amp = 0: at the equinox the Sun's centre sets due west, 270°T, in any latitude.

questions.q: You check the steering compass by amplitude on your present heading. What deviation do you log?
questions.why: Amp W23.4°S → 246.6°T; error 246.6° − 255° = 8°W; deviation = error − variation = 8°W − 11°W = 3°E.

questions.q: You take a sunrise amplitude on the way to the Azores. What is the Sun's true bearing?

figure.title: Sunrise, 21 June
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

questions.why: sin Amp = sin 23°26′ / cos 38° → Amp 30.3°, east toward N: 090° − 30° = 060°T. The higher the latitude, the bigger the amplitude.

questions.q: You take the Sun's bearing mid-morning for a compass check. Which true azimuth do you compare it with?
questions.why: Zn = atan2(−cos Dec sin LHA, cos Lat sin Dec − sin Lat cos Dec cos LHA) = 127°; LHA over 180° puts the Sun in the east.

questions.q: You check the compass by the Sun's azimuth on your way to Antigua. What is the deviation on this heading?

figure.title: Afternoon sun, 1 December
lines: Sun bears 246°C over the steering compass

questions.q: You want the Sun's azimuth for a compass check today. Which of these times do you choose?
options: 1145 — the Sun is high and bright to sight
0730 — the Sun is low, its bearing easy to take
1215 — just after noon, the Sun is steady
Any of them — the azimuth is computed anyway
questions.why: A high Sun is hard to bear accurately and near noon in the tropics its bearing swings fast: take the azimuth with the Sun low.

questions.q: Bound for Cape Town, you use HO 249 for the Sun's azimuth to check the compass. What Zn do you take?
questions.why: South latitude, LHA less than 180°: Zn = 180° + Z = 180° + 97° = 277°T.

questions.q: At evening twilight you take Sirius over the steering compass. What deviation do you log for this heading?

figure.title: Evening twilight, 15 February
lines: Sirius bears 145°C over the steering compass

questions.q: You check the compass by the Sun's azimuth in the South Atlantic. What is the compass error?

figure.title: Morning sun, 15 January
lines: DR 25°S 6°E, Cape Town to St Helena
Sun bears 094°C over the steering compass

questions.why: LHA = GHA + longitude east = 297°41′ + 6° = 303°41′ → Zn 098°T; error = 098° − 094° = 4°E (compass least, error east).

questions.q: Two days from Saint Lucia you check the steering compass on Polaris. What is the compass error?

figure.title: Evening twilight, ARC route
lines: Polaris bears 357° by the steering compass

questions.why: In low latitudes Polaris is within about 1° of true north: error = 000° − 357° = 3°E; the compass reads low.

questions.q: You plan your compass checks for the next week on this passage. Which of these is no use to you here?

figure.title: Marquesas to the Tuamotus
lines: Clear nights, sharp horizon at twilight

options: The azimuth of a bright star
The Sun's azimuth in the morning
questions.why: Polaris lies within about 1° of the north celestial pole: south of the equator it is below your horizon.

questions.q: You use Polaris to check the steering compass on this heading. What deviation do you log?

figure.title: Polaris check, 40°N
lines: Bermuda to the Azores, evening twilight
Polaris bears 006° by the steering compass

questions.why: Error = 359.2° − 006° = 6.8°W; deviation = error − variation = 6.8°W − 12°W = 5.2°, about 5°E.

questions.q: Making landfall in the Azores, you steer along this transit. What deviation do you log for this heading?
questions.why: A transit needs no almanac: error = 248° − 252° = 4°W; deviation = error − variation = 4°W − 7°W = 3°E.

questions.q: Crossing the Indian Ocean, the Sun's azimuth this morning gives this compass error on your present heading. What is the deviation?
questions.why: Deviation = error − variation = 6°W − 4°W = 2°W (west counted negative).

questions.q: You have steered this compass course all watch on the ARC. What true course do you plot on the plotting sheet?
questions.why: True = compass + deviation + variation, east +, west −: 263° + 2°E − 16°W = 249°T.

questions.q: In the trades you gybe onto a new heading. What do you now take as the deviation?

figure.title: Deviation log, day 6
lines: No check yet on the new heading

options: 1°E — it was found only this morning
Unknown until you check it on 200°C
questions.why: Deviation changes with the ship's head: a value found on 260°C does not hold on 200°C — check again or use the card for that heading.

questions.q: You load the boat in Las Palmas for the Atlantic crossing. What do you do about the steering compass?

figure.title: Las Palmas, the day before the start
lines: Spare anchor and chain in the cockpit locker
Two dive tanks lashed beside the binnacle
Compass checked and carded last spring

options: Check its deviation again on several headings
Use last spring's card — the compass hasn't moved
Allow a flat 5° on every heading for the steel
Rely on the fluxgate — it ignores nearby steel
questions.why: New steel near the compass changes its deviation: move it away if you can, then check the deviation afresh on several headings.

questions.q: You fill in the deviation log on the crossing. What else do you need to find the deviation?
options: The log reading at the time
The Sun's altitude at the time
The height of eye on deck
questions.why: Deviation = error − variation: read the variation for your DR position from the pilot chart or the chart.

questions.q: Crossing westward from the Canaries, you check the compass on the same heading. What does the log tell you?
options: The compass is failing and needs a swing
questions.why: Deviation = error − variation: 7 − 6, 12 − 11 and 16 − 15 all give 1°W. The growing error is the variation across the ocean.

questions.q: You need the variation for tonight's compass check. What value do you use?

figure.title: Pilot chart, North Atlantic
lines: Your DR: 3/5 of the way from 10°W to 15°W

questions.why: Interpolate between the isogonic lines: 10° + 3/5 × 5° = 13°W.

questions.q: You take the variation for your compass checks from the chart's compass rose. What do you use?
You fit a new autopilot with a fluxgate compass before an ocean passage and find this. What do you do?
options: Apply 8° to every heading shown on the fluxgate
Run its calibration turns in calm water, then compare
Move the steering compass until the two agree
Trust the fluxgate — electronic compasses have no deviation
questions.why: A fluxgate also senses the boat's magnetism: its calibration (slow full circles) compensates it; then check it against the steering compass.

questions.q: With the electrics down for the rest of the passage, what do you steer by?
options: The fluxgate on the engine battery
questions.why: The magnetic steering compass needs no power: keep it lit at night with a torch and keep checking its error.

questions.q: The autopilot shows true heading. What is the steering compass's deviation on this heading?
questions.why: True to magnetic: 253°T + 12°W = 265°M; deviation = magnetic − compass = 265° − 262° = 3°E.

questions.q: You switch on the backup GPS mid-ocean and see this. Why is there no position yet?

figure.title: GNSS status page
lines: Antenna clear of the rig, open sky

options: It needs a fourth satellite to solve its clock error
Three satellites give only a line, not a point
It needs one satellite in each quadrant of the sky
It needs six — two for each of three axes
questions.why: Each satellite gives a range from the signal's travel time; with the receiver's clock unknown, three ranges and the clock need four.

questions.q: You plan to enter the lagoon using the plotter. What does this GNSS status tell you?

figure.title: Approaching a Tuamotu pass
lines: Satellites used: 5, all low to the north
Pass 150 m wide, reef on both sides

options: An HDOP over 5 means the fix is good to 5 m
Poor geometry: the fix may be tens of metres out
The fix is good; HDOP affects only height
The plotter would warn you of any bad fix
questions.why: HDOP multiplies the range error and bunched satellites give a high HDOP: enter the pass by eye in good light, not by the plotter.

questions.q: You fit this receiver for the ocean passage. What do you gain by leaving all the systems on?
options: A separate datum for each system
An accurate fix without any clock
More satellites: better geometry, fewer gaps
A fix that cannot be jammed
questions.why: GPS (USA), Galileo (EU), GLONASS (Russia) and BeiDou (China) all give ranges: more satellites mean a lower DOP and more resilience.

questions.q: Approaching the atoll at dusk, the plotter shows you safely 0.4 M off the reef. What do you do?

figure.title: Chart of a Pacific atoll
lines: Note: positions may be 1 M in error
Plotter: boat 0.4 M from the reef

options: Change the plotter's datum and carry on
Carry on: GPS is accurate to a few metres
Shift the GPS position 1 M and carry on
Stand off until daylight: the chart may be a mile out
questions.why: GPS is good to metres, but an old survey can put the reef a mile from where it lies: keep sea room, use radar and your eyes.

questions.q: Your old paper chart of a Pacific island uses a local datum and carries this note. Which position do you plot?
questions.why: In south latitude moving north reduces the latitude; in west longitude moving west increases it: 26.40′ − 0.15′, 36.10′ + 0.42′.

questions.q: Bound for the Indian Ocean, you see this at night. What do you do?
options: Restart all the receivers until one gets a fix
Treat it as jamming: DR from the last fix, radar, log it
Heave to until the GPS signal comes back
Steer for the last waypoint on the plotter
questions.why: Every receiver losing the fix at once points to jamming: navigate by DR, radar and sights, and report and log the outage.

questions.q: Crossing the Arabian Sea at night, you see this. What do you do?

figure.title: Gulf of Oman approach, 0200
lines: AIS: two ships shown at an airport ashore
Radar: coast 12 M off, not as on the plotter

options: Trust the GPS position — the log must be fouled
Average the GPS and DR positions and carry on
Treat all GNSS as spoofed: DR, radar ranges, sights
Reboot the plotter and carry on navigating by it
questions.why: A frozen, plausible position that disagrees with the log and radar is spoofing: navigate independently of GNSS and report it.

questions.q: Halfway across the Atlantic, the receiver shows this. How far can you trust the position?
options: Not at all until SBAS comes back
To 1 cm — SBAS is no longer needed
Only to about a mile without SBAS
To within about 10 m — ample for the ocean
questions.why: SBAS (EGNOS, WAAS) corrects only within its service area; plain GPS with a good HDOP is good to metres — ample offshore.

questions.q: On passage from the Bahamas to Beaufort, North Carolina, you receive this warning. What do you plan?

figure.title: NAVAREA IV warning
lines: GPS testing: signals may be unreliable

options: A good fix before, then DR, and the sextant ready
Nothing — the warning is for ships, not yachts
Steer by GPS COG, which is not affected
Reset the receiver at 1300 to clear the fault
questions.why: In an outage window, start DR from a known fix, keep the log and compass courses, and check with sights or radar.

questions.q: Crossing the doldrums at night, what do you do with the handheld GPS and the spare VHF?

figure.title: ITCZ, 0100
lines: Lightning every few seconds, 2–3 M off
Handheld GPS and VHF on the chart table

options: Keep them on deck in the grab bag
Put them in the oven, disconnected
Switch them on to log the position
Plug them into ship's power to stay charged
questions.why: A strike can kill everything wired to the boat: a closed metal box like the oven shields unconnected spares as a Faraday cage.

questions.q: You find this on the watch log. What is the most likely fault?
options: The whole GPS system is down
The plotter's chart card has failed
The shared GPS antenna or its cable
The AIS transponder is being jammed
questions.why: The handheld has a fix, so the satellites are fine; plotter and AIS share one antenna, so check it and its cable first.

questions.q: You review the boat's systems before a 3,000-mile passage. What is the best change?

figure.title: Navigation wiring
lines: One GPS antenna on the stern arch
It feeds plotter, AIS, autopilot, DSC VHF
All on one house battery bank

options: Fit a bigger house battery bank instead
Add a second plotter on the same antenna
Carry a spare antenna cable, nothing else
Give the DSC VHF its own GPS and carry a handheld
questions.why: One antenna and one battery feed everything, even the DSC distress position: add an independent source and a handheld.

questions.q: You check the grab bag before leaving the Canaries. What do you add for the handheld GPS?

figure.title: Ocean grab bag check
lines: Handheld VHF, flares, water, first-aid kit
Handheld GPS in a waterproof pouch

options: Spare lithium batteries, sealed in the bag
Nothing — it lasts weeks on one set
A paper chart of the destination
A charging lead for the ship's 12 V
questions.why: There is no charging in the raft: a tested handheld GPS with sealed spare batteries gives your position to rescuers.

questions.q: Mid-Atlantic, your family sees your AIS position online. How does it reach them?

figure.title: Message from home, day 9
lines: Family: 'We see you on a tracking website'
Nearest ship on your AIS: none for 2 days

options: Ships within VHF range relay it by DSC
Satellites pick up your AIS signal and relay it
Your EPIRB transmits it every six hours
Your AIS sends it by HF radio every hour
questions.why: Satellites in orbit receive AIS transmissions and pass them ashore; ships still see you only within VHF range, some 20 M.

questions.q: Mid-ocean, how do you get the next GRIB file?

figure.title: Weather at sea
lines: Need: GRIB for the next 5 days

options: Download it by VHF from the nearest coast station
Wait for the GPS to update the forecast
Request a small GRIB by email over the Iridium link
Receive it on NAVTEX at 518 kHz
questions.why: Iridium covers the whole globe: a small compressed GRIB by email arrives in minutes; NAVTEX and VHF reach only near the coast.

questions.q: You plan this high-latitude summer passage. What do you do about communications?

figure.title: Summer passage to Svalbard
lines: Route north of 75°N for two weeks

options: Keep Inmarsat alone: it covers the whole globe
Rely on VHF DSC: it reaches satellites overhead
Rely on NAVTEX: it carries email up there
Add Iridium: Inmarsat's satellites sit over the equator
questions.why: Inmarsat's geostationary satellites sit low on the horizon and are lost beyond about 75° of latitude; Iridium's polar orbits cover the poles.

questions.q: You check the EPIRB before the Atlantic crossing. What must you do?

figure.title: Pre-departure check
lines: 406 MHz EPIRB, came with the boat
Registration: previous owner's name and boat
Battery and hydrostatic release in date

options: Register it to you and this boat
Test it with a full activation in harbour
Reprogramme it to transmit on 121.5 MHz only
Nothing — it sends your position anyway
questions.why: Cospas-Sarsat decodes the beacon's ID: the MRCC uses the registration to know the boat, the crew and whom to call ashore.

questions.q: You are choosing an EPIRB for an ocean passage. What does model B give you?

figure.title: Choosing an EPIRB
lines: Model A: 406 MHz, no GNSS receiver
Model B: 406 MHz with built-in GNSS

options: Your position in its first bursts, within minutes
No need to register the beacon
A stronger signal for ships close by
questions.why: Without GNSS the satellites must work out the position from the signal, more slowly and coarsely; with GNSS it goes out in the alert.

questions.q: Adrift in the liferaft, how does the search aircraft find you in the last few miles?

figure.title: Day 3 in the liferaft
lines: Search aircraft heard, not yet seen

options: It hears you on VHF channel 16 by itself
It reads your AIS signal by satellite
It homes on the EPIRB's 121.5 MHz signal
It follows the 406 MHz position alone
questions.why: The 406 MHz alert goes via Cospas-Sarsat to the MRCC; the 121.5 MHz homing signal leads aircraft and ships to the raft.

questions.q: A crew member asks why the GPS position goes in the logbook every hour. What do you answer?

figure.title: Skipper's standing orders
lines: Every hour: time, GPS position, log
Noon: sun sight compared with GPS

options: The plotter needs it to check its datum
It keeps the GPS receiver calibrated
The insurer needs it to settle any claim
If the GPS fails, DR starts from a recent known position
questions.why: With an hourly position, course and log reading on paper, a GPS failure costs you less than an hour of DR.

questions.q: Your crew questions the daily sun sight. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Day 4, GPS working well
lines: Noon sight vs GPS: 1.8 M apart

options: It keeps the skill and the kit ready for a failure
It is more accurate than GPS offshore
The almanac must be used once a day
It corrects the GPS for its datum
questions.why: Celestial navigation is the backup: practise it daily and compare with GPS, so you can trust it when the electronics fail.

questions.q: Your only GPS failed after the last hourly entry. What DR position do you plot at 1500?
questions.why: 21 M on 260°: d.lat 3.6′S; departure 20.7′W ÷ cos 15.3° = d.long 21.4′W.

questions.q: You are south of the equator and want a night check on the compass. What do you use where you once used Polaris?

figure.title: Night check, Rio to Cape Town
lines: Clear sky, Southern Cross well up

options: Canopus whenever it is in the south
The Pointers at any time of the night
The Southern Cross when its long axis is vertical
Sigma Octantis, the faint south pole star
questions.why: With its long axis vertical the Cross is on your meridian and bears 180°T; σ Octantis, at the pole, is too faint to take.

questions.q: On passage from New Zealand to Tonga you take this bearing of Acrux. What deviation do you log?

figure.title: Night, 33°S 176°E
lines: Southern Cross upside down, low in the south
Acrux on your meridian, below the pole

questions.why: On the meridian Acrux bears 180°T; error 180° − 165° = 15°E; deviation = error − variation = 15°E − 19°E = 4°W.

questions.q: Bound from Tahiti to Rarotonga, you check the steering compass on Canopus, low in the south-east. What deviation do you log?
Bound for Mauritius, you want a star to check the compass tonight. Which one do you take?
options: Canopus — nearly due south, easy to use
Acrux — low enough to bear over the compass
Rigel — high and clear of any haze
Sirius — the brightest star in the sky
questions.why: A bearing is good only of a low body: at 60°–80° you cannot hold the compass level and sight the star. Acrux at 19° is right.

questions.q: Bound from Panama to New Zealand, you find the steering compass card tilting and dragging as you go south. Why?

figure.title: Steering compass, 38°S
lines: Card tilted, sticks on one side
Fine in the Caribbean and on the equator

options: Variation is too large for it near New Zealand
Its fluid is too cold in the southern winter
It is balanced for the north: magnetic dip pulls it
Its magnets weakened as it crossed the equator
questions.why: A compass card is balanced for one magnetic zone; far south the dip of the field tilts a northern card. Fit a southern or global one.

questions.q: Jupiter is setting over a clear western horizon. At what moment do you take its bearing for an amplitude?

figure.title: Jupiter setting
lines: Bright, low over a clear western horizon

options: With it half a Sun's diameter above the horizon
With it 5° up, well clear of the haze
As it touches the visible horizon
With it about a Sun's diameter above the horizon
questions.why: On the celestial horizon, refraction (34′) and dip (3′) lift a point body about 0.6° — one Sun's diameter — above the visible horizon.

questions.q: On the way to the Azores you take the amplitude of Venus as it sets. What true bearing do you use?
questions.why: sin Amp = sin 22°10′ / cos 35° → Amp 27.4°, from west toward N: 270° + 27° = 297°T. Amp ≈ Dec only near the equator.

questions.q: In mid-Atlantic you check the steering compass as Rigel rises. What deviation do you log?
questions.why: sin Amp = sin 8°10′ / cos 30° → E9.4°S, 099.4°T; error 099.4° − 106° = 6.6°W; deviation 6.6°W − 12°W = 5.4°E, about 5°E.

questions.q: Approaching the Western Approaches from the Azores on 21 June, you take a sunrise amplitude. What true bearing do you use?

figure.title: Sunrise, 21 June
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

questions.why: sin Amp = sin 23°26′ / cos 50° → Amp 38.2°, from east toward N: 090° − 38° = 052°T. At 50°N the amplitude is far more than the Dec.

questions.q: Bound for Norway, you take the sunrise bearing late, with the Sun's centre about 1° higher than it should be. How far out is your check?

figure.title: Sunrise, 21 June, 58°N
lines: Here the Sun takes 11 minutes to climb 1°

options: About ¼°: as it would be near the equator
None: the Sun rises at a fixed bearing
