About 1°: one degree for each degree up
About 2½°: the Sun climbs at a slant up here
questions.why: At 58°N the Sun's path is oblique: its Zn goes from 041.4° on the horizon to 043.7° at 1° up; near the equator it would move 0.2°.

questions.q: On the Cape to Rio route you take an amplitude at sunset. What is the compass error?
questions.why: sin Amp = sin 23°26′ / cos 33° → W28.3°S, 241.7°T; error = true − compass = 241.7° − 250° = 8°W.

questions.q: You take the Sun's bearing for this compass check. How far out could the azimuth you work for it be?

figure.title: Compass check, 15°N
lines: Watch error unknown, up to 2 minutes

options: About ½°: 2 minutes is ½° of hour angle
About 3°: near the zenith the bearing swings fast
About 1°: as for any Sun on a morning check
Under 0.1°: the azimuth hardly changes with time
questions.why: At 84° up the Sun's Zn goes from 057° to 055° in 2 minutes (LHA 355° → 355.5°); mid-morning it moves under 0.1°. Use a low Sun.

questions.q: South of the equator on the Puddle Jump, the Sun is north of you after noon. What is its true azimuth for your compass check?
questions.why: LHA = 150°51.5′ − 131°20′W = 19°31.5′; LHA under 180° puts the Sun west of your meridian: Zn = 327°T, to the north-west.

questions.q: On passage from Fiji to Vanuatu you check the steering compass on the morning Sun. What deviation do you log?

figure.title: Morning sun, west of the date line

questions.q: At evening twilight on the way to the Azores you take Jupiter over the steering compass. What deviation do you log?
On the ARC you use HO 249 Volume 1 for a star's azimuth at dusk. What is the compass error?
questions.why: Volume 1 gives Zn directly for its selected stars: error = true − compass = 091° − 098° = 7°W (the deviation would be 4°E).

questions.q: Mid-ocean, you want a fresh deviation card for the main headings. How do you get it?

figure.title: Compass swing at sea
lines: Calm sea, clear sky, morning Sun
No land or transit for 1,500 M

options: Compare the compass with the GPS track for a day
Take one Sun bearing and apply it to every heading
Steer each heading in turn and bear the Sun on each
Wait for a transit at the landfall to swing it
questions.why: Deviation changes with heading: steer each heading, bear the Sun, work its Zn for that time and log error − variation.

questions.q: You swing the compass on four headings between 0900 and 0940. A crew member wants to use the 0900 azimuth for every bearing. What do you tell them?
options: Take all four bearings at 0900 on the same heading
Fine: use the mean azimuth of 133° for all four
Fine: the Sun's bearing changes little in 40 minutes
Work an azimuth for each bearing: the Sun moves 7°
questions.why: The Sun's Zn moves 7.3° in those 40 minutes: one azimuth for all would put up to 7° of false deviation into the card.

questions.q: You swing the compass in the Indian Ocean with the morning Sun. What is the deviation on 090°C?
questions.why: On 090°C: error = 066° − 071° = 5°W; deviation = 5°W − 1°W = 4°W. Use each time's own Zn, not the 0800 one.

questions.q: Your new deviation card has the four cardinal headings. What deviation do you apply steering 045°C?
questions.why: Deviation runs smoothly between headings: halfway from 000°C (2°E) to 090°C (5°W) it is (+2° − 5°) ÷ 2, about 1½–2°W.

questions.q: Your swing at sea shows large deviation on east and west headings. A crew member offers to adjust the corrector magnets now. What do you do?
options: Move the compass to where the error is smallest
Turn the correctors until the Sun's bearing agrees
Steer by the card; leave the magnets to an adjuster
Take the correctors out and start again from zero
questions.why: Adjusting at sea without a full swing can make it worse: steer by the card, keep checking, and have it adjusted in port.

questions.q: You check the compass twice on the same heading and get these results. What explains them?

figure.title: Same heading, 240°C
lines: Next day, heeled 20° to port: error 2°W

options: The compass card sticks when she heels
The Sun's azimuth was worked wrongly once
Variation changed with the boat's heel
Heeling error: heel shifts the boat's magnetism
questions.why: Heel moves the keel, engine and rig relative to the compass: deviation changes with heel as well as heading — log it per tack.

questions.q: Beating to windward, you go about onto port tack. What true course do you plot?
questions.why: Port-tack deviation 4°W and variation 6°W are both west, so subtract: 310°C − 4° − 6° = 300°T.

questions.q: On the night watch the compass error on the same heading has jumped by 10°. What do you check first?

figure.title: Compass check, 0400
lines: Crew restowed the cockpit lockers at dusk

options: Whether the compass fluid has leaked
What has been stowed near the compass
Whether the Sun's tables are right
questions.why: Steel, magnets or electronics moved near the compass change its deviation at once: move them away, then check again.

questions.q: Six days out of Cape Town you notice you still apply the departure variation. What true course have you been steering?

figure.title: Cape Town to St Helena, day 6

questions.why: True = compass − westerly variation: 315° − 19°W = 296°T, not the 290°T you planned — 6° to the right of your track.

questions.q: A crew member suggests checking the compass against the GPS course over ground instead of the Sun. When is that good enough?

figure.title: Mid-Atlantic, day 9
lines: Trade wind F5, 1 kn of current likely
Leeway on a broad reach: unknown

options: Always, if the GPS shows a good HDOP
Always: COG is the boat's true heading
Never: GPS COG is a magnetic value
Only with no current and no leeway
questions.why: COG is the track over the ground: current and leeway set it off the heading, so the difference is not the compass error.

questions.q: Your new satellite compass gives true heading from two GNSS antennas. What is its weak point on an ocean passage?

figure.title: Satellite compass
lines: True heading: no deviation, no variation
Feeds the autopilot and the radar overlay

options: It loses its heading when GNSS is lost or jammed
It drifts and must be reset each day at noon
It shows only magnetic heading, never true
It needs swinging for deviation like a compass
questions.why: A GNSS compass needs satellite signals: jamming or an antenna fault kills its heading, so keep the magnetic compass checked.

questions.q: After a wave fills the cockpit, the EPIRB in its bracket starts flashing. What does that mean?
options: It is only showing that its GPS has a fix
It has activated and is sending a distress alert
Its battery is low and needs replacing
It is running a self-test after getting wet
questions.why: A water-activated EPIRB switches on when it gets wet in its bracket: the strobe means a 406 MHz distress alert is going out.

questions.q: Your EPIRB has gone off by accident, 900 miles from land. What do you do?

figure.title: False alert, day 12
lines: EPIRB set off by a wave 20 min ago

options: Leave it on until a ship comes to check
Take out its battery and note it in the log
Call an MRCC at once and report the false alert
Switch it off quietly: no harm has been done
questions.why: A false alert launches a search: switch the beacon off and call an MRCC at once by satphone with its ID, your position and time.

questions.q: You call the MRCC to cancel your false EPIRB alert. What do they need from you?
options: Your MMSI and the VHF channel you keep
The EPIRB's make and battery expiry date
Only the boat's name and her home port
The beacon's hex ID, boat's name, position and time
questions.why: The hex ID matches the alert to your beacon; with the time, position and 'all well', the MRCC can stand the search down.

questions.q: Adrift after abandoning ship, you watch the EPIRB. This blue light comes on. What does it tell you?
options: The system has received your alert and position
The beacon has just found a GPS fix
A rescue unit is now on its way to you
The battery is half used and failing
questions.why: Galileo's Return Link Service only confirms that Cospas-Sarsat has your alert and position; it does not mean help is close.

questions.q: In the liferaft, an aircraft flies over and rocks its wings. A crew member wants to switch off the EPIRB to save its battery. What do you do?
options: Switch it off now that they have found you
Leave it on until you are picked up
Switch it off until night falls
Switch it off and on again every hour
questions.why: The ship sent to you homes on 121.5 MHz and the 406 MHz position: leave the EPIRB on until you are aboard.

questions.q: At night you have one radar target and one AIS target ahead. What do you navigate by?

figure.title: Night, 0230, 40 M off Cape Verde
lines: No other target on radar or AIS

options: The mean of the radar and AIS positions
Her AIS: the radar target is sea clutter
Radar and your eyes: her AIS position is wrong
Her AIS: it is more accurate than radar
questions.why: AIS shows where the ship's own GPS puts her; when it disagrees with radar and eyes, the AIS may be wrong (Rule 7: no scanty data).

questions.q: A ship's compass bearing has been steady for 12 minutes, but her AIS shows a comfortable CPA. What do you do?

figure.note: Bearing 040° steady 12 min · AIS CPA 1.8 M

options: Call her to correct her AIS, then stand on
Stand on: the AIS says she passes 1.8 M off
Wait for the AIS CPA to update, then decide
Treat it as a risk of collision and act early
questions.why: A steady compass bearing means risk of collision (Rule 7); AIS CPA rests on GPS and heading data that may be wrong. Act in ample time.

questions.q: A ship calls you on VHF about your AIS. What do you do?

figure.title: VHF call, mid-Atlantic
lines: Ship: 'Your AIS puts you on Barbados'
Your plotter: 280 M east of Barbados
The AIS transponder has its own GPS

options: Give her your position, then check the AIS's GPS
Re-enter your MMSI so the error clears
Switch the AIS off for the rest of the passage
Ignore it: ships see you on radar anyway
questions.why: Your AIS sends its own GPS's position: tell the ship where you are, then check the AIS GPS antenna and its status page.

questions.q: You plan to cross ahead of this container ship using her AIS. Where is her bow relative to the AIS position?

figure.title: AIS target: container ship, 330 m
lines: Static data: A 260, B 70, C 20, D 28 (m)
Plotter draws a dot at her AIS position
Night, she is end-on to you

questions.why: AIS reports the position of the ship's GPS antenna; A is the distance from it to the bow, so her bow is 260 m ahead of the dot.

questions.q: You compare the noon-to-noon runs. What do they tell you?

figure.title: Noon to noon, day 7
lines: Log checked against GPS in slack water

options: A GPS error of about 18 M in the fix
A current of about ¾ kn setting against you
A current of about ¾ kn setting with you
A current of about 1½ kn setting with you
questions.why: 158 M over the ground − 140 M through the water = 18 M in 24 h: a favourable current of 0.75 kn.

questions.q: Today's noon latitude is 14 miles from the GPS, after a week of agreement within 2 miles. What do you do first?

figure.title: Noon, day 8, ARC route
lines: Days 1–7: sight and GPS within 2 M

options: Reset the GPS and accept its next fix
Navigate by the sextant: the GPS has failed
Recheck the sight: the Dec, index error, arithmetic
questions.why: A sudden 14′ gap after a week of agreement usually means a slip in the sight — wrong Dec, IE, a misread degree. Check before doubting GPS.

questions.q: The main GPS and the handheld now disagree by 4 miles. How do you decide which to trust?
options: Check both against your DR, and a sight if you can
Trust the handheld: it has its own antenna
Trust the main set: it has the bigger antenna
Plot the mean of the two and carry on
questions.why: Two sources that disagree cannot tell you which is wrong: a third — your DR from log and compass, or a sun line — decides.

questions.q: The GPS loses its fix every time you send email over the satellite terminal. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: Watch log, day 5
lines: Both antennas on the same pushpit rail

options: The email software resets the GPS receiver
The satcom antenna transmits too close to the GPS one
The satellites are below the horizon at those times
The batteries sag under the satcom's load
questions.why: Iridium and Inmarsat transmit just above the GPS L1 band: mount the GPS antenna well away from the satcom one, not level with it.

questions.q: You suspect jamming. A crew member wants to set the receiver to Galileo only. Will it help?

figure.title: GNSS receiver, Red Sea
lines: GPS, Galileo and GLONASS all lost
Signal strength low on every satellite

options: Yes: Galileo signals cannot be jammed
Yes: one system needs fewer satellites
Little: all the systems share the same L-band
Yes: Galileo uses a separate datum
questions.why: GPS, Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou all send weak L-band signals near 1.2–1.6 GHz: a jammer blocks them all. Navigate by DR and radar.

questions.q: The plotter's boat symbol is still moving, but the status reads 'No fix — DR'. What is the position shown?
options: A fix from the AIS transponder's GPS
A fix corrected by the SBAS signal
A GNSS fix from fewer satellites
An estimate from the last fix, COG and SOG
questions.why: Without a fix the plotter dead-reckons on the last COG and SOG: note the time of the last real fix and start your own DR from it.

questions.q: You receive this warning on the way to Antigua. What do you plan for the next day?
options: A fix before it, then DR and sights; expect HF gaps
Switch every receiver off until it passes
Rely on HF weatherfax instead of satellites
Nothing: space weather affects only aircraft
questions.why: A geomagnetic storm upsets the ionosphere: GNSS fixes may jump or drop out and HF fades. Keep DR going and the sextant ready.

questions.q: Your Iridium terminal shows no signal tonight. What do you check first?

figure.title: Iridium terminal, day 3
lines: Antenna moved under the hard top

options: That the antenna points towards the equator
That the antenna has a clear view of the sky
That the next satellite pass is due at noon
That the SIM card has not expired
questions.why: Iridium satellites cross the whole sky in low orbits: the antenna needs a clear view overhead. Pointing at the equator is for Inmarsat.

questions.q: The Inmarsat terminal drops out on one heading only. What is the likely cause?

figure.title: Inmarsat dome on the stern arch

options: The heel tilts the dome beyond its range
The satellite sets below the horizon at sea
The mast and sails block its view of the satellite
The radar beam jams it on that heading
questions.why: An Inmarsat satellite sits over the equator: with it dead ahead, the mast and mainsail stand between the stern dome and the satellite.

questions.q: The satellite phone has died mid-Atlantic. How do you still get the forecast?
options: GRIB files over the GPS receiver
VHF forecasts from the nearest coast station
High-seas bulletins and weatherfax on the SSB
questions.why: Mid-ocean only HF reaches you without a satellite: high-seas forecasts and weatherfax charts on the SSB receiver. NAVTEX reaches ~300 M.

questions.q: Your satcom has failed and your shore contact expects a daily email. What do you do?

figure.title: Day 6 of 20, mid-Atlantic
lines: Float plan: daily email by 1800 UT

options: Ask the ship on VHF to email your shore contact
Set off the EPIRB briefly so they see you are well
Send a DSC distress alert, then cancel it
Nothing: they will call the MRCC on day 7 anyway
questions.why: Any ship can relay a routine message; never use an EPIRB or a distress alert for it. Your float plan should say a missed email is no distress.

questions.q: Just south of the equator you get ready for a sunrise amplitude. Where do you expect the Sun to rise?
options: About 090° — due east on the equator
questions.why: Near the equator cos Lat ≈ 1, so the amplitude ≈ the Dec: the Sun rises about E15°S, 105°T.

questions.q: The pilot chart shows no variation at your position. What does today's Sun check give you?

figure.title: Compass check on the agonic line

options: Nothing until you know the variation
questions.why: Error = variation + deviation; with variation 0° the whole 3°E error is deviation on this heading.

questions.q: Your watches have stopped and you know UT only to about 20 minutes. Which compass check can you still make?

figure.title: No reliable time
lines: Deck watch and GPS both dead
UT known only to about ±20 min

options: A planet's azimuth in the night
A star's azimuth at evening twilight
The Sun's amplitude at sunrise or sunset
questions.why: The amplitude needs only the Dec, which changes slowly; an azimuth needs the hour angle, and so the exact time.

questions.q: Before the Indian Ocean crossing a crew member looks at the plotter and asks why the great-circle track, which curves far south of the straight line on the chart, is the shorter one. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Plotter: Cape Town → Fremantle
lines: GC track bows south to about 44½°S

options: Its plane passes through the Earth's centre — the shortest way on a sphere
The plotter allows for the east-going current in the forties
It follows the line along which magnetic variation stays the same
It keeps one course, so no miles are lost in turns
questions.why: A great circle is cut by a plane through the Earth's centre; its shorter arc is the shortest route between two points on the globe.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the shortest route

questions.q: You draw a straight line from Halifax to Falmouth on this gnomonic chart. What does the line show?
options: The rhumb line — one course all the way
The great-circle track between the two ports
The track along the parallel of mean latitude
The route the pilot chart recommends for June
questions.why: On a gnomonic chart every great circle is a straight line; a rhumb line on it is curved.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the gnomonic chart

questions.q: With the great circle drawn on the gnomonic chart, a crew member picks up the protractor and dividers to take the course and the distance off it. What do you tell them?
options: The course is true; measure the distance on the edge
Fine — courses and distances are both true on it
Neither is true on this chart: transfer the points or compute
The distance is true; take the course from the rose
questions.why: A gnomonic chart shows great circles as straight lines but distorts angles and distances; use it only to pick the points.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the gnomonic chart

questions.q: Which of the three tracks on this Mercator chart is the great circle from Cape Town to Fremantle?

figure.note: Mercator chart, south Indian Ocean (north up)

options: A — it bows north, towards the equator
B — the straight line between the ports
A or C — it depends on the way you sail
C — it bows south, towards the pole
questions.why: On a Mercator chart a great circle bows towards the nearer pole — south in the southern hemisphere; the straight line B is the rhumb line.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — on the Mercator chart

questions.q: You have drawn the great circle from Halifax to Falmouth on the gnomonic chart. How do you put it on the Mercator chart you navigate by?
options: Read its latitude on every 10° meridian and plot those points
Lay off the distance along the rhumb line
Copy the straight line across at the same angle
Measure the initial course and lay it off from Halifax
questions.why: Take the latitude where the GC crosses each meridian 5° or 10° apart, plot the points on the Mercator chart and join them with short rhumb lines.

questions.q: You rule this straight line from Mindelo to Barbados on the Mercator chart and set the autopilot to the one course it gives. What track are you sailing?
options: A parallel sailing along one latitude
A rhumb line, crossing every meridian at the same angle
A great circle, the shortest track
A composite track along a limiting latitude
questions.why: A straight line on a Mercator chart is a rhumb line: one course, the same angle with every meridian — but not the shortest track.

questions.q: Heading south through the Atlantic you have this leg in the plotter. Your watch leader suggests switching it to GC to save miles. How much does it save?
options: About 120 M — about 10 % of the leg
About 12 M — about 1 % of the leg
Nothing — a meridian is itself a great circle
About 60 M — about 5 % of the leg
questions.why: Meridians and the equator are great circles and rhumb lines at once: on a due north–south leg GC and RL are the same track.

questions.q: You compare four ocean passages. On which does the great circle save the most miles over the rhumb line?
questions.why: The saving grows with latitude and east–west distance: about 214 M Cape Town–Fremantle, 32 M St John's–Falmouth, 10 M ARC, 0 M north–south.

questions.q: From this waypoint you could run due east along the parallel to Falmouth or take the great circle. How much shorter is the great circle?
questions.why: Parallel: 1,796′ of DLo × cos 50.15° = 1,151 M; the GC is 1,143 M. Even a due-east leg is not the shortest away from the equator.

questions.q: On the Puddle Jump you wonder whether to switch the plotter to GC. How much shorter is the great circle?
questions.why: GC 2,996 M against RL 2,997 M: so close to the equator the two tracks almost coincide.

questions.q: You are about to leave St John's for Falmouth with the plotter set as shown. How many miles would the great circle save?
questions.why: GC by cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo: 1,855 M; 1,886 − 1,855 = 31 M saved.

questions.q: You are planning the ARC crossing and want the great-circle distance from Las Palmas to Rodney Bay. What is it?
You leave Las Palmas on the great circle for Rodney Bay. What initial course do you set?
questions.why: GC formula: S 81.3° W = 261°T, north of the rhumb-line course 252°T; it ends at 244°T off St Lucia.

questions.q: You are planning the South Atlantic crossing from Cape Town to Brazil. What is the great-circle distance?
questions.why: DLo = 18°25′E + 38°31′W = 56°56′ (east and west add); cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo → 55.50° = 3,330 M.

questions.q: You plan the trade-wind crossing from Cocos (Keeling) to Mauritius. What is the great-circle distance?
You plan the long leg from Panama to the Marquesas, across the equator. What is the great-circle distance?
You leave St George's, Bermuda, for Horta on the great circle. What initial course do you steer?
questions.why: DLo 36°02′E; GC formula → N 67.9° E = 068°T. The rhumb line is 078°T; the GC course reaches 089°T at Horta.

questions.q: You leave Cape Town on the great circle for Fremantle. What initial course do you steer?
questions.why: Both latitudes south; GC formula → S 59.2° E = 121°T, south of the rhumb line (089°T): the track bows towards the South Pole.

questions.q: You leave Falmouth westbound on the great circle for Newport, Rhode Island. What initial course do you steer?
questions.why: GC formula: N 74.3° W = 286°T — north of the rhumb line 259°T: in the north the great circle bows towards the pole.

questions.q: You set off from Auckland on the great circle for Tahiti. What initial course do you steer?
questions.why: DLo across the date line: 5°14′ + 30°26′ = 35°40′ east; GC formula → N 68.1° E = 068°T, 2,209 M to Papeete.

questions.q: You are sailing the great circle from Newport to Falmouth and reach V, its most northerly point. What is your course there?
questions.why: At the vertex the great circle runs at right angles to the meridian: the course is 090° or 270°.

questions.q: Before leaving Halifax you work out the vertex of the great circle to Falmouth. Where is it?
questions.why: cos Lv = cos 44.65° × sin 60.4° → 51°47′N; cos DLo = tan 44.65° / tan Lv → DLo 38°57′E, so 024°37′W.

questions.q: Leaving Cape Town for Fremantle on the great circle, you check how far south it will take you. What is the latitude of the vertex?
questions.why: cos Lv = cos 33.92° × sin 120.8° (= sin 59.2°) → Lv 44°32′S — on the polar side, so named like the start: south.

questions.q: Sailing this great circle from Bermuda, where on the track are you furthest north?
options: North of the Azores, at about 45°N
Near Bermuda — the track runs south of east
At Horta — the vertex lies just beyond it
questions.why: The course is still north of east (089°T) on arrival, so the track climbs all the way: the vertex (38°32′N 027°26′W) is past Horta.

questions.q: You set great-circle waypoints every 10° of longitude for the passage to Falmouth. What latitude does the waypoint on 40°W get?
questions.why: tan L = tan Lv × cos (DLo from the vertex) = tan 51.78° × cos 15.38° → 50°46′N.

questions.q: With only the two ports' positions to go on, you work out the great-circle waypoint on the 40°W meridian. What is its latitude?
questions.why: Initial course 55.4°; cos Lv = cos 41.48° sin 55.4° → 51°55′N at 025°11′W; tan L = tan Lv cos 14.82° → 50°58′N.

questions.q: You sail the great circle as rhumb-line legs between waypoints every 10° of longitude. How much farther is that than the true great circle?

figure.title: GC Halifax → Falmouth
lines: GC 2,337 M · one rhumb line 2,396 M

questions.why: Short rhumb legs hug the curve: about 1.5 M over 2,337 M, against 59 M for one rhumb line all the way.

questions.q: On the great circle from Halifax the plotter's course to steer creeps round day by day, with no current and no wind shift. Why?
options: The Earth's rotation pulls the track to the right
The plotter corrects for the Gulf Stream each hour
Magnetic variation changes along the route
The great circle cuts each meridian at a different angle
questions.why: Only a rhumb line keeps one angle to the meridians; on a great circle the course changes all the way, here from 060° to 105°.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the course changes

questions.q: Reaching the waypoint on 50°W, you check the great-circle course from here. What is it?

figure.title: GC Halifax → Falmouth
lines: You are at the waypoint now

questions.why: sin C = cos Lv / cos L = cos 51.78° / cos 48.93° → N 70.3° E = 070°T: 060° at Halifax, 090° at the vertex.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the course changes

questions.q: Three days out of Bermuda a gale has pushed you south of the planned great circle. What great-circle course do you now steer for Horta?

figure.title: Bermuda → Horta, day 3
lines: GC course out of Bermuda was 068°T

questions.why: Start a new great circle from the fix: DLo 26°42′E; GC formula → N 70.7° E = 071°T, 1,312 M to go.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the course changes

questions.q: You plan the passage from Cape Town to Hobart. Which track do you lay off?

figure.title: Cape Town → Hobart
lines: Your limit: no further south than 45°S

options: The great circle — the shortest track is the best
The rhumb line — it is shorter at this latitude
GC to 45°S, along the parallel, then GC to Hobart
Two rhumb lines that meet at the vertex
questions.why: Composite sailing: great circles to and from the limiting latitude, joined along it — the shortest track that keeps out of the ice.

questions.q: You plan a composite track to Fremantle with 40°S as the limit. What initial course do you steer out of Cape Town?
questions.why: The first GC has its vertex on 40°S: sin C = cos 40° / cos 33.92° → S 67.4° E = 113°T.

questions.q: On your composite track to Fremantle, at what longitude does the first great circle bring you down to the 40°S limit?
questions.why: The vertex is on 40°S: cos DLo = tan 33.92° / tan 40° → DLo 36°45′E; 018°25′E + 36°45′ = 055°10′E.

questions.q: On your composite track to Hobart, how far do you sail along the 45°S parallel?
questions.why: DLo 59°24′ = 3,564′; departure = DLo × cos 45° = 2,520 M.

questions.q: You decide not to go south of 45°S on the way to Hobart. What is the total distance of the composite track?
questions.why: GC legs: cos d = sin L / sin 45° → 2,274 + 946 M; along 45°S 2,520 M; total 5,740 M (direct GC 5,408 M).

questions.q: On the last night before landfall you lay off the short leg to the channel waypoint by plane sailing. What course and distance?
The sky is overcast at noon, so you work up the noon DR by plane sailing. Where is it?

figure.title: Noon to noon in the trades

questions.q: On passage from Cape Town to St Helena you have these two noon fixes. What course and distance have you made good?
questions.why: dLat 90′N; DLo 2°30′W (east and west add across Greenwich) × cos 25.9° = dep 135′; C = N 56.3° W = 304°T, 162 M.

questions.q: Bound across the South Pacific, you have sailed these two legs since noon. By plane sailing, where is your DR now?
You want the single rhumb-line course from Mindelo to Bridgetown by Mercator sailing. What is it?
Working the rhumb line from Horta to Falmouth by Mercator sailing, what distance do you get?
questions.why: tan C = DLo 1,414′ / DMP 976.1 → C N 55.4° E; distance = dLat 697′ / cos C = 1,227 M.

questions.q: You lay off the rhumb line from Cape Town to Jamestown, St Helena. What course and distance does Mercator sailing give?

figure.title: Cape Town → St Helena, rhumb line

questions.q: Bound from Cape Verde to Brazil across the equator, you work the rhumb line by Mercator sailing. What course and distance do you get?
questions.why: Contrary names add: dLat 1,791′, DMP 1021.2 + 779.5 = 1800.7; DLo 812′W; C = S 24.3° W; d = 1,791 / cos C.

questions.q: You have reached Bermuda's latitude and will run due west along it to St George's. How far do you have to go?
questions.why: Parallel sailing: distance = DLo × cos lat = 390′ × cos 32.38° = 329 M.

questions.q: You run your easting down along 40°S for a day. What is your longitude at noon tomorrow?
questions.why: 168 M of departure; DLo = departure / cos lat = 168 / cos 40° = 219.3′ = 03°39′E → 062°19′E.

questions.q: You leave Las Palmas for St Lucia in late November. Why does your route head SSW for days instead of following the great circle?
options: To keep clear of the Canary Current
To find the steady NE trade wind further south
To pass the vertex of the great circle
To sail a shorter track than the great circle
questions.why: The GC runs through light, fickle winds north of the trades; going south first ('until the butter melts') finds the steady NE trade.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when not to use it

questions.q: You leave Honolulu for San Francisco in July. The NE trade blows straight down the great circle (054°T, 2,078 M) and the Pacific High lies across its middle. How do you route?

figure.note: GC: on the wind, then calms

options: Along the rhumb line, then motor through the calms
Along the great circle — the shortest is the fastest
North on starboard tack round the high's west side, then east
South of the high, then north up the Californian coast
questions.why: Calms at the high's centre and a beat on the GC: sail north on the trade round the high, then east in the westerlies — more miles, fewer days.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when not to use it

questions.q: You plan the passage from Cape Town to Salvador in February. The great circle runs close to the centre of the South Atlantic high. Which route do you choose?

figure.title: Cape Town → Salvador, February
lines: SE trade and current north of 25°S

options: South into the westerlies, then north up the Brazilian coast
The great circle — the shortest track is the quickest
West along 34°S, then north along the coast to Salvador
North with the SE trade towards St Helena, then west to Brazil
questions.why: Calms at the high's centre; the SE trade and the South Equatorial Current to its north give a fast run — more miles, fewer days.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when not to use it

questions.q: You enter the passage from Horta to Falmouth into the plotter as one leg. Which leg setting gives the shorter track?
options: GC — the plotter follows the great circle
RL — GC works only on a gnomonic chart
RL — the straight line on the screen is shorter
Either — both settings give the same miles
questions.why: GC makes the plotter compute the great circle; RL keeps one course — a straight line on its Mercator screen, but longer.

questions.q: Checking the route before leaving Newport, you see the plotter leg is set to RL. How many extra miles does that cost over the great circle?
questions.why: GC by cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo: 2,725 M; RL 2,811 M — 86 M, about half a day's run.

questions.q: A new crew member asks why the great circle from Yokohama to Victoria, the shorter track, swings up towards the Aleutians on this chart. What is the reason?
options: A great circle is drawn curved on every kind of chart
The track is bent to keep inside the Aleutian ice limit
Mercator stretches latitude towards the poles, so a GC plots as a curve
The plotter bends the track for the set of the Kuroshio current
questions.why: Only rhumb lines are straight on a Mercator chart; the GC (4,104 M) bows poleward of the rhumb line (4,374 M).
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — on the Mercator chart

questions.q: You compare four legs, each 40° of longitude long and each sailed along a parallel. On which does switching the plotter to GC save nothing at all?

figure.title: Four legs in the plotter, type RL

questions.why: Only the equator is a great circle: the GC saves 0 M on A, 1.5 M on B, 10.9 M on C and 18.7 M on D.

questions.q: Running your easting down in the Southern Ocean, a crew member says that holding 50°S, with the latitude never changing, must be the shortest track. What do you tell them?
options: No — a parallel is a small circle; the great circle is shorter
No — the rhumb line along 50°S is shorter still
Yes — every parallel of latitude is a great circle
Yes — a steady course is always the shortest track
questions.why: Only the equator is both a parallel and a great circle: along 50°S from 080°E to 120°E the parallel is 1,543 M, the GC 1,524 M.
questions.ref: Parallel sailing — and the great circle

questions.q: On this gnomonic chart centred on the South Pole you rule the great circle from Bluff to Cape Horn. Which of the marked points is its vertex?

figure.note: Gnomonic chart centred on the South Pole

options: None — the vertex is off this chart
B — the point of the line nearest the pole
A — where the line first crosses 60°S
C — where the line climbs back over 60°S
questions.why: On a gnomonic chart the vertex is where the GC line comes nearest the pole — here about 69°53′S, deep in the ice.

questions.q: On this gnomonic chart you have ruled the great circle from Sydney to Nelson and run the line on to its vertex X. Where on the passage itself are you furthest south?
options: At Sydney — the track climbs north all the way
Halfway across, where the line dips lowest
At Nelson — the vertex lies beyond it, off the track
At X, the vertex, at about 43°45′S
questions.why: The course is still south of east at Nelson (106°T), so the track descends all the way; the vertex 43°45′S 163°10′W is beyond.

questions.q: Bound from Salvador in Brazil to Grenada, you cross the equator. Which of the three tracks on this Mercator chart is the great circle?
options: C — bowed towards the pole you are heading for
C — bowed north of the straight line all the way
B — the straight line between the two ports
A — south of the straight line, then north of it
questions.why: A GC bows towards the nearer pole: south of the rhumb line in the south, north of it past the equator — an S on the Mercator chart.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — across the equator

questions.q: You plan the South Indian Ocean crossing from Durban to Fremantle. What is the great-circle distance?
questions.why: DLo 84°42′E, both latitudes south: cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo → 70.60° × 60 = 4,236 M.

questions.q: Clearing the breakwater at Durban, bound for Fremantle by the great circle, you want the first course to steer. What is it?
questions.why: Both latitudes south: GC formula → S 63.5° E = 117°T, south of the rhumb line 092°T: the track bows towards the pole.

questions.q: You leave Durban on the great circle for Fremantle with no current and no wind shift. How will the course to steer change on the way?
options: It stays at 117°T — a great circle holds one course
It swings further south of east than 117°T
It comes round through 090° at the vertex to north of east
It comes round through 180° to west of south
questions.why: Eastbound in the south the GC bows to the pole: 117°T at Durban, 090° at the vertex (39°06′S), 066°T at Fremantle.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the course changes

questions.q: To see how far south the great circle to Fremantle will take you, you work out its vertex. Where is it?
questions.why: cos Lv = cos 29.87° × sin 116.5° → 39°06′S; cos DLo = tan 29.87° / tan Lv → DLo 45°02′E, so 076°05′E.

questions.q: Before the Indian Ocean crossing you list the great-circle waypoints from the vertex. What latitude goes against the 060°E meridian?
questions.why: tan L = tan Lv × cos DLo from the vertex = tan 39.10° × cos 16.08° → 37°59′S, named south like the vertex.

questions.q: Coming up to the 100°E waypoint on this sheet, you check the great-circle course onward from it. What is it?
questions.why: sin C = cos Lv / cos L = cos 39.10° / cos 36.62° → 75.2°; past the vertex in the south it is N 75° E = 075°T.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the course changes

questions.q: After days of southerly gales you are far north of the planned track. Rather than claw back to it, you start a fresh great circle from the fix. What course does it begin on?

figure.title: Durban → Fremantle, day 9
lines: Planned GC crosses 060°E 169 M further south

questions.why: New GC from the fix: DLo 55°25′E; GC formula → S 77.3° E = 103°T, 2,740 M to go; the old GC ran 100°T at 060°E.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the course changes

questions.q: Planning the North Pacific crossing from Japan to British Columbia, you need the great-circle distance. What is it?
questions.why: DLo across 180°: 40°21′ + 56°38′ = 96°59′E; cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo → 68.40° = 4,104 M.

questions.q: Your first course out of Yokohama on the great circle for Victoria, across the date line — what is it?
questions.why: DLo 96°59′ east across 180°; GC formula → N 45.1° E = 045°T, far north of the rhumb line 080°T; 120°T on arrival.

questions.q: Checking how close the great circle to Victoria runs to the Aleutians, you work out its vertex. Where is it?
questions.why: cos Lv = cos 35.45° × sin 45.1° → 54°45′N; cos DLo = tan 35.45° / tan Lv → 59°48′ east of Yokohama = 160°33′W.

questions.q: Your next great-circle waypoint is where the track to Victoria crosses the date line. What latitude do you give it?
questions.why: DLo from the vertex to 180° = 19°27′; tan L = tan 54.75° × cos 19.45° → 53°09′N.

questions.q: A crew member sets the autopilot to the plotter's first course on this great circle and means to hold it all the way to Victoria. What happens?
options: You end up south of Victoria, off Oregon
You reach Victoria by a longer, southern route
You stay on the great circle — it starts on 045°T
You sail a rhumb line that passes far north of Victoria
questions.why: A steady 045°T is a rhumb line, not the GC: it crosses every meridian at 45° and would reach 60°N near 177°E, in the Bering Sea.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — the course changes

questions.q: Planning Japan to British Columbia, you look at the great circle running up past the Aleutians. Which route do you choose?

figure.title: Yokohama → Victoria, routing
lines: GC runs close south of the Aleutians
Near the Aleutians: fog, cold, frequent gales
Winter: deep lows across the whole route

options: South of the GC, along about 40–45°N in summer, then east
South to the trades near 20°N, then north up the coast
The great circle in January, for the strongest westerlies
The great circle past the Aleutians — the shortest
questions.why: By the Aleutians the GC meets fog, cold and gales; a summer route along 40–45°N has steady westerlies and a fair current for a few more miles.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

questions.q: Before working the great circle from Nouméa to Rarotonga, you need the difference of longitude. What is it?
questions.why: Across 180° add the two distances from it: (180° − 166°26′) + (180° − 159°47′) = 13°34′ + 20°13′ = 33°47′, eastbound.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — DLo across the date line

questions.q: Crossing the Tasman from Sydney Heads to Nelson on the great circle, what course do you set first?
questions.why: Both south: GC formula → S 60.4° E = 120°T; the rhumb line is 113°T and the GC course is 106°T on arrival.

questions.q: Bound from Mauritius to Durban on the great circle, you work out the vertex to see how far south the track goes. Where is it?
questions.why: cos Lv = cos 20.17° × sin 62.7° → 33°28′S; DLo 56°16′ west of Port Louis → 001°14′E: beyond Durban, off the track.

questions.q: Planning the great circle from Cabo San Lucas to the Marquesas, which crosses the equator, you work out its northern vertex. Where is it?

figure.title: GC Cabo San Lucas → Nuku Hiva

questions.why: cos Lv = cos 22.88° × sin 46.3° → 48°14′N; it lies 67°51′ east of Cabo, behind you: from the start the track only descends.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — across the equator

questions.q: On the same great circle from Cabo San Lucas, where do you cross the equator, and on what course?

figure.title: GC Cabo San Lucas → Nuku Hiva

questions.why: Lv 48°14′N at 042°03′W; the GC cuts the equator 90° of longitude from the vertex: 132°03′W; sin C = cos Lv → S 41.8° W.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — across the equator

questions.q: You leave Honolulu for Fiji on the great circle, across both the equator and the date line. What course do you set first?
questions.why: DLo 22°08′ + 1°34′ = 23°42′ west across 180°; Suva's latitude negative; GC formula → S 32.2° W = 212°T.

questions.q: You plan the long leg from Hawaii to New Caledonia, across both the equator and the date line. What is the great-circle distance?
questions.why: DLo 22°08′ + 13°34′ = 35°42′W; Nouméa's latitude negative; cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo → 55.77° = 3,346 M.

questions.q: Before the Southern Ocean leg from New Zealand to Cape Horn, you compute the great-circle distance. What is it?
questions.why: DLo 11°39′ + 112°43′ = 124°22′E across 180°; both south; cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo → 67.34° = 4,040 M.

questions.q: You are on this composite track from Bluff to Cape Horn and have come down to the limiting latitude. What course do you steer along it?
questions.why: Between the two great circles you run along the parallel: course 090°, distance = DLo × cos 58°.

questions.q: With 58°S as your ice limit, what course do you steer out of Bluff on the composite track?
questions.why: The first GC has its vertex on 58°S: sin C = cos 58° / cos 46.60° → S 50.5° E = 130°T.

questions.q: You will turn east along 58°S where the first great circle out of Bluff touches it. Which meridian is that?
How many miles of the composite track to Cape Horn do you spend running along 58°S?

figure.title: Composite, Bluff → Cape Horn
lines: Along the parallel for 53°32′ of DLo
Then a GC up to the Horn

questions.why: DLo 53°32′ = 3,212′; departure = DLo × cos 58° = 1,702 M.

questions.q: Keeping north of 58°S all the way to the Horn, how long is your composite track?
questions.why: GC legs: cos d = sin L / sin 58° → 1,863 + 732 M; along 58°S 1,702 M; total 4,297 M (direct GC 4,040 M).

questions.q: Your plotter route to Cape Horn is a single GC leg, but your ice limit is 58°S. How do you set up the route?
options: Add one waypoint at the vertex, with RL legs to it
Switch the leg to RL — the shortest that clears 58°S
Two GC legs to and from 58°S, joined by an RL along it
Leave it — a GC leg keeps north of the ice
questions.why: Composite sailing: GC to the limit, a rhumb line along the parallel, GC to the Horn — the shortest track that stays north of 58°S.

questions.q: Planning your great-circle waypoints, you can space them every 10° of longitude or closer. Where does closer spacing matter most?

figure.title: Waypoints for a great circle
lines: Option: every 5° on part of the route

options: At the start, whatever the latitude
Nowhere — the extra miles are the same
Near the equator, where the course changes fastest
In high latitudes, where the course changes fastest
questions.why: The course turns by about DLo × sin lat: over 10° of DLo it turns 1.7° at 10° but 8.2° at 55°, so long rhumb legs cut more corner there.

questions.q: From the positions of the two ports alone, you work out where the great circle from Rio crosses the Greenwich meridian. What latitude?

figure.title: GC Rio de Janeiro → Cape Town

questions.why: Initial course 116.3°; cos Lv = cos 22.90° sin 63.7° → 34°19′S at 008°35′E; tan L = tan Lv cos 8.59° → 34°01′S.

questions.q: From the Falklands you are heading for Cape Town on the great circle. How far is it?
questions.why: DLo = 57°50′W + 18°25′E = 76°15′ (west and east add); cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo → 55.94° = 3,356 M.

questions.q: You work the single rhumb line from Fremantle to Mauritius by Mercator sailing. What course and distance do you get?
Across the date line from Fiji to the Cook Islands, you want the rhumb line by Mercator sailing. What course and distance?
You want one rhumb-line course from Honolulu to Suva by Mercator sailing, across the equator and the date line. What course and distance?
questions.why: Contrary names add: DMP 2399.4, dLat 2,366′S; DLo 23°42′W = 1,422′; C = S 30.7° W; d = 2,366′ / cos C.

questions.q: Your mate has worked the long rhumb line to Cape Town by plane sailing. You check it by Mercator sailing with the MPs. What do you find?
options: Same course and distance — both exact
questions.why: Mercator: DMP 1463.7, DLo 4,575′ → 072°T, 3,498 M. Over a long leg the mean-latitude departure goes wrong.

questions.q: You are about to cross the Bay of Biscay from Ushant to Cape Finisterre. Which sailing do you use to work the course and distance?

figure.title: Ushant → Cape Finisterre
lines: About 380 M across the Bay of Biscay

options: Parallel sailing — along the mean latitude
Composite sailing — to keep out of the bay
Plane sailing — on a leg this short it is close enough
Great circle sailing — nothing else is accurate
questions.why: Plane sailing gives 208°T, 378 M and the GC is 378 M: over a few hundred miles the difference is a fraction of a mile.

questions.q: You work the Biscay crossing from Falmouth to A Coruña by plane sailing, with no current or leeway to allow for. What course and distance?
You work the overnight hop from Sydney to Lord Howe Island by plane sailing. What course and distance do you get?
Westbound from Tonga, you have these two noon fixes, either side of the date line. What course and distance have you made good?

figure.title: Two noon fixes, Tonga to Fiji

questions.q: East of Fiji you are on the parallel of Savusavu and will keep to it, across the 180° meridian, into the harbour. What distance is left?
questions.why: DLo 2°30′ + 0°40′ = 3°10′ = 190′ across 180°; distance = DLo × cos lat = 190 × cos 16.78° = 182 M.

questions.q: You plan to cross the Bay of Bengal westbound from Phuket to Galle in Sri Lanka. When do you go?

figure.title: Phuket → Galle, Sri Lanka
lines: NE monsoon Dec–Mar: fair, NE F3–5
SW monsoon Jun–Sep: W–SW F6–7, rain

options: Any month — the miles are the same
July — with the SW monsoon behind you
August — the SW monsoon is easing by then
January — with the NE monsoon on the quarter
questions.why: Westbound at 265°T the NE monsoon is on the quarter; in the SW monsoon the same great circle is a beat into F6–7 and rain.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

questions.q: In early June you are in Galle, bound for Salalah and the Red Sea. The great circle runs straight into the monsoon. What do you do?

figure.title: Galle → Salalah, early June
lines: SW monsoon setting in: W–SW F6–8
July–August: the monsoon at its strongest

options: Wait for the NE monsoon and go in January or February
Go in August, when the monsoon has eased
Go now and motor close along the Indian coast
Go now on the great circle — it is the shortest
questions.why: In the SW monsoon the 295° track is a beat into F6–8 for 1,672 M; from December to March the NE monsoon puts the wind on the quarter.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

questions.q: Leaving Fremantle for Mauritius in October, you compare the great circle with the trade-wind belt to the north. Which way do you route?

figure.title: Fremantle → Mauritius, October
lines: Along 32°S: variable winds under the high

options: North to the equator, then west along it
North-west into the SE trade, then west with it on the quarter
South into the westerlies, then north to Mauritius
The great circle, due west along about 32°S
questions.why: The GC runs through the light variables under the high; the SE trade to the north gives a fast reach — a few more miles, fewer days.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

questions.q: You plan Rio de Janeiro to Cape Town. The great circle runs east-south-east under the South Atlantic high, shown here. Which route do you take?
options: The rhumb line, motoring through the calms
The great circle — the shortest is the fastest
South of the high into the westerlies, then east to the Cape
North of the high with the SE trade, then south
questions.why: Light winds lie under the high; to its south, near 35–40°S by Tristan da Cunha, the westerlies carry you east to the Cape.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

questions.q: In May you leave New Zealand for Tahiti. The great circle heads north-east, straight into the SE trade. How do you route?

figure.title: Opua → Papeete, May
lines: GC: north-east, into the SE trade

options: North into the trade first, then east along 20°S
The great circle — beat up it through the trade
North to Tonga, then east along 18°S to Tahiti
East in the westerlies to about 150°W, then north to Tahiti
questions.why: Make your easting in the westerlies south of 30°S, then turn north and reach up through the SE trade: more miles, but no long beat.
questions.ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

questions.q: You are three days out of Las Palmas on the ARC route, in the trade-wind belt. Why does the wind blow from the NE and not straight from the N?

figure.title: Leaving Gran Canaria, late November
lines: Air flows south towards the equator

options: The Earth's rotation turns it to the right
The Sahara's heat pulls it in from the east
The Azores High spins it anticlockwise
The Canary Current drags it to the west
questions.why: Coriolis turns moving air to the right in the north: the flow back to the equator becomes the NE trade.

questions.q: You left Madeira for the Cape Verdes and the wind has died. Why is there so little wind here?

figure.title: Becalmed at 30°N 25°W
lines: Sky clear, air dry, sea glassy

options: The trades and the westerlies cancel each other
Air from the Hadley cell sinks here under a high
The cold Canary Current stops the air moving
Air rises here and the cloud smothers the wind
questions.why: Air lifted at the ITCZ sinks again near 30°: a belt of high pressure, light winds and dry air — the horse latitudes.

questions.q: You leave Santa Cruz for Hiva Oa on the Pacific Puddle Jump. What wind do you expect for most of the passage?
options: The NE trade, on the starboard quarter
The westerlies, close-hauled all the way
The SE trade, on the port quarter
The calms and squalls of the doldrums
questions.why: South of the ITCZ the SE trade blows: from about 135° on a course of 250° it is on the port quarter.

questions.q: You plan the run south from the Cape Verdes to Brazil. Where do you expect to meet the doldrums?

figure.title: Mindelo to Salvador, 1 March
lines: Course south, crossing the equator at 28°W

options: Right off the Cape Verdes, at about 15°N
Around 10–12°N, where it lies in August
Around 0–5°N, the ITCZ at its farthest south
questions.why: The ITCZ follows the Sun with a lag: in the Atlantic it lies nearest the equator in Feb–Apr and farthest north in Aug–Sep.

questions.q: You leave Bermuda for Horta in early June, and the Azores High lies across the rhumb line, as here. Which way do you go?
options: North of the centre, where the westerlies blow
South of the centre, along its southern side
Wait in Bermuda until the high has moved away
Straight through the centre, the shortest way
questions.why: Round a northern high the wind turns clockwise: westerlies on its north side, easterlies on its south side, calm in the middle.

questions.q: You are planning the passage home from Hawaii to California. Which route do you take?
options: Through the middle of the high, motoring the calms
North on starboard tack, round the top of the high, then east
The rhumb line, beating NE into the trade all the way
South of the high in the trade, then up the coast
questions.why: Clockwise flow round the high: sail north across the trade, reach the westerlies above it, then run east to the coast.
questions.ref: Subtropical highs — the North Pacific High

questions.q: You are two days out of Cape Town, north-east of the South Atlantic High, steering for St Helena. What wind do you expect?
questions.why: A southern high turns anticlockwise: on its NE side the air flows to the NW — the SE trade, astern on a course of 320°.
questions.ref: Subtropical highs — the St Helena High

questions.q: You plan to run east along 40°S across the Indian Ocean. What weather do you prepare the boat for?

figure.title: Cape Town to Fremantle along 40°S
lines: Pilot chart: gales 10 % of the time

options: Easterlies on the nose most of the way
A steady SE trade under settled skies
Mostly calms under a permanent high
Fair westerlies, with a gale as each low passes
questions.why: No land stops the Southern Ocean lows: the roaring forties give strong westerlies and a gale every few days.

questions.q: Your 24 m expedition yacht leaves Iceland for Svalbard, north of the storm track of the westerlies. Which prevailing wind do you plan for near 75°N?
options: Easterlies blowing out of the polar high
The NE trade, steady at force 4
The SW monsoon of high summer
questions.why: Beyond about 60° cold air flows out of the polar high and Coriolis turns it west: the polar easterlies.

questions.q: It is early June in Galle and a crew member suggests leaving now for Oman. What does the pilot chart for June tell you?

figure.title: Pilot chart, June: Arabian Sea
lines: Wind rose: SW, F6–7 most of the month

options: The monsoon is over: easy trade-wind sailing to the west
The SW monsoon has set in: F6–7 on the nose and a rough sea all the way
The NE monsoon is still blowing: a fast run with the wind astern
It is the transition: light airs, motoring most of the way
questions.why: From June to September the SW monsoon blows hard across the Arabian Sea: a westbound passage is a beat into a big sea.

questions.q: You are ready to cross to the Bahamas. When do you go?

figure.title: Fort Lauderdale, 1800
lines: Bimini: 45 M east, across the Gulf Stream
Gulf Stream setting N at 3 kn
Cold front due 2000, then N 20–25 kn

options: Tomorrow morning, in the N 20–25 kn
Tonight, while the front is passing
Tomorrow evening, once the northerly has eased
Now, to get across ahead of the front
questions.why: Wind against a 3 kn current raises short, steep, breaking seas: never cross the Gulf Stream with a wind from the north.

questions.q: You are running west in the trade wind. What is your run over the ground in 24 hours?

figure.title: ARC, day 10, 16°N 45°W
lines: Pilot chart: current 0.5 kn, setting W

questions.why: The North Equatorial Current sets west with you: (6.5 + 0.5) × 24 = 168 M over the ground.
questions.ref: Ocean currents — the North Equatorial Current

questions.q: You are waiting to sail down the South African coast. What do you decide?

figure.title: Richards Bay, bound SW for East London
lines: 300 M: about 30 h with the current
Now: NE 15–20 kn for the next 36 h
Then a cold front: SW 35–40 kn

options: Go now: in port about 6 h before the change
Go now and stay in the current when it turns SW
Go as the front passes: the current calms the sea
Wait, then go with the SW wind behind the front
questions.why: A SW gale against the 2–4 kn Agulhas raises huge, steep seas: sail in the NE window and be in port before the change.

questions.q: Your crew expected tropical heat this close to the equator. What explains this weather?

figure.title: Callao, Peru, 12°S, February
lines: Low grey cloud, no rain for months

options: The ITCZ lying overhead in February
The cold Humboldt Current flowing north
The Canary Current crossing from Africa
questions.why: The Humboldt (Peru) Current brings cold water north along South America: cool, stable air, low cloud and almost no rain.

questions.q: You are sailing north-east along the coast of Japan. Where do you put the boat?

figure.title: Amami to Tokyo Bay, May, 450 M NE
lines: Pilot chart: Kuroshio sets NE, 2–4 kn

options: Inshore of it, out of the current's set
Well offshore, south of the current
In the Kuroshio, wind and current both NE-going
In the Kuroshio only if the wind turns NE
questions.why: The Kuroshio is Japan's Gulf Stream: with a SW wind ride its axis for 2–4 kn more; never stay in it in a NE blow.

questions.q: On a circumnavigation you will hear storm warnings in each of these places. What does each forecast call a tropical revolving storm?

figure.title: One kind of storm, four oceans
lines: D: the Bay of Bengal, November

questions.why: Atlantic and NE Pacific: hurricane; NW Pacific: typhoon; Indian Ocean and South Pacific: (tropical) cyclone.

questions.q: Your crew want to stay in the Caribbean until October. Which plan fits the North Atlantic hurricane season?

figure.title: Antigua, end of April
lines: Plan: cruise the Leewards into autumn
Pilot charts Aug–Oct: TRS tracks across them
Insurer: no named-storm cover in season

options: Leave the belt by June; the season runs to November
Leave by September; the season is only Aug–Sep
Stay; hurricanes never reach the Leewards
Stay; storms are rare before October
questions.why: The North Atlantic season runs 1 June – 30 November, peaking Aug–Oct: be out of the hurricane belt by June.

questions.q: What do you tell the crew about the South Pacific cyclone season?

figure.title: Neiafu, Tonga, mid-October
lines: Next stop on the plan: New Zealand in May

options: It runs May–October, in the southern winter
It runs November–April: be in New Zealand by then
There is none: no cyclones form south of the equator
It runs June–November, as in the Caribbean
questions.why: Southern-hemisphere cyclones come in the southern summer, Nov–Apr: most boats leave Tonga for New Zealand in Oct–Nov.

questions.q: Which months carry the highest risk of a cyclone on this crossing?

figure.title: Galle to Phuket, across the Bay of Bengal
lines: Sea warm enough for storms all year
Months being discussed: Jan, May, Aug, Nov

options: July–August, at the height of the SW monsoon
None: the Bay of Bengal has no cyclones
May and Oct–Nov, as the monsoon changes
questions.why: North Indian Ocean cyclones peak at the monsoon changes, Apr–Jun and Oct–Dec; the strong SW monsoon's shear stops most in Jul–Aug.

questions.q: Each area shows a cluster of thunderstorms. Which one could grow into a hurricane?
options: D: in the South Atlantic, in its winter
C: the farthest north, in the westerlies
A: the warmest sea of the four
B: warm sea, far enough from the equator
questions.why: A TRS needs a sea of about 26.5 °C or more and Coriolis spin, so at least 5° from the equator: only B has both.

questions.q: You have hired a weather router for the crossing. Who decides each day when to reef and which way to go?

figure.title: Routing service, Canaries to Antigua
lines: Advice from the latest model runs

options: You: the router advises, the skipper decides
The router, unless the GRIB disagrees
Whoever is on watch when the e-mail comes
The router: they see the full model output
questions.why: A router sees models, not your sky, sea and barometer: the advice is one input, and the decisions stay with the skipper.

questions.q: You are three days from Martinique. What do you make of these signs?

figure.title: 15°N 55°W, early September
lines: NE trade 15 kn, as for a week
New long swell from ESE, period 14 s
Cirrus streaks fanning out from the ESE
Barometer 1012 hPa, normal for the hour

options: A normal trade-wind day: carry on as before
A TRS may lie to the ESE: log the glass hourly
The ITCZ is moving north towards you
A cold front is coming down from the north
questions.why: A long swell and cirrus radiating from one point are the first signs of a TRS, often before the barometer moves.

questions.q: You log this reading in the hurricane season. How far below normal is it, and what does it mean?

figure.title: Barometer at 1000 local, 16°N
lines: Pilot chart mean for the month: 1013 hPa

options: 3.0 hPa below the mean: only the daily swing
No fall at all once the daily swing is allowed
4.5 hPa below normal for 1000: suspect a TRS
1.5 hPa below normal: within the daily swing
questions.why: Normal at 1000 = 1013 + 1.5 = 1014.5; 1014.5 − 1010 = 4.5 hPa. 3 hPa or more below normal in the tropics warns of a TRS.

questions.q: A crew member is alarmed by a fall of 3 hPa in six hours. What do you tell them?
options: A cold front is coming: expect a sharp veer
A TRS is near: 3 hPa in six hours is the sign
The barometer is faulty: tropical pressure never moves
Normal: the glass peaks near 1000 and dips near 1600
questions.why: Tropical pressure has a twice-daily tide of about 3 hPa: highs near 1000 and 2200, lows near 0400 and 1600.

questions.q: Your crew say a hurricane heading NW will pass well west of Bermuda. What is its most likely path over the next few days?
options: It recurves north, then north-east, speeding up
It turns west-south-west, back into the Caribbean
It stalls and fills where it is within a day
It keeps going NW until it reaches the US coast
questions.why: North Atlantic storms move W–NW round the high, then recurve N and NE into the westerlies, faster — often towards Bermuda.

questions.q: The depression is north-west of you. Which path does a storm born here typically take?
options: South-west at first, then on to the west
West-south-west at first, then recurving south-east
West-north-west at first, then recurving north-east
East along 10°S at first, then turning north
questions.why: Southern storms move west and poleward, then recurve S and SE into the westerlies: the mirror of the northern track.

questions.q: This hurricane east of the Leeward Islands is moving west. Which side of it is the dangerous semicircle?
options: The west side, ahead of the centre
The south side, left of the track
The north side, right of the track
The east side, behind the centre
questions.why: North of the equator it is the right-hand half, looking along the track: the storm's speed adds to the wind, which blows you into its path.

questions.q: This cyclone north-east of Mauritius is moving south-west. Which side of it is the dangerous semicircle?
options: The south-west side, ahead of the centre
The north-east side, behind the centre
The north-west side, right of the track
The south-east side, left of the track
questions.why: South of the equator the dangerous half is the left-hand one, looking along the track: on a SW track that is the SE side.

questions.q: You face the wind to find the typhoon's centre. Roughly which way does it bear?

figure.title: South China Sea, typhoon warning
lines: Centre about 10 points (112°) from the wind

questions.why: North of the equator, face the wind and the centre is on your right, about 10 points at first: 040° + 112° ≈ 150°.
questions.ref: Tropical revolving storms — Buys Ballot's law

questions.q: Sailing from Nouméa towards Brisbane, you need to know where the cyclone's centre lies. Which way does it bear from you?

figure.title: Coral Sea, cyclone warning
lines: Centre about 10 points (112°) from the wind

questions.why: South of the equator, face the wind and the low is on your left: 330° − 112° ≈ 220°.
questions.ref: Tropical revolving storms — Buys Ballot's law

questions.q: You log the wind and barometer every two hours as the storm comes closer. Where are you relative to it?
options: Right in its path: the wind is holding steady
In the navigable semicircle: the wind is backing
In the dangerous semicircle: the wind is veering
In the dangerous semicircle: the wind is backing
questions.why: E → ESE → SE turns clockwise, a veer: north of the equator a veering wind puts you in the right-hand, dangerous half.

questions.q: The wind shifts like this as the hurricane approaches. What do you do?

figure.title: Hurricane to the SE, moving NW

options: Put the wind on the starboard bow, close-hauled
Heave to on port tack and wait for it to pass
Put the wind on the port quarter and run
Put the wind on the starboard quarter and run
questions.why: NE → N is backing: the navigable half in the north. Run with the wind on the starboard quarter, away from the centre.

questions.q: You have logged these over the last six hours in the South China Sea. What does it tell you, and what do you do?

figure.title: Typhoon to the SE, moving NW
lines: Wind NE 7, direction steady for 6 h

options: On its track: run, wind on the starboard quarter
Dangerous half: close-hauled, wind on starboard bow
Navigable half: hold your course and wait
On its track: run, wind on the port quarter
questions.why: A steady wind and a falling glass put you on the track; north of the equator run with the wind on the starboard quarter.

questions.q: Your plot puts you here, 150 M north of a hurricane that is moving west. Which action is right?
options: Run with the wind on the port quarter
Close-hauled on starboard tack, wind on the starboard bow
Run with the wind on the starboard quarter
Close-hauled on port tack, wind on the port bow
questions.why: North of a westbound storm is its right, dangerous half: in the north keep the wind on the starboard bow and claw away.

questions.q: You log these as a cyclone approaches Tonga. Where are you, and what do you do?
options: Dangerous half: close-hauled on starboard tack
Navigable half: run, wind on the port quarter
Dangerous half: close-hauled on port tack
Navigable half: run, wind on the starboard quarter
questions.why: SE → E → NE is backing; south of the equator that is the left-hand, dangerous half: keep the wind on the port bow.

questions.q: A cyclone is tracking west across the Coral Sea, and the plot puts you on its north side, as here. What do you do?
options: Run with the wind on the starboard quarter
Close-hauled on starboard tack, wind on the starboard bow
Close-hauled on port tack, wind on the port bow
Run with the wind on the port quarter
questions.why: In the south the right-hand half of a westbound storm, its north side, is navigable: run with the wind on the port quarter.

questions.q: You are south-west of Fiji with these readings. Where are you, and which action do you take?

figure.title: Cyclone to the NE, moving SW
lines: Wind SE 7, direction steady for 5 h

options: On its track: run, wind on the port quarter
Dangerous half: close-hauled, wind on the port bow
Navigable half: hold your course and wait
On its track: run, wind on the starboard quarter
questions.why: A steady wind and a falling glass: you are on the track. South of the equator run with the wind on the port quarter.

questions.q: You plot the advisory using the mariner's 1-2-3 rule. What radius round the 48-hour forecast position do you keep out of?
questions.why: 1-2-3 rule: add 100, 200, 300 M of forecast error at 24, 48, 72 h to the 34-kn radius: 120 + 200 = 320 M.

questions.q: Using the 1-2-3 rule, is your plan safe?

figure.title: Storm plot, 48 h ahead
lines: Your DR in 48 h: 280 M from it

options: Yes: the 48-h zone is only 250 M
Yes: you would be outside the 150 M radius
No: you would be inside the 350 M zone
Yes: you stay more than 200 M from the centre
questions.why: At 48 h: 150 + 200 = 350 M; at 280 M your DR is inside the zone — re-route now, while the storm is still far off.

questions.q: If you stay where you are, how long before the 34-knot winds reach you?
questions.why: (330 − 120) ÷ 14 = 15 h: the gale arrives with the edge of the 34-kn radius, long before the centre.

questions.q: How far from the centre are you after 24 hours?

figure.title: Hurricane 360 M due east of you
lines: You run 225° at 6 kn for 24 h

questions.why: The storm runs 288 M to 72 M E of your start; you run 144 M SW: √(173.8² + 101.8²) ≈ 201 M, clear of the 34-kn winds.

questions.q: You are north of the equator. What wind do you expect at your position?

figure.title: Advisory: 34-kn wind radii
lines: You: 130 M NE of the centre

options: Under 34 kn: outside the 60 M SW radius
34 kn or more: inside the NE radius
64 kn or more: inside the hurricane core
Under 34 kn: beyond the 105 M mean radius
questions.why: The radii are given per quadrant and are widest on the right of the track in the north: 130 M NE is inside 150 M.

questions.q: How long before the squall reaches you?

figure.title: Trade winds, night, 0230
lines: Stars vanishing under a line of cloud
Squalls move with the trade at 15 kn
You: running at 7 kn, poled-out genoa

questions.why: It closes at 15 − 7 = 8 kn: 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 h = 45 min — time to reef before it arrives, not in it.

questions.q: You are crossing from Newport to the Azores, and this depression is passing north of you. How does the wind change when its cold front comes through?
options: It veers from NW to NE, then falls calm
It backs from SW to SE, with drizzle
It backs from NW to SW, the glass falling
It veers from SW to NW, in squalls
questions.why: North of the equator a cold front brings a sharp veer, SW to W or NW, squalls, then a rising glass and clearer air.
questions.ref: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing

questions.q: You are running east to Fremantle. How does the wind shift as the front passes?

figure.title: Southern Indian Ocean, 40°S
lines: Low passing to the south, moving E

options: It backs from NW to SW, in squalls
It holds NW and slowly eases
It drops to a calm, and fog sets in
It veers from NW to NE, with rain
questions.why: Lows turn clockwise in the south: NW ahead of a cold front, SW behind it — a back, with squalls and a rising glass.
questions.ref: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing

questions.q: You are eastbound across the North Atlantic, and this faster low will overtake you. You can alter north or south now. Which do you choose?
options: Neither: heave to and let it pass over you
South, so its centre passes north of you
North, so its centre passes south of you
North, to meet its warm front sooner
questions.why: With the centre passing north of you the wind runs SW → W → NW, all fair eastbound; north of it you meet easterlies.
questions.ref: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing

questions.q: The GRIB file and the advisory disagree about tomorrow. Which do you plan by?

figure.title: Two forecasts for tomorrow
lines: GRIB (GFS, 0.5°): NE 20 kn on your route
NHC: moving W at 12 kn, 34-kn radius 100 M

options: The GRIB, unless the barometer has fallen
An average of the two forecasts
The advisory: a GRIB blunts a small, intense storm
The GRIB: it is the newer and finer data
questions.why: A GRIB is raw model output on a coarse grid: it underplays a tropical storm's winds and track. Trust the forecaster's advisory.
questions.ref: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

questions.q: Why has the NAVTEX gone quiet, and where do you now get the official high-seas forecast?
options: Faulty set: retune it to 490 kHz
No warnings issued: keep waiting for NAVTEX
Out of range: VHF Ch 16 every four hours
Out of range: SafetyNET and HF weatherfax
questions.why: NAVTEX reaches only about 300–400 M from its station: offshore the METAREA forecasts come by SafetyNET, charts by HF weatherfax.

questions.q: You are planning the trade-wind crossing. What wind do you plan for in this square?

figure.title: Pilot chart, January, 15°N 35°W
lines: Arrows fly with the wind, to the circle
Longest arrow, on the NE side: 48 %

options: From the NE, force 5, about half the time
From the E, force 5, nearly all the time
From the SW, force 5, about half the time
From the NE, force 1, calm most days
questions.why: Pilot-chart arrows fly with the wind towards the circle: length = frequency (48 %), feathers = mean force (5).

questions.q: Your great-circle route crosses this area. What does the pilot chart tell you to do?

figure.title: Halifax to Cork, June
lines: Fog 20 % of the time on the Grand Banks

options: Keep the great circle and post a lookout
Route south of the iceberg limit there
Keep the great circle: radar shows every berg
Go north of it to shorten the route further
questions.why: The ice limit marks how far south bergs drift that month; growlers hide from radar in a sea and in fog, so route outside it.

questions.q: You log the wind and the glass every six hours as a cyclone comes closer, south of the equator. Where are you, and what do you do?
options: Dangerous half: close-hauled on starboard tack
Navigable half: run, wind on the starboard quarter
Navigable half: run, wind on the port quarter
Dangerous half: close-hauled on port tack
questions.why: SW → WSW → W turns clockwise, a veer; south of the equator that is the right-hand, navigable half: run, wind on the port quarter.

questions.q: Every three hours you work out the hurricane's bearing from the wind. What do the bearings tell you to do?

figure.title: Hurricane warning, 20°N 62°W
lines: Wind NNW 7, glass falling 1 hPa an hour

options: On its track: run with the wind on the port quarter
Dangerous half: close-hauled, wind on the starboard bow
Navigable half: run with the wind on the port quarter
Navigable half: run with the wind on the starboard quarter
questions.why: The centre's bearing moves anticlockwise (096° → 083°): you are left of its track, the navigable half in the north.
questions.ref: Tropical revolving storms — the centre's bearing

questions.q: You plot the cyclone's bearing every three hours. Which heading do you steer now?
options: About 225°, the wind on the port quarter
About 315°, the wind on the starboard quarter
questions.why: Bearing moving anticlockwise: left half, dangerous in the south. Wind on the port bow: 090° + 50° = 140°, away from the centre.

questions.q: Your crew want to keep going until the typhoon is on the radio. Where is it, and what do you do?
options: About 270°: dangerous half, wind on the starboard bow
About 130°: dangerous half, wind on the starboard bow
About 310°: navigable half, wind on the port quarter
About 130°: navigable half, wind on the starboard quarter
questions.why: Face the wind, the centre is about 10 points right: 020° + 112° ≈ 130°, as the swell says. Veering in the north: the dangerous half.
questions.ref: Tropical revolving storms — finding the centre

questions.q: You must choose one of the two courses. Which is it, and how close will the centre pass?

figure.title: Hurricane plot, 0000 UT, 17°N
lines: Moving 290° at 12 kn, straight at you
You can make 7 kn on 200° or on 020°

options: 020°: about 175 M off, in the dangerous half
200°: about 175 M off, in the navigable half
200°: about 150 M off, in the navigable half
020°: about 150 M off, in the navigable half
questions.why: Relative motion gives a CPA of about 151 M on either course, in about 19 h; 200° is left of the track, the navigable half.

questions.q: This Coral Sea cyclone was moving south-west and has now recurved. Which side of it is now the dangerous semicircle?
options: The south-east side, as before the turn
The north-west side, behind the centre
The south-west side, right of the new track
The north-east side, left of the new track
questions.why: South of the equator the dangerous half is always left of the track: once the track turns SE, that is the NE side.

questions.q: The forecast says the hurricane will recurve and pass north-west of you. Which way do you go now?

figure.title: Hurricane advisory, 1500 UT
lines: You: 33°N 61°W, bound east for the Azores

options: South-east, away from the right side of the new track
North, to cross ahead of it to its left side
Heave to and let it pass to the north-west
East as planned: it will pass behind you
questions.why: Once it recurves NE you would sit right of the track, the dangerous half: head SE now to open the distance.

questions.q: The hurricane has stopped moving. What do you do with the time it gives you?

figure.title: Hurricane advisory, 0900 UT
lines: Centre 250 M east of you, stationary
Your glass and wind steady for 6 h

options: Stay put: a stalled storm dies where it stands
Open the distance now: it may move off any way
Close it now to pass behind it while it waits
Heave to and wait until it picks a direction
questions.why: A stalled storm can drift or lurch off in any direction once it is steered again: use the pause to put sea room between you.
questions.ref: Tropical revolving storms — a stalled storm

questions.q: Your crew want to wait for the next advisory in 12 hours. How do you use the boat?

figure.title: 14 m catamaran, hurricane ahead
lines: Centre crosses your position in 30 h
Clear of 34-kn winds: 150 M off the track
Navigable side: a reach at 8 kn
Dangerous side: a beat at 5 kn

options: Heave to and let her ride it out where she is
Beat for the dangerous side: clear in about 30 h
Reach for the navigable side now: clear in about 19 h
Wait 12 h, then reach: still clear in time
questions.why: 150 M at 8 kn ≈ 19 h, inside the 30 h; waiting 12 h first leaves no margin (31 h). A catamaran's speed is her escape.
questions.ref: Tropical revolving storms — a catamaran's options

questions.q: You are caught in the storm and this happens. What comes next?

figure.title: Hurricane, 0300
lines: Wind NE 70 kn for the last 4 h

options: The wind returns from the NE, but lighter
The storm has passed: the glass will now rise
It is weakening: the worst of it is over
The far wall: the wind returns from the SW, as hard
questions.why: You are in the eye: when it passes, the other wall arrives, with the wind as strong from the opposite direction.

questions.q: It is 1600 in the hurricane season and you correct the reading for the time of day. What do you make of it?

figure.title: Barometer at 1600 local, 14°N
lines: Pilot chart mean for the month: 1012 hPa

options: 2.0 hPa below normal: under 3, keep logging
2.0 hPa below normal: over 1, suspect a TRS
3.5 hPa below normal: over 3, suspect a TRS
5.0 hPa below normal: a TRS is near, act now
questions.why: Normal at 1600 = 1012 − 1.5 = 1010.5; 1010.5 − 1008.5 = 2.0 hPa. Suspect a TRS at 3 below normal, act at 5.

questions.q: Your crew say the afternoon fall is just the daily tide of the barometer. What do the two readings tell you?
options: A 6 hPa fall by 1600 is the normal daily swing
5.5 hPa below normal and falling: a TRS is close
7.0 hPa below normal: you are inside the storm
Only 2.5 hPa below normal: the 1600 dip explains it
questions.why: Normal 1014.5 at 1000, 1011.5 at 1600: 2.5 then 5.5 hPa below. The normal swing is 3 hPa, not 6: a TRS is close.
