questions.q: A new swell has been building for two days. What does it tell you?
options: Nothing: a swell in the trades means nothing
A storm is moving away: the period is falling
A storm is closing on a steady bearing, about 100°
A storm lies about 280°, where the swell runs to
questions.why: Swell runs out from a storm, so it comes from its bearing; a steady direction, a shorter period and a higher sea: it is coming at you.

questions.q: When did this swell leave the storm that made it?

figure.title: Anchored at Nuku Hiva, 9°S
lines: New swell from the SSW, period 18 s
Fax: a storm near 40°S, 1900 M away

questions.why: 1.5 × 18 s ≈ 27 kn; 1900 M ÷ 27 kn ≈ 70 h: the swell left the storm about three days ago.
questions.ref: Ocean swell — from a distant storm

questions.q: Both swells came from the same distant storm. Roughly how far away was it?
questions.why: 18 s runs at 27 kn, 14 s at 21 kn; the 12-h gap gives D(1/21 − 1/27) = 12, so D ≈ 1130 M.
questions.ref: Ocean swell — from a distant storm

questions.q: You cannot get farther away than this. What wind do you prepare for at the closest point?

figure.title: Advisory: Hurricane 'Mara', Cat 2
lines: Forecast closest approach to you: 100 M

questions.why: 100 M is inside the 160 M of the 34-kn radius but outside the 80 M of the 50-kn one: plan for 34–49 kn, more in gusts.

questions.q: You plot an advisory with the mariner's 1-2-3 rule, adding 100, 200 and 300 M to the 34-knot radius at 24, 48 and 72 hours. Why does the margin grow?
options: Your own DR error grows with time
The storm speeds up as it recurves
The forecast track error grows with time
The storm itself grows as it ages
questions.why: The 100–200–300 M are the average forecast track errors at 24, 48 and 72 h: the further ahead, the less sure the position.

questions.q: Your crew know the South Pacific season runs November to April. What do you tell them about this coast?

figure.title: Salvador to Rio, February
lines: South Atlantic hurricanes on record: one

options: They form, but turn away before Brazil
Its season runs June to November
Same season here: November to April
The South Atlantic almost never breeds them
questions.why: Strong wind shear aloft and no ITCZ south of the equator stop them forming; Catarina (2004) is the only known hurricane.
questions.ref: Tropical revolving storms — where they form

questions.q: Planning the leg to the Azores, your crew read the pilot chart like this. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Pilot chart, North Atlantic, July
lines: Red lines: tracks of past storms
Crew: "So no hurricanes on our route"

options: Not quite: rare there in July, not impossible
Yes: the red lines are this year's forecast
Yes: no storm has ever crossed it in July
No: the red lines show where storms never go
questions.why: Pilot-chart storm tracks are history for that month: an empty route means storms are rare there, not impossible. Watch the advisories.

questions.q: You compare the two routes on the pilot chart. How many days of gale should each one expect?

figure.title: Pilot chart, May: Bermuda to the Azores

options: Both about 0.8 days: the miles even it out
questions.why: Gale % is the share of observations at force 8 or more: 8 × 0.15 = 1.2 days north, 11 × 0.03 = 0.33 days south.

questions.q: You plan the delivery south through the South China Sea. When do you go?
options: September–October, before the NE monsoon sets in
April–May, in the calms between monsoons
December–March, with the NE monsoon behind you
June–August, with the SW monsoon behind you
questions.why: On 215° the NE monsoon (Nov–Mar) is a fair wind, and it falls outside the typhoon season; the SW monsoon would be on the nose.

questions.q: You arrive late from Thailand and still want to go west. What do you expect?

figure.title: Uligan, Maldives, 25 April
lines: Plan: 1300 M west to Salalah, Oman
NE monsoon has died: light, variable
SW monsoon due late May, 25–30 kn

options: The SW monsoon behind you as it sets in
The NE monsoon will return for a few weeks
Steady light easterlies all the way to Oman
Calms and squalls, then the SW monsoon on the nose
questions.why: Between the monsoons come calms and squalls; the SW monsoon then blows from where you are going. Go west by March, or wait for autumn.

questions.q: You plan to take the boat north up the Red Sea. Which season do you choose?

figure.title: Djibouti to Suez, 1200 M north
lines: North of 20°N: NNW 15–25 kn all year
Gulf of Aden: NE or SW monsoon

options: Winter, when SSE winds fill the southern half
Spring, when the northerlies stop for a month
Summer, when the SW monsoon blows up the sea
Any season: it blows from the south all year
questions.why: In the NE monsoon (Oct–May) air drawn in from the Gulf of Aden gives SSE winds in the south; in summer NNW blows the whole length.

questions.q: You join the Puddle Jump fleet from Mexico. Where do you plan to cross the doldrums?

figure.title: Puerto Vallarta to Nuku Hiva, late March

options: Near 140°W, just north of Nuku Hiva
Near 125–130°W, where the band is narrower
Wherever the rhumb line meets the band
questions.why: In March the ITCZ lies a few degrees north of the equator and is wider in the east: sail SW in the NE trade and cross it further west.

questions.q: You plan to motor through the light airs. How much fuel do you allow for them, before any reserve?

figure.title: Balboa to San Cristóbal, mid-March
lines: Light airs expected for 360 M of it

questions.why: 360 M ÷ 6 kn = 60 h; 60 h × 3 L/h = 180 L, before the reserve.
questions.ref: The ITCZ — Panama to the Galápagos

questions.q: You planned to sit out the season in French Polynesia. What does the El Niño change?

figure.title: Papeete, Tahiti, October
lines: Season ahead: strong El Niño declared
Plan: the cyclone season in the Tuamotus
Most years: few cyclones east of 150°W

options: The season ends early: no cyclones after January
Nothing: El Niño only changes the rainfall
Cyclones form further west: the Tuamotus are safer
Cyclones form further east: the Tuamotus are at risk
questions.why: In an El Niño the warm water and the cyclones shift east: French Polynesia, usually spared, had several in 1982–83.
questions.ref: El Niño — cyclones and the trades

questions.q: The forecasters have declared an El Niño. How does it change the trade-wind passage ahead?

figure.title: Galápagos, March, El Niño year
lines: Puddle Jump to the Marquesas, 3000 M

options: Weaker, less steady trades, with more calms
Stronger, steadier trades all the way
The trades swing round to the NE
No change: El Niño stays near South America
questions.why: El Niño weakens the Pacific trades, which can even reverse in the west: plan more fuel and a slower passage.
questions.ref: El Niño — cyclones and the trades

questions.q: The eddy turns like every warm-core ring north of the Gulf Stream. Where do you put the boat?

figure.title: Newport to Bermuda, course 165°
lines: SST chart: an eddy pinched off a meander
its centre 20 M west of your rhumb line

options: Through its centre, where the current is strongest
On its east side, where it sets south with you
On its east side, where it sets north against you
On its west side, where it sets south with you
questions.why: A warm-core ring in the north turns clockwise: its east side sets south, a fair current on 165°.

questions.q: Which side of the cold ring gives you a fair current home?

figure.title: Bermuda to Newport, course 345°
lines: south of the Gulf Stream, 80 M across
Your rhumb line runs through its centre

options: Neither: cold rings carry no current
Its centre: the current is strongest there
Its east side: it turns anticlockwise
Its west side: it turns clockwise
questions.why: A cold-core ring is a cyclonic eddy, anticlockwise in the north: its east side sets north, fair for 345°.

questions.q: You hold your heading straight across the Stream. How far north-east has it carried you by the time you are out?

figure.title: Gulf Stream off Cape Hatteras
lines: You head 135° across it at 6 kn

questions.why: 50 M ÷ 6 kn ≈ 8.3 h across; 8.3 h × 3 kn = 25 M set to the NE.
questions.ref: Ocean currents — crossing the Gulf Stream

questions.q: The front's timing has held for two days of forecasts. Do you carry on into the Stream at 0800?

figure.title: Bermuda to Newport, Gulf Stream ahead
lines: Stream 60 M wide, setting NE at 3 kn
You reach its south edge at 0800
Across it at 6 kn over the ground
Front, then N 25 kn, reaches it at 1600

options: Out at 1800, 2 h after the front: wait
Out at 1600, just as the front arrives: go
Out at 1800, but a north wind is harmless: go
Out at 1440, ahead of the front: go
questions.why: 60 M ÷ 6 kn = 10 h: in at 0800, out at 1800 — two hours of north wind against a 3-kn current. Wait until the northerly has gone through.

questions.q: Your watch reports this change. Where are you?
options: On the edge of the Grand Banks
Just out across the Gulf Stream's north wall
Just into the Gulf Stream from the south
In the middle of a warm-core eddy
questions.why: The Stream's north wall is a sharp drop to the cold slope water: northbound, the sea cools fast and the Stream's chop eases.

questions.q: The south-westerly buster is coming sooner than forecast. Where do you take the boat?

figure.title: Agulhas Current, off the Wild Coast
lines: Core on the 200 m line: SW-going, 4 kn
You: on the 200 m line, 60 M from port
SW gale, 40 kn, arriving in 2 h

options: Along the 200 m line, to keep the current's lift
Further out, into the core of the current
Inshore of the 200 m line, out of the current
Back NE along the 200 m line, running before it
questions.why: A SW gale against the 4-kn current builds the steep, breaking seas of the shelf edge: get out of the stream, inshore.
questions.ref: Ocean currents — the Agulhas and a cold front

questions.q: You are riding the Agulhas south-west. What do these signs tell you?

figure.title: Durban to East London, day 1
lines: NE wind 25 kn, now dying to calm
Glass fell to 1004 hPa, now steady
Fog patches; cloud bank in the SW

options: A sea breeze is setting in: carry on
A high is building: the calm will last
The NE will fill in again: carry on
A SW buster within hours: make for port
questions.why: The NE dies as a coastal low passes; fog and a cloud bank in the SW mean the cold front's SW gale is hours away.
questions.ref: Ocean currents — the Agulhas and a cold front

questions.q: You are running east at 42°S, and this low will catch you tomorrow. You can alter north or south now. Which do you choose?
options: North, so its centre passes south of you
Hold your latitude and let it pass over you
Heave to now until it has gone through
South, so its centre passes north of you
questions.why: South of the equator, north of a low the wind runs NW → W → SW, all fair for the east; south of it, NE → E → SE on the nose.
questions.ref: Southern Ocean — lows and their sequence

questions.q: The front has just gone through. What do you expect over the next day or two?
options: SW for a week now that the low has stalled
SW easing as a ridge passes, then NW for the next low
The eye passes next, then NE as hard
SE and a falling glass as the low comes back
questions.why: Southern Ocean lows come in a train: after the cold front the SW eases under a brief ridge, then NW and a falling glass bring the next.
questions.ref: Southern Ocean — lows and their sequence

questions.q: You are eastbound as a depression goes by. Where is its centre passing?
questions.why: North of the equator a wind that backs (SE → E → NE) under a falling glass means the low's centre is passing south of you.
questions.ref: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing

questions.q: Four days out, the GRIB shows the Azores High has shifted. What do you do?
options: Bear away south of the high for its easterlies
Keep north to 38°N, as the plan says
Turn east sooner, at about 34°N, in the westerlies
questions.why: The westerlies lie on the high's north side, wherever it is: with the centre at 30°N you find them at 33–34°N, not 38°N.
questions.ref: Subtropical highs — the Azores High's movement

questions.q: The high has moved north-east and is sitting on your destination. How do you plan the passage?

figure.title: Bermuda to Horta, mid-June
lines: Azores High 1035 hPa centred on the Azores
Calms within 300 M of the centre

options: Stay north in the westerlies, then motor in
Run along 32°N, through the middle of the high
Pass south of the centre in its easterlies
Take the rhumb line: the high will move on
questions.why: Round a northern high the westerlies are on its north side: ride them as far as you can, and carry fuel for the last 300 M of calm.
questions.ref: Subtropical highs — the Azores High's movement

questions.q: Your crew think a storm is coming. What is this wind?

figure.title: English Harbour, Antigua, late December
lines: Pilot chart: no TRS in December

options: The reinforced winter trades, the 'Christmas winds'
A cold front's northerly from America
questions.why: In mid-winter a strong Azores–Bermuda High tightens the gradient: the trades blow 25–30 kn for days under clear skies.

questions.q: The funnel is heading your way. What do you do?

figure.title: Gulf Stream, summer afternoon
lines: Cumulonimbus 2 M to the W, moving E
A funnel dropping from its base to the sea

options: Steer towards it to pass close behind it
Heave to: they never move faster than 5 kn
Steer away across its track and shorten sail
Hold on: a waterspout collapses before it arrives
questions.why: A waterspout moves with its parent cloud and can carry violent winds: alter across its track, reef and close the hatches.

questions.q: The watch leader wants to keep the spinnaker up until the squall arrives. What do you do?
options: Keep it up until the first rain arrives
Keep it up: squall winds are steadier
Keep it up and bear away in the gusts
Drop the spinnaker now, before the squall arrives
questions.why: At night and short-handed, shorten sail before the squall: in 35-kn gusts a spinnaker can broach the boat or be lost.

questions.q: Your crew want to keep full sail: she sails flat and fast. How do you set her up for the night?

figure.title: 13 m catamaran, trade-wind night
lines: True wind 18 kn, full main and genoa
Builder's chart: first reef at 20 kn true

options: Reef before dark for the squall gusts, not the mean
Reef only when the first squall arrives
Full sail: she will heel and warn you in a gust
Full sail, and luff up into each squall
questions.why: A catamaran does not heel to spill a gust: reef for the 35-kn squall gusts, by true wind, before night falls.

questions.q: You plot the squall's echo twice. What do you expect?
options: It hits you at about 0240: reef now
It hits you at about 0300: reef now
It passes astern: the bearing is steady
It passes ahead of you at about 0300
questions.why: Steady bearing, closing 2 M in 20 min (6 kn): the last 4 M take 40 min, so it reaches you about 0300.

questions.q: The crew trust the GRIB and want full sail all night. Why will it not show the squalls?

figure.title: GRIB for tonight: GFS, 0.25°
lines: ENE 16–18 kn all night, no change

options: The file is three hours old by the time it arrives
GRIB files leave out the wind under rain
A squall is smaller than the 15 M grid spacing
Squalls form after midnight, past the forecast
questions.why: 0.25° of latitude is 15 M: a model with that spacing averages a 3-M squall away. Set sail for the squalls, not the GRIB.
questions.ref: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

questions.q: You set the boat up for the night from this file. What do you plan for?
options: 20 kn at most: the GRIB is the maximum
A steady 20 kn: the GRIB shows the gusts
Under 20 kn: GRIB files overstate the trades
Gusts near 28 kn, and more in the squalls
questions.why: A GRIB gives the mean wind over its grid; gusts run some 40 % higher (20 × 1.4 = 28 kn), and squalls add more.
questions.ref: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

questions.q: You must decide today whether to leave port for a 4-day passage. How do you use the two forecasts?

figure.title: Two models, front on day 3
lines: ECMWF: front at 0000 next day, 40 kn

options: Plan for the worse one and check each new run
Average them: about 32 kn at about 1800
Trust GFS: it is updated more often
Ignore both until the front is in sight
questions.why: When the models and the ensemble disagree, confidence is low: plan for the stronger case and watch how each new run moves.
questions.ref: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

questions.q: The chart took hours to reach you. Where along 40°N is the front now?
You have just crossed onto the cold Labrador water over the Grand Banks. What do you prepare for?
options: Fog only once the wind drops tonight
A cold front, with the wind veering NW
Thick fog that this wind will not clear
Clear air: the cold water dries it out
questions.why: Warm, moist SW air chilled over the cold Labrador Current gives advection fog: it forms in a breeze and lasts. Radar, AIS, horn.

questions.q: Sailing up the Namibian coast, you log the sea temperature on three stretches. Where do you expect fog?

figure.title: Lüderitz to Walvis Bay, SE 20 kn

options: Over C, within a degree of the dew point
Over A, where the warm sea adds moisture
Over all three: this coast is always in fog
Over B, the only sea colder than the dew point
questions.why: Fog forms when air is cooled to its dew point: only B (10°C) is below 13°C. The cold Benguela upwelling does this.

questions.q: You are planning your first trade-wind crossing from the Canaries to the Caribbean. When do you leave?

figure.title: Planning the crossing
lines: Las Palmas → St Lucia, about 2 700 M
N Atlantic hurricane season: 1 Jun – 30 Nov
NE trades: steady from late Nov–Dec

questions.why: Leave as the hurricane season closes (30 Nov) and the NE trades set in; the ARC sails in late November, when the risk on its route is very low.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You want to keep cruising the Caribbean through the summer and stay insured. Your policy has this clause. What do you plan?
options: Stay in Antigua with doubled mooring lines
Sail south to Grenada or Trinidad before 1 June
Sail north to the Virgin Islands before 1 June
Stay in Antigua: storms rarely come before August
questions.why: The policy decides: be south of the line (Grenada 12°N, Trinidad 10°N) before the exclusion starts, or haul out as agreed.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You leave Las Palmas for the Caribbean in December, and the pilot chart for the month gives this. How do you plan the route?
options: The rhumb line due west along 26–28°N
The great circle direct: the shortest is fastest
Head SSW to about 20°N, then west in the trades
questions.why: The direct route skirts the Azores high: light winds and calms. Go south till the trades are steady, then turn west.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You are in Panama planning the Pacific Puddle Jump and a season in the islands. When do you leave, and when must you be in New Zealand?

figure.title: Puddle Jump plan
lines: Then Tahiti, Tonga and on to New Zealand

options: Leave in June; reach New Zealand by January
Leave in December; reach New Zealand by May
Leave Sep–Oct; reach New Zealand by March
Leave Feb–Apr; reach New Zealand by early November
questions.why: Arrive in Polynesia as the cyclone season ends, cruise the austral winter, and be out of the tropics before it starts again.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You are crossing the northern Indian Ocean westbound towards the Red Sea. When do you sail?
options: January–February, the NE monsoon behind you
October, as the SW monsoon eases
May, in the calm between the monsoons
July, in the steady SW monsoon
questions.why: Westbound you want the NE monsoon astern; the SW monsoon is a gale on the nose, and the changeovers bring cyclones.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You leave Bermuda for the Azores in late May, and the high sits across the direct route. Which route do you plan?
options: North to 50°N for the strongest westerlies
North of the high to about 38–40°N, then east
The rhumb line straight through the high
South of the high, in the NE trades
questions.why: Round a high on its poleward side for fair westerlies; its centre is calm, its south side is foul easterlies, 50°N is gales.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: The rigger’s survey before your Atlantic crossing finds this. What do you do?

figure.title: Rig survey
lines: Cap shroud: hairline crack at lower swage
Rest of the rigging: same age, 12 years

options: Ease that shroud and reef early all the way
Replace that one shroud only and go
Re-rig all of it, and carry a spare shroud
Tape over the swage and check it daily
questions.why: One crack in 12-year-old wire says the rest is as tired: replace it before 3 weeks of rolling, and carry spare wire and fittings.

questions.q: You are planning three weeks of trade-wind running with these figures. How do you steer the boat?

figure.title: Self-steering
lines: Autopilot, big following sea: 6 A average

options: Hand-steering in 2-hour tricks by all three
The autopilot by day, hand-steering at night
The autopilot full-time; run the engine as needed
The windvane day and night; the autopilot as backup
questions.why: Autopilot 6 A × 24 h = 144 Ah + 70 = 214 Ah against 120 Ah: a windvane steers downwind with no power at all.

questions.q: You are drawing up the energy budget for the crossing from these loads. How much must you put back into the batteries each day?

figure.title: Energy budget, per day
lines: Fridge 5.0 A, running 40 % of the time
LED tricolour 1.0 A, 12 h; the rest 14 Ah

questions.why: 96 (autopilot) + 5 × 0.4 × 24 = 48 (fridge) + 36 (instruments) + 12 (light) + 14 = 206 Ah a day.

questions.q: Ten days out, your energy log settles at these figures. How long do you run the engine each day to keep up?
options: None: the 400 Ah bank covers it
questions.why: Deficit 180 − 110 = 70 Ah ÷ 50 A = 1.4 h. The bank’s usable 160 Ah would be gone in about 2 days without it.

questions.q: You are planning drinking water for a 3-week crossing, with washing and dishes done in sea water. What daily allowance do you plan per person?
options: About 1 litre: you drink little at sea
About 3 litres, for drinking and cooking
About 25 litres, as you use at home
questions.why: Plan about 3 L a person a day for drinking and cooking — more in the tropics — and a reserve on top.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

questions.q: You are filling up with water for the crossing, as on the card. How much do you carry in cans on top of the tanks?

figure.title: Water plan
lines: Crew 5; allowance 3 L per person per day
Reserve can’t rely on the watermaker

options: None: the watermaker makes up any gap
questions.why: 5 × 3 × 18 × 1.5 = 405 L must be aboard without the watermaker: 405 − 350 = 55 L in cans, kept apart from the tanks.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

questions.q: You are writing the provisioning list for the crossing. For how many person-days do you provision?
questions.why: 2 000 ÷ 125 = 16 days; +50 % = 24 days for calms and breakdowns; × 4 crew = 96 person-days.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

questions.q: You are working out your range under power for the crossing. How far can you motor?

figure.title: Fuel
lines: Diesel: tank 180 L + 4 cans of 20 L
Keep 25 % reserve for landfall and charging

questions.why: 260 L × 0.75 = 195 L ÷ 3.0 L/h = 65 h × 5.5 kn = 358 M, with the reserve still in the tank.

questions.q: You are approaching the doldrums on the way from the Canaries to Brazil. What is your plan for crossing them?

figure.title: Doldrums ahead
lines: ITCZ ahead: about 200 M of calms and squalls
Diesel left 150 L; keep 50 L for landfall
GRIB: puffs of 8–12 kn in the squalls

options: Motor straight through: the fuel covers 200 M
Drift without motoring until the trades fill in
Sail every puff, motor only in the calms
Motor through, using the 50 L reserve as well
questions.why: 100 L ÷ 3.5 L/h × 6 kn ≈ 171 M — short of 200 M without the reserve; so motor only when the sails can’t do it.

questions.q: A crew applicant for your ocean crossing tells you this. What do you require before you accept them?

figure.title: Crew application
lines: Passage 21 days, up to 1 000 M from help
Fridge on board: one 12 V unit

options: Nothing extra: the pump manages it, and they are an adult
Only a letter from their GP saying they are fit
Nothing: refuse — no insulin user can sail offshore
Double supplies, a backup cool store, a doctor’s plan, a briefed crew
questions.why: A medical condition is planned for, not ignored or barred: spares, insulin kept cool if the fridge fails, a hypo plan, crew who know it.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: You are choosing a watch system for a three-week trade-wind crossing. How many hours on deck does each watchkeeper stand per day in each option?

figure.title: Watch systems
lines: Crew of 5: skipper on call, not in the rota
A: two watches of two, 4 on 4 off
B: four solo watches of 3 h, in turn

questions.why: A: half of 24 h each = 12 h. B: 24 h shared by four = 6 h (two 3-h watches) — far more rest over three weeks.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: You set up this rota for a 20-day crossing. Which watches does Anna stand from then on, and what do you change?

figure.title: Watch rota
lines: Crew of 4, solo watches of 3 hours

options: 0000 and 1500 every day; swap pairs each week
0000 and 1200 every day; split one into two dog watches
0000 and 1200 every day; four can’t be rotated
0000, then 0300 on day 2: it rotates by itself
questions.why: Eight watches a day among four repeat daily (0000, 1200). Split 1800–2100 into two dog watches: nine a day, and the hours rotate.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: At 0310 the AIS shows a tanker passing at CPA 1.6 M. The skipper had a long day. You are on watch with these standing orders. What do you do?

figure.title: Standing orders
lines: Call me: any ship with CPA under 2 M
Call me: wind > 20 kn or baro −3 hPa in 3 h
Clip on at all times at night

options: Let him sleep: the tanker will pass clear
Alter course, and tell him in the morning
Call the skipper now, as the orders say
Call him only if the CPA falls below 1 M
questions.why: Standing orders exist so the watch doesn’t have to judge alone: CPA under 2 M means the skipper is called.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: This is your crew on day 3 of the crossing. What is your first fix as skipper?

figure.title: Day 3
lines: Two crew can’t sleep off watch
You: 5 hours’ sleep in the last 48

options: Coffee and double watches until it passes
Heave to every night until everyone is rested
Push on: crews adjust by about day 10
Guard off-watch sleep, and name a deputy so you sleep too
questions.why: Fatigue causes the mistakes: quiet bunks and protected sleep, and a skipper who sleeps — a tired skipper is the biggest risk aboard.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: This is the mood aboard two weeks into the crossing. What do you do as skipper?

figure.title: Day 14
lines: Rows over galley and clean-up duty

options: A fair duty rota, a crew talk, a halfway treat, a word with the quiet one
Give the quiet one the galley to keep them busy
Keep out of it: adults sort these things out
Shorten watches so people see less of each other
questions.why: Morale is the skipper’s job: clear fair duties, air the grievances, mark the halfway, and check privately on anyone withdrawn.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: Your group of six boats is crossing together and wants a daily check-in with positions and weather, far beyond VHF range and without paying for airtime. What do you set up?
options: AIS text messages to each boat at noon
A daily HF/SSB net: a set UT time, frequency and controller
A VHF channel 72 schedule at 0800 every day
A DSC group call on VHF every evening
questions.why: HF (SSB) radio reaches hundreds to thousands of miles free of airtime; VHF and AIS reach only about 20–30 M.

questions.q: You download your GRIB by satellite email each morning mid-ocean. Which request do you send?
options: The whole North Atlantic: 0.25°, hourly to 16 days
The route box: every parameter, 0.25°, hourly to 10 days
The route box only: wind and pressure, 1°, 12-hourly to 5 days
The world: wind only, 3-hourly at 0.5° to 7 days
questions.why: At 2.4 kbit/s every kilobyte costs: the area you’ll sail, the fields you use, a coarse grid and days the model can still forecast.

questions.q: You are leaving this float plan ashore before the crossing. What instruction is still missing?

figure.title: Float plan
lines: Shore contact: your sister in Bristol
Plan: boat, crew, raft, EPIRB ID, route, ETA

options: A list of the provisions on board
The crew’s home addresses and employers
When to call the MRCC if reports stop, and which one
questions.why: A float plan needs a trigger: e.g. no report for 48 h → call MRCC Falmouth with this plan. Without it the alarm comes late or too soon.

questions.q: You are checking the navigation pack for this crossing. What do you do about the almanac?
options: Add the 2027 almanac: January isn’t in the 2026 one
Nothing: the Sun’s data repeats every year
Use the 2026 one and add a day to each date
Nothing: 2026 data is close enough in January
questions.why: The almanac covers one calendar year: sights after 31 Dec need next year’s (or a long-term) almanac aboard.

questions.q: You are packing the sight reduction tables for this route. Which volumes do you take?
options: Vol 1 only: stars cover every sight
questions.why: Vol 1 reduces star sights; Vol 2 the Sun, Moon and planets for latitudes 0°–39° — the whole route lies below 39°N.

questions.q: This is the state of the boat after a night of thunderstorms. What is your navigation plan for the rest of the crossing?

figure.title: After the lightning
lines: In the oven: handheld GPS and batteries

options: The handheld GPS left on full-time; the sextant stays boxed
A position from the MRCC by sat phone each day
Handheld GPS fixes a few times a day, sights as a check, a paper DR
DR only, until the plotter is repaired ashore
questions.why: The backup chain: the handheld (kept in the oven from the lightning), used sparingly for its batteries, with celestial and DR behind it.

questions.q: This is your daily routine on the crossing. Which check is still missing from it?

figure.title: Daily routine
lines: 0700 UT: GRIB download, check the routing
Noon: noon position and the day’s run
Daily: water, fuel and battery state

options: A second GRIB download each midnight
An hourly sounding of the water tanks
A weekly check of the chart datum
A compass check by the Sun’s amplitude or azimuth
questions.why: On an ocean passage the compass is checked daily (sunrise or sunset amplitude, or an azimuth) and the error logged.

questions.q: At the noon position you update the ETA from the last three days’ runs. When do you expect to arrive?

figure.title: Noon, day 12
lines: Noon 2 Dec: 1 310 M to Rodney Bay

questions.why: Average (148 + 139 + 151) ÷ 3 = 146 M a day; 1 310 ÷ 146 = 8.97 days ≈ 8 d 23 h 20 min after noon on 2 Dec.

questions.q: You are reviewing the medical kit for the crossing. What do you add?

figure.title: Medical kit
lines: On board: a coastal first-aid kit
Crossing: 18 days, 4–6 days from a doctor

options: More plasters and bandages: the same kit doubled
Prescription drugs and a medical guide, agreed with a doctor
A defibrillator in place of extra medicines
Nothing: radio advice replaces a bigger kit
questions.why: Days from help, you must treat, not just patch: antibiotics, strong painkillers, wound closure — chosen with a doctor, with a guide.

questions.q: One of your crew is ill, as on the card. What do you do first?

figure.title: Day 9: medical
lines: Crew: severe pain, lower right abdomen
Sat phone and HF on board

options: Head for the nearest port and tell nobody yet
Give antibiotics and painkillers, then wait 24 h
Call the MRCC for radio medical advice from a doctor
Call PAN-PAN on VHF channel 16 for any ship
questions.why: Mid-ocean the MRCC connects you to a telemedical doctor (TMAS) by sat phone or HF, and arranges help if evacuation is needed.

questions.q: This is Tom on the first day of the crossing. What do you do?

figure.title: Day 1
lines: Tom: vomiting for 6 hours, cold, quiet

options: Keep him on watch: it passes faster that way
Send him below to his bunk in the bow
Give him a big meal to settle his stomach
Off the rota; in the cockpit, clipped on, sipping fluids
questions.why: Seasick crew are a MOB and dehydration risk: off watch, warm, clipped on in the cockpit (or aft bunk), small sips, watch their fluids.

questions.q: You are choosing the liferaft for an Atlantic crossing. Which do you take?

figure.title: Liferaft options
lines: B: ISO 9650-1 Group A, >24 h pack
C: no raft; the dinghy and a grab bag

options: A, with a bigger grab bag
questions.why: Rescue may take days far offshore: an offshore raft with the >24 h (SOLAS-style) pack — water, food, flares, a sea anchor.

questions.q: You bought this boat in the summer and are preparing her for the crossing. What do you do about the EPIRB?

figure.title: EPIRB check
lines: EPIRB: registered to the previous owner, UK
Today: Nov 2026; boat now on the Malta flag

options: Register it for Malta; the old battery still works
Recode and register it for Malta, and renew the battery
Nothing: any 406 MHz beacon alerts the MRCC
Renew the battery; registration doesn’t matter
questions.why: The MRCC uses the registration to call your contacts and know the boat; an expired battery may not last the 48 h a rescue needs.

questions.q: You are equipping the lifejackets of your crew of four for an ocean crossing. Which device on each lifejacket gets your own boat back to a person overboard at night fastest?
options: A personal strobe light on its own
An AIS MOB beacon, seen on your own plotter
A 406 MHz PLB, alerting the MRCC
questions.why: Mid-ocean the rescue is your own boat: an AIS MOB beacon alarms and shows the casualty on your plotter; a PLB alerts an MRCC days away.

questions.q: At 0200 in 20 kn of trade wind a halyard fouls at the masthead and you must go forward. What do you do?
options: Clip on once you reach the mast
Clip to the guardrail as you go forward
Go quickly unclipped: it takes a minute
Wake a second crew and clip on before leaving the hatch
questions.why: Far from help you cannot count on recovery: the jackstay from the companionway, a second person awake, a lifejacket and a light.

questions.q: This happens on your night watch in the trades. What are your first actions?

figure.title: Man overboard!
lines: Crew of 4; one overboard, with a light

options: MOB button, danbuoy and light, a pointer, then the kite down
MAYDAY first, then turn when the MRCC replies
Keep sailing while you plan a search pattern
Gybe at once under the kite, back to him
questions.why: At 8 kn you lose 250 m a minute: mark the spot, give him a buoy, keep eyes on him, then drop the spinnaker and return under power.

questions.q: This is the situation aboard. What do you do?

figure.title: Day 12: leak
lines: Leak at a seacock; water rising slowly
Electric and manual pumps keep up

options: Set off the EPIRB and step into the raft
Stay aboard, fight the leak, alert the MRCC; the raft only if she sinks
Wait for the leak to ease, and alert no one
Abandon now, while it is calm and daylight
questions.why: The boat is the best liferaft: step up into the raft only when she is going down. Tell the MRCC early (PAN-PAN) and keep pumping.

questions.q: This is your coastal grab bag. What do you add for an ocean crossing, with rescue possibly days away?

figure.title: Grab bag (coastal)
lines: Passports, phone in a dry bag

options: Fishing gear and a book for the wait
More flares and a second handheld VHF
A PLB, a sat phone, water and a hand watermaker
A bigger first-aid kit and more torches
questions.why: Days in a raft mid-ocean: water first (a hand watermaker), a way to alert (PLB/EPIRB) and to talk to the MRCC (sat phone).

questions.q: You are approaching an atoll in the Tuamotus. What speed do you make good from now?

figure.title: Landfall timing
lines: Plan: in the pass at 0800, sun high
No lights; charts from old surveys

options: About 4.0 kn: at the pass at 0400
About 2.0 kn: the pass at 1600 tomorrow
About 6.0 kn: in the pass by midnight
About 3.0 kn: reef down, or heave to for part of the night
questions.why: 1600 to 0800 is 16 h: 48 M ÷ 16 h = 3.0 kn. At 7 kn you’d be at an unlit reef pass at about 2250.

questions.q: You are making a night landfall after 19 days at sea. At about what range do you expect to raise this light?
questions.why: Geographical range 2.08 × (√52 + √2.5) = 2.08 × 8.79 ≈ 18 M: the curve of the Earth hides it before its 26 M nominal range.

questions.q: You are sailing between low atolls at night. How do you navigate this stretch?
options: Steer the plotter’s waypoint through the gap
Keep 10 M off, radar and DR, the gap in daylight
Close to 1 M to see the reef in the moonlight
Trust the plotter: GPS is good to 5 m
questions.why: GPS is precise but the old chart may be offset by a mile, and the current is unknown: keep a wide margin and pass in daylight.

questions.q: You anchor in Atuona after the Pacific crossing. What do you do first?

figure.title: Arrival
lines: Arrived: Hiva Oa, Marquesas, after 24 days

options: Courtesy flag only: the Q flag is history
Everyone ashore first; clear in tomorrow
Q flag up; nobody ashore but the skipper, to clear in
Anchor in a quiet bay first, clear in later
questions.why: Arriving from abroad: straight to a port of entry, the yellow Q flag flying, and nobody ashore until cleared, except to clear in.

questions.q: You are preparing the paperwork for clearing in. Which document do officials expect that you should have brought from Mindelo?
options: A fishing licence for the crossing
Your Yachtmaster logbook of miles sailed
The outward clearance from your last port
questions.why: Customs and immigration want proof you left your last port legally: the outward clearance (zarpe), with the crew list.

questions.q: You are two days out from Opua with this food aboard. What do you plan for it?

figure.title: Biosecurity
lines: Aboard: fresh fruit, eggs, honey, salami

options: Eat what you can and declare the rest on arrival
Throw it all overboard in the harbour
Hide it in the bilge: small amounts are fine
Nothing: food from the Pacific is exempt
questions.why: Quarantine rules come with clearing in: declare all food; biosecurity removes what is banned. Hiding it brings heavy fines.

questions.q: This is your situation mid-ocean. What do you do?

figure.title: Gale, mid-ocean
lines: Gale from astern: 40 kn, breaking seas

options: Turn and beat into it to stop the surfing
Stream a drogue astern to slow her and hold her stern-to
Lie ahull: all sail down, helm lashed
Carry on as fast as she will go downwind
questions.why: With sea room to leeward, a drogue slows her to a safe speed and keeps the stern to the seas, stopping the broaches.

questions.q: This is your situation on day 6 of the crossing. What do you do?

figure.title: Day 6
lines: Sea room: 400 M in every direction

options: Motor head to wind all night
Run back 100 M the way you came
Heave to, rest the crew, keep a watch
questions.why: With sea room all round, heaving to stops the slamming and lets the crew sleep; the lookout goes on.

questions.q: You are approaching your landfall after three weeks, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: Landfall and a gale
lines: Dusk; 50 M east of the island, E 20 kn
Forecast: 40 kn squally gale within 12 h
Harbour on the west side; night entry

options: Close the coast for radar fixes on the way in
Push on to arrive before the gale, at night
Anchor off the east coast and wait it out
Stay at sea with sea room: reef, heave to, land in daylight
questions.why: The island is a lee shore in an E gale: the open ocean is safety. Keep your offing, ride it out, and enter by day.

questions.q: An owner offers you command of his 28 m sailing yacht for an Atlantic crossing. What does your Yachtmaster Ocean let you do?
options: Decline: it covers yachts up to 24 m
Take it: the limit is 30 m on any ocean
Take it: the certificate has no size limit
Decline: it covers coastal waters only
questions.why: Yachtmaster Ocean: command of yachts up to 24 m on any ocean. A 28 m yacht needs a different, larger-vessel qualification.

questions.q: You are the skipper. The owner insists you leave today, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: Departure day
lines: Owner aboard; his flight home is booked
Forecast: 45 kn gale on the route for 36 h

options: Leave, and heave to if the gale hits
Delay: the safety of crew and boat is your call
Leave: the owner decides, he pays
Put it to a crew vote and follow it
questions.why: The skipper carries responsibility for the boat and everyone aboard; a schedule never outranks a forecast gale.

questions.q: You leave Cape Town for Salvador, Brazil, in January, and the South Atlantic high sits across the direct route. Which route do you plan?

figure.note: St Helena high; you at Cape Town

options: North along the African coast, then west near the equator
SW into the westerlies first, then north
NW up the high’s east side via St Helena, then west
The great circle direct, across the high’s centre
questions.why: In the south a high turns anticlockwise: S–SE winds on its east side carry you north, the SE trades on its north side west.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You are crossing the southern Indian Ocean, and its cyclone season runs from November to April. How long can you stay in Mauritius?

figure.title: Indian Ocean plan
lines: Plan 140 M a day; be in by 1 November
Keep 7 days in hand for weather windows

questions.why: Mauritius ≈ 2 Oct (2 350 ÷ 140 = 16.8 d). Leave by 1 Nov − 10.7 d − 7 d ≈ 14 Oct: a stay of about 12 days.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You are in Antigua after a winter in the Caribbean and are sailing the boat home to Europe. When do you leave?

figure.title: Going home
lines: N Atlantic hurricane season from 1 June

options: Early May, to be clear of the tropics by June
September, with the trades behind you
Mid-July, in the most settled weather
questions.why: Leave the Caribbean in May: north of the hurricane belt before 1 June, with the gales at 40°N easing for the leg to the Azores.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You are bound from the Galápagos to the Marquesas in March. With these pilot-chart figures, which way do you head first?
options: North-west first, into the ITCZ squalls
SW to about 5°S, then west in the SE trades
The rhumb line: the trades are the same everywhere
Due west along the equator, then SW at the end
questions.why: Near the equator the winds are light and patchy; a few degrees south the SE trades and the west-going current are steady.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You are choosing between two routes from Lanzarote to Antigua with these figures. Which is faster, and by how much?

figure.title: Two routes
lines: B: south to 20°N, then west: 2 850 M

questions.why: A: 2 650 ÷ 4.8 = 552 h = 23.0 days. B: 2 850 ÷ 6.3 = 452 h = 18.8 days. The longer route in the trades wins by 4 days.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You are in Falmouth in July, bound for the ARC start in Las Palmas. When do you cross Biscay?

figure.title: Getting to the start
lines: Biscay: gales more frequent from late Sept

options: Early November, straight to Las Palmas
Mid-November, with the other ARC boats
Early October, after the summer calms
By early September, then down the Iberian coast
questions.why: Cross Biscay in settled late summer before the autumn gales begin, then cruise Spain and Portugal south to the Canaries.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

questions.q: You are planning the cooking gas for the crossing from these figures. How many full cylinders do you carry, at the least?

figure.title: Cooking gas
lines: Shakedown week: 0.35 kg of gas a day

questions.why: 0.35 kg × 22 days × 1.5 = 11.6 kg ÷ 4.5 kg = 2.6: three full cylinders, stowed in the gas locker.

questions.q: You are adding the solar panels to your energy budget for the trade-wind crossing. What daily charge do you plan from them?

figure.title: Solar charging
lines: Trade-wind sun: about 5 peak hours a day

questions.why: 300 W × 5 h = 1 500 Wh ÷ 12 V = 125 Ah, less 25 % losses = about 94 Ah a day.

questions.q: You are working out how far you can motor in calms on the crossing, as on the card. What range do you plan?

figure.title: Fuel plan
lines: Charging: 1.5 h a day at 1.2 L/h, 20 days

questions.q: Your boat has wheel steering, and you are preparing her for an ocean crossing. Which steering check do you do with the crew in harbour?
options: Turn the wheel from lock to lock once
Grease the wheel brake and the pedestal
Check the autopilot shows the heading
Fit the emergency tiller and steer with it
questions.why: A broken cable or quadrant mid-ocean means steering by the emergency tiller: fit it and use it before you need it, and know where it is.

questions.q: This is what you find on your morning deck check. What do you do?

figure.title: Morning deck check
lines: Genoa sheet half worn through at the pole
Same chafe point since the start

options: End-for-end it, pad the pole end, ease it a little daily
Sheet it in hard so it stops moving
Roll the genoa away and sail on under main
Tape it over and leave it until the Caribbean
questions.why: Weeks on one tack wear through anything: move the chafe point every day (“freshen the nip”), pad it, and check every morning.

questions.q: You are checking the engine spares before the crossing, as on the card. What do you add?

figure.title: Engine spares
lines: Engine: 1.5 h a day for charging, 20 days
Spares box: oil, one fuel filter, gaskets

options: A second gasket set and more oil
Fuel filters, an impeller and an alternator belt
A spare propeller and a shaft seal
Nothing: 30 hours of running needs no spares
questions.why: Your charging depends on the engine: carry what fails at sea — fuel filters (dirty diesel), raw-water impellers and belts.

questions.q: You run this watch system on a crossing with a crew of six. Which watches does A stand from 1900 on day 2?

figure.title: Watch bill
lines: Swedish system, two watches A and B

questions.why: Five watches a day, taken in turn by two teams: A stands 1st, 3rd, 5th on day 1, then 2nd and 4th — so the times swap daily.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: Your crew of six will stand in two watches of three for four weeks. You want short watches at night and watch times that change from day to day. Which system do you choose?
options: 3 on, 3 off: eight watches of 3 h a day
6 on, 6 off: four watches of 6 h a day
4 on, 4 off: six watches of 4 h a day
Swedish: five a day, 4 h at night and 6 h by day
questions.why: With two teams the times rotate only if the day has an odd number of watches; the Swedish five do, with short night ones.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: You are taking three crew you met on a crewing website across the Atlantic. What do you do before you commit to the passage with them?
options: A shakedown of two or three days offshore, with night watches
An afternoon sail in the bay to see them handle the boat
Nothing: their sailing certificates say what they can do
An interview and their references; the sea will do the rest
questions.why: Only a few days and nights at sea show seasickness, skill and character — while you can still change crew or fix the boat.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: This is what your 48-hour shakedown sail shows. Whom do you leave ashore for the crossing?

figure.title: Shakedown, 48 h offshore
lines: Ana: seasick day 1, on watch again day 2
Carl: 2 crossings; unclipped twice at night

options: No one: all three will settle in
Carl: he ignores the standing orders
Ana: her seasickness rules her out
Ben: he has no ocean miles
questions.why: Seasickness passes and keenness learns; a crew who won’t follow the clip-on rule is a risk to himself and to everyone who goes back for him.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: You write the night orders for the rest of the crossing after this. Which order prevents it happening again?

figure.title: Night watch, 0200
lines: 0200: squall line astern on the radar
Watch: “the last ones were only 25 kn”

options: Two on watch after midnight, kite or not
Hand-steer whenever the spinnaker is up
No spinnaker after dark; call me for any squall
Radar off at night to save the batteries
questions.why: Trade-wind squalls come at night and can double the wind: a night sail plan you can hold in one, and the skipper called early.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: You are handing over the watch at 0300 and have said this. What else does the new watch need from you?

figure.title: Watch handover, 0300
lines: One reef in, genoa poled out
Ship astern on AIS, overtaking, CPA 2.5 M

options: The day’s run so far and the ETA
The engine hours since the service
The water left in the tanks
The barometer trend and any squalls you have seen
questions.why: A handover gives what the next watch must act on: course and sails, traffic, and what the weather is doing — pressure and squalls.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

questions.q: A crew who gets seasick tells you they will take a tablet “if I start to feel ill” once you are out of Las Palmas. What do you tell them?
options: Take it before we leave, as the leaflet directs
Take it with a big meal after your first watch
Wait until you are sick, then take two
Skip it: the body adapts in the first hour
questions.why: Seasickness tablets prevent rather than cure: start them before departure, at the time the leaflet gives; once vomiting starts they stay down poorly.

questions.q: You are about to call for radio medical advice, as on the card. What do you have ready before you call?

figure.title: Day 11: injury
lines: Day 11: crew fell against a winch
Sat phone; MRCC will connect a doctor

options: The insurance policy number and his passport
Position, pulse, breathing, temperature, history, the kit list
Only the position: the doctor asks the rest later
Nothing: call first, then examine him
questions.why: The doctor can only work from what you report: vital signs, what happened, medicines given or allergies, and what your kit holds.

questions.q: Your crew have been saving water, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: Day 10: dehydration?
lines: Day 10, 28 °C; crew rationing 2 L a day
Water aboard: 260 L; 9 days to go; crew 4

options: Keep the ration: the water has to last
Raise the ration to 3–4 L, with rehydration salts
Let them rinse their faces in sea water
questions.why: These are signs of dehydration. 260 L ÷ (4 × 9) ≈ 7 L a person a day: there is water to drink 3–4 L in the tropics.

questions.q: You are at the market in Las Palmas, buying fresh food for a 3-week crossing with no room in the fridge. Which basket lasts into the third week?

figure.title: Market, Las Palmas
lines: B: cabbage, onions, potatoes, unwashed eggs

questions.why: Hard vegetables, onions, potatoes and unwashed, unrefrigerated eggs keep for weeks; soft and ripe food lasts days.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

questions.q: You are stowing the fresh food for the crossing, as on the card. How do you stow it?

figure.title: Fresh food aboard
lines: No fridge space; 3 weeks to go

options: Dry and airy, wrapped singly, checked daily
Sealed in plastic bags in the cool bilge
All together in one deep locker
Washed and stowed damp in a hanging net
questions.why: Air and dryness keep it; one rotten fruit spoils its neighbours. A whole stem of bananas ripens at once — buy hands at different stages.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

questions.q: One of your water tanks is contaminated, as on the card. What daily ration do you set per person?

figure.title: Day 8: water
lines: Day 8 of 20 expected: 12 days to go
Port tank (180 L) tastes of diesel: shut off
Clean: starboard tank 125 L + cans 25 L

questions.why: Clean water 125 + 25 = 150 L, less 20 % = 120 L ÷ (4 × 12) = 2.5 L. This is why the water is split between tanks and cans.
questions.ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

questions.q: This is your situation, with 10 days still to go. How do you get the weather from now on?

figure.title: Day 9: no sat phone
lines: Day 9, mid-Atlantic: the sat phone is dead
SSB receiver and a laptop with a fax app
NAVTEX receiver; VHF; 1 100 M to land

options: Ask passing ships on VHF once a day
NAVTEX: it carries the high-seas forecast here
HF weatherfax charts and high-seas forecasts on the SSB
The old GRIB: it runs out to 16 days
questions.why: The SSB receiver needs no airtime: surface analyses and forecasts by HF fax, the high-seas bulletin by voice — with your barometer log.

questions.q: You want the official high-seas forecasts and navigational warnings on the whole route, as on the card. What do you fit?

figure.title: Weather backup
lines: Sat phone: GRIB by email (can fail)
NAVTEX on board: coastal range only
Route: 2 800 M, far from any coast

options: A second NAVTEX receiver, as a spare
An AIS receiver with a chart display
questions.why: SafetyNET broadcasts the high-seas forecasts and warnings by satellite to EGC receivers ocean-wide; NAVTEX reaches only a few hundred miles.

questions.q: You are mid-Atlantic, westbound, and keep the ship’s clocks to the zone, as on the card. At what ship’s time do you send the report?
questions.why: Zone +4: UT = zone time + 4 h, so zone time = 1800 − 4 = 1400. Keep reports in UT so the shore never has to guess.

questions.q: It is 0700 UT on day 12, and you are all well, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: Day 12: silence
lines: Day 12: the sat phone dead since day 10
Shore plan: no report for 48 h → call MRCC
HF net at 0800 UT; a boat on it has email

options: Set off the EPIRB briefly so they get your position
Ask a boat on the HF net to email home that all is well
Nothing: the MRCC can see you are fine on AIS
Turn for the nearest port to phone home
questions.why: The 48-h trigger falls at 1800 UT today: relay a short report before then, or a needless search starts. Never use the EPIRB as a message.

questions.q: A crew member suggests this mid-ocean. What do you do?

figure.title: AIS mid-ocean
lines: Crew: “Switch the AIS to silent, save power”
Shipping: 2–3 ships a day on the route

options: Switch it off and keep a radar watch
Silent mode: receiving them is all you need
Keep it transmitting: ships and satellites see you
Transmit at night only, silent by day
questions.why: 0.4 A × 24 h ≈ 10 Ah, a small part of the budget: ships see you at night, and the satellite AIS track helps a search if needed.

questions.q: You are about to send this daily report to your shore contact. What must you add?

figure.title: Daily report
lines: “flying fish for breakfast. Love to all.”

options: The menu and the fish you have caught
The crew’s moods and the watch rota
The engine hours and the fuel used
Position, course, speed and the next report time
questions.why: A report must let the shore and the MRCC find you and know when to worry: UT, position, course and speed, conditions, next report.

questions.q: You are writing the navigation routine for an ocean crossing with a working GPS and plotter. How often do you check the steering compass?
options: Daily at sunrise or sunset, and after a big change of heading
Weekly at noon, from the Sun’s meridian altitude
Once before leaving: deviation doesn’t change at sea
Only if the GPS fails, to find the error then
questions.why: Log the compass error daily (amplitude or azimuth) on the heading you steer: if the GPS fails you need it for steering and DR.

questions.q: You are checking the navigation pack for the crossing, as on the card. What do you add for the landfall?
options: A second ocean chart, in case one gets wet
A large-scale paper chart and a pilot book for the approach
A star chart for night arrivals
More plotting sheets for the last 100 M
questions.why: The ocean chart can’t show a harbour: if the plotter fails at landfall you need the approach and harbour on paper, with the lights.

questions.q: At the noon position you check whether the crew will make their flights. What daily run must you average from now?

figure.title: Noon, 18 December
lines: Crew flights: must arrive by noon 30 Dec

questions.why: Noon 18 Dec to noon 30 Dec is 12 days: 1 640 ÷ 12 ≈ 137 M a day, or 5.7 kn.

questions.q: You are writing the day’s run in the log, as on the card. What average speed do you enter?

figure.title: Day’s run
lines: Westbound; clocks put back 1 h at midnight
Noon yesterday to noon today (ship’s time)

questions.why: Putting the clocks back makes this noon-to-noon day 25 hours long: 150 M ÷ 25 h = 6.0 kn.

questions.q: You want to stop the boat and let everyone sleep, lying bow to the seas, as on the card. What do you stream, and from where?

figure.title: Gale: stopping
lines: 45 kn, breaking seas; crew of 3 exhausted
Sea room: 600 M in every direction
Aboard: series drogue, parachute sea anchor

options: The parachute sea anchor, from the bow
The series drogue astern, and keep running
The parachute sea anchor, from the stern
The series drogue, from the bow
questions.why: A sea anchor from the bow holds her head to the seas almost stopped; a drogue astern only slows her while she runs on.

questions.q: You are among the atolls when this gale arrives. How do you ride it out?

figure.title: Gale near the reefs
lines: Gale from the north, about 30 h to come
Drift on the sea anchor: 0.4 kn

options: Heave to and keep a good watch
Lie to the sea anchor from the bow
Run off before it with the drogue
questions.why: Hove to: 1.8 kn × 30 h = 54 M — on the reef after 20 h. On the sea anchor: 0.4 × 30 = 12 M, well short of it.

questions.q: You are back alongside your man overboard, as on the card. How do you get him aboard?

figure.title: Recovery
lines: Freeboard 1.2 m; two of you left aboard
His lifejacket has a lifting loop

options: Drop the ladder and tell him to climb
Both haul him over the guardrail by his arms
A halyard to his lifting loop, and winch him up
Tow him astern to calmer water first
questions.why: A cold, exhausted casualty can’t climb, and two people can’t lift 90 kg up 1.2 m: a halyard and a winch can — horizontally if you can.

questions.q: You must abandon the boat, as on the card. In what order do you do it?

figure.title: Abandon ship
lines: Grab bag and EPIRB by the hatch

options: Raft over, then make the painter fast as it inflates
Cut the painter at once to drift clear of the fire
Raft over, jump in, then the MAYDAY from the raft
MAYDAY, painter made fast, raft over, step in dry, cut free
questions.why: Alert first (MAYDAY, EPIRB), secure the painter before launching or the raft blows away, board from the deck, then cut.

questions.q: Your liferaft’s service record reads like this, a few weeks before the crossing. What do you do?
options: Have it serviced before you leave
Go: a sealed raft lasts ten years
Have it serviced in the Caribbean
Open it on deck to check it yourself
questions.why: Overdue by a year: the gas, pack and seals are no longer certified. The raft you may live in for days is serviced before departure.

questions.q: You are planning the landfall at an atoll, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: Landfall timing
lines: Noon: 214 M to the reef pass
Best speed in this wind: 6.0 kn
Pass: daylight only; diesel for 8 h

options: Motor-sail at 7 kn to be in before sunset
Ease to about 5 kn, at the pass soon after dawn
Keep 6 kn and enter at about 2340 by GPS
Heave to for 24 h now, then sail in at 6 kn
questions.why: At 6 kn: 214 ÷ 6 = 36 h, the pass at 2340 tomorrow. Sunset needs 7.1 kn for 30 h; 0630 the day after needs 214 ÷ 42.5 h ≈ 5 kn.

questions.q: Your GPS has failed and your position comes from sun sights, good to about 8 M. You are closing this low, featureless coast. Where do you aim?
options: Point B, 15 M up-current of the harbour
Point C, 15 M down-current of the harbour
questions.why: Aim off deliberately: at landfall you know the harbour is south, and you run down to it with the current, not search both ways.

questions.q: You are planning a landfall in a remote island group, as on the card. How do you plan it?

figure.title: Remote landfall
lines: are often unlit or off station”

options: Enter on the light: it is on the chart
Steer for the light’s charted position on the plotter
Close to 3 M of the coast and look for it
As if unlit: stand off and close the coast by day
questions.why: In remote groups lights fail and go unrepaired: plan the landfall without them, keep offshore in the dark and close the land in daylight.

questions.q: You email your arrival notice to Tongan customs before leaving Niue, as on the card. What ETA do you give?

figure.title: Niue → Tonga
lines: Customs want the ETA in Tonga time

questions.why: Leave 9 June 1900 UT; + 50 h = 11 June 2100 UT; Tonga (+13) = 12 June 1000. Same clock time, but a day later across the date line.

questions.q: You are sailing to Australia, as on the card. When do you send the advance notice of arrival?

figure.title: Arrival notice
lines: Border Force: notice ≥ 96 h before arrival

options: Halfway across, by sat phone email
On arrival, from the quarantine dock
questions.why: 96 hours is four days — about the whole passage: the notice goes in before departure, or you arrive unannounced and face penalties.

questions.q: You have cleared in, as on the card. What do you do before Jo leaves?

figure.title: Crew change
lines: Cleared in at Bridgetown: 5 crew on the list
Immigration: crew stay on the boat’s list
The rest sail on to Grenada next week

options: Nothing: once cleared, crew come and go
Give Jo the boat’s papers for the airport
Sign Jo off the crew list with immigration
Let Jo go and fix the list when you clear out
questions.why: The skipper answers for everyone on the crew list: sign a leaving crew off with immigration, or you may have to explain a missing person.

questions.q: Customs and immigration have cleared you in at Horta, in the Azores. What do you do with the flags?
options: Leave the Q flag up until you leave the country
Courtesy flag at the port spreader, Q flag above it
Your own ensign at the starboard spreader
Q flag down; Portuguese courtesy flag at the starboard spreader
questions.why: The Q flag says you are not yet cleared; once cleared it comes down and the host country’s courtesy flag goes up to starboard.

questions.q: Your new storm trysail and storm jib have never been set. When do you try them?
options: In harbour or a fresh breeze before you leave
Never: a deep-reefed main does the job
Halfway across, on a calm day
The first time a gale comes
questions.why: In a gale is no time to find the track won’t take the slides or the sheets don’t lead: rig and set them before departure.

questions.q: You are preparing for the gale, as on the card. What else do you do now?

figure.title: Gale in 12 h
lines: Done: two reefs, storm jib hanked on

options: Drop all sail now and lie ahull
Lash all below, food in flasks, crew rested
Motor at full speed to outrun the gale
Take out the washboards for ventilation
questions.why: Before a gale: everything heavy secured below, hot food and drink ready, the crew fed and asleep in turn — tired crew make the mistakes.

questions.q: The MRCC asks if you can help, as on the card. What do you do?

figure.title: Call from the MRCC
lines: Rally day 8; you lie 3rd in your class
MRCC: dismasted yacht 55 M upwind, injured
Your crew of 5: rested, boat sound

options: Relay the call and hold your course
Decline: a racing yacht may carry on
Go: you must assist if you can do so safely
Decline: the ship will be there in 20 hours
questions.why: A skipper must go to people in distress when able to without serious danger to their own boat; the race and the place come second.

questions.q: This is your situation after the evacuation. How do you sail on?

figure.title: After the evacuation
lines: Two crew taken off by a ship after injury
Left aboard: you and one crew

options: Turn back 900 M upwind to the start
Both sleep at night with the AIS alarm on
Full sail day and night to finish fast
Short watches, less sail at night, AIS and radar alarms set
questions.why: Two can sail on with care: shorter watches so neither is worn out, a sail plan one person can handle, alarms backing up the lookout.
